## 1. Title of the Work

# When Crises Converge: Why the Greater Horn of Africa Needs a New Framework for Humanitarian Survival

## 2. Creative Work

Humanitarian disasters are frequently understood as separate emergencies requiring separate solutions. Drought is treated as an environmental problem, epidemics as public health emergencies, armed conflicts as political crises, and rising food prices as economic disturbances. This division allows governments and international organizations to assign responsibility, mobilize specialized resources, and develop targeted interventions. Yet it becomes dangerously inadequate when these pressures occur simultaneously and reinforce one another. In the Greater Horn of Africa, the convergence of climate instability, prolonged warfare, disease threats, economic disruption, and declining humanitarian assistance demonstrates the limitations of responding to interconnected disasters as though they were independent events. The region's growing vulnerability is not simply the consequence of unusually severe natural hazards. It reflects a deeper failure of political institutions and international systems to recognize how environmental, economic, and security pressures interact. Preventing widespread human suffering therefore requires a fundamental shift from fragmented emergency relief toward coordinated prevention, conflict accountability, resilient local institutions, and long-term humanitarian preparedness.

The most important feature of an interconnected humanitarian emergency is that its consequences cannot be understood by examining each contributing factor in isolation. A drought may reduce agricultural production and increase demand for food assistance. A conflict may interrupt transportation routes and prevent farmers from cultivating their land. An epidemic may overwhelm hospitals and disrupt local commerce. A sudden rise in fuel prices may make essential goods more expensive. Each development can cause substantial hardship independently. When they occur together, however, the damage can become much greater than the sum of their individual effects.

Consider a farming community already struggling with declining rainfall. Reduced harvests leave households with less food and fewer opportunities to earn income. If armed violence then forces families to abandon their farms, the community loses both its immediate food supply and its capacity for future production. Rising transportation costs make imported food increasingly expensive, while weakened health services leave malnourished children more vulnerable to disease. Displacement places additional pressure on neighboring communities, which may themselves face declining resources. A crisis initially associated with rainfall can consequently develop into a broader breakdown of livelihoods, public health, social stability, and food security.

This pattern illustrates why the concept of a polycrisis is particularly useful. The term describes a situation in which multiple crises interact through shared systems, producing outcomes that cannot be adequately explained by their separate causes. Its significance lies not in identifying a large number of problems, but in recognizing the relationships that cause those problems to intensify one another. Effective humanitarian policy must therefore focus on these relationships rather than simply increasing the number of isolated interventions.

Climate instability is an especially important source of vulnerability in the Greater Horn of Africa. Millions of people depend directly or indirectly upon rainfall for agriculture, livestock production, water access, and household income. When seasonal precipitation becomes unreliable, the consequences extend far beyond reduced crop yields. Grazing land deteriorates, livestock health declines, water collection becomes more difficult, and rural markets experience disruptions. Families that rely upon agricultural labor may lose employment precisely when the price of food begins to rise.

The prospect of strong El Niño conditions adds another layer of uncertainty. Changes in regional weather patterns can produce severe drought in some areas and destructive flooding in others. These apparently opposite hazards can have similarly devastating consequences. Drought gradually erodes productive resources and household savings, while floods can rapidly destroy homes, roads, crops, and essential infrastructure. Both can force people to migrate and increase their dependence upon external assistance.

A particularly dangerous feature of climate-related emergencies is their capacity to undermine recovery from previous disasters. Households rarely begin each agricultural season with unlimited reserves. Families may already have sold livestock, borrowed money, reduced food consumption, or withdrawn children from school to survive earlier shortages. When another climatic shock arrives before these resources have been restored, the ability to adapt becomes progressively weaker. What might once have been a manageable period of poor rainfall can become a life-threatening emergency because previous crises have exhausted the community's capacity to respond.

Yet climate change and weather variability do not automatically produce famine. Food insecurity becomes catastrophic when environmental pressures intersect with political violence, economic exclusion, and inadequate institutions. This distinction matters because it challenges the tendency to portray hunger as an unavoidable consequence of nature. Rainfall may influence how much food is produced, but political decisions determine whether people can reach markets, access assistance, move to safer locations, and receive protection during emergencies.

Armed conflict therefore occupies a central position in understanding the region's vulnerability. Prolonged violence in Sudan, South Sudan, Ethiopia, and Somalia has weakened public institutions, disrupted agricultural activity, damaged infrastructure, and displaced communities. Military insecurity restricts transportation and complicates humanitarian access. Farmers may abandon productive land because cultivation has become dangerous. Traders may avoid important routes, reducing the availability of essential goods in isolated markets.

Conflict also transforms ordinary economic pressures into threats to survival. A sudden increase in food prices is difficult for a household with stable employment and functioning markets. For a displaced family that has lost its income, possessions, and agricultural resources, the same increase may make adequate nutrition impossible. A shortage of medical supplies can strain a functioning health system, but in a conflict-affected region where clinics have been damaged and healthcare workers displaced, it can leave entire communities without essential treatment.

These consequences reveal that warfare does not merely accompany humanitarian crises. It actively shapes their severity and determines whether available resources can prevent suffering.

The international dimensions of economic disruption further complicate the situation. The Greater Horn of Africa is connected to global markets through food imports, fuel supplies, agricultural inputs, transportation systems, and financial networks. Conflicts beyond the region can therefore influence household survival even when they occur thousands of kilometers away.

Disruptions to energy markets and shipping routes may increase transportation costs, while shortages of fertilizer can reduce agricultural productivity in subsequent growing seasons. The combination is particularly damaging because it affects both the cost of producing food and the price at which food reaches consumers. Farmers may be unable to afford necessary inputs, leading to smaller harvests. At the same time, consumers face higher prices for domestic and imported products.

This creates a difficult economic contradiction for agricultural communities. Food becomes more expensive, but many rural households do not necessarily become wealthier. Families producing insufficient crops for their own needs may have to purchase food at elevated prices. Agricultural laborers may lose employment when farmers reduce cultivation, even as their living expenses increase. Economic disruptions thus concentrate hardship among those with the fewest resources to absorb it.

The global nature of these pressures also exposes the limitations of relying exclusively upon international food markets as a safeguard against regional shortages. When several food-producing areas experience climatic or economic disruption simultaneously, surplus production elsewhere may become less available or more expensive. Countries facing domestic shortages may encounter international markets that offer little meaningful relief. Strengthening local and regional agricultural resilience is therefore essential, but it must occur alongside efforts to maintain reliable trade and affordable agricultural inputs.

Public health emergencies introduce another dangerous interaction. Infectious disease outbreaks can spread more easily when communities are displaced, sanitation deteriorates, and healthcare services become inaccessible. A weakened hospital system may struggle to identify and contain an outbreak, especially when trained personnel, diagnostic supplies, and transportation networks are limited.

The consequences of epidemic risk also extend into food security and humanitarian operations. Fear of infection can restrict travel and economic activity. Quarantine measures, when necessary, may complicate the movement of goods and assistance. Healthcare workers may be redirected away from routine services, reducing access to maternal care, childhood vaccination, and treatment for other illnesses. Malnutrition can further increase vulnerability to disease, creating a destructive relationship between hunger and declining health.

These interactions demonstrate why early disease surveillance and functional public health institutions should be considered fundamental components of humanitarian preparedness. Waiting until an epidemic has spread widely before restoring monitoring systems is both ethically and economically shortsighted.

Unfortunately, the region faces these overlapping threats during a period of serious weakness in international humanitarian capacity. Reductions in foreign assistance have placed considerable pressure on organizations and public programs responsible for emergency relief, disease monitoring, food distribution, and essential services. Funding shortages may force agencies to reduce operations, dismiss experienced staff, close facilities, and withdraw from vulnerable communities.

The consequences cannot be reversed simply by restoring financial commitments after a disaster has intensified. Humanitarian capacity is not a reserve of money that can be activated instantaneously. It consists of trained professionals, trusted local relationships, functioning supply chains, transportation arrangements, monitoring systems, and institutional knowledge. Once these resources are dismantled, rebuilding them requires substantial time and sustained coordination.

This distinction reveals why abrupt funding reductions are particularly dangerous when severe crises are foreseeable. A humanitarian system already weakened by financial contraction may struggle to expand precisely when additional capacity becomes most necessary. Delayed intervention can allow preventable problems to develop into emergencies requiring far greater resources.

There is also a broader ethical contradiction in dismantling preventive assistance while recognizing that foreseeable hazards are accumulating. Governments and international donors frequently emphasize fiscal restraint and competing domestic priorities when reducing humanitarian commitments. Such concerns cannot be dismissed entirely. Public resources are limited, and aid programs should be evaluated for effectiveness and accountability. However, financial responsibility must include the consequences of withdrawing support.

If cuts to disease surveillance contribute to larger outbreaks, or the closure of food assistance programs accelerates malnutrition and displacement, the apparent savings may produce substantially greater humanitarian and economic costs. Preventive assistance should therefore be assessed not only according to immediate expenditure but also according to the suffering and future emergency spending it can avert.

Nevertheless, a renewed humanitarian strategy cannot depend exclusively on restoring the previous international aid model. External assistance remains essential, particularly during emergencies that exceed local resources. Yet systems dominated by distant donors and large international organizations may fail to recognize the knowledge, priorities, and capabilities of affected communities.

Local people are rarely passive recipients of humanitarian aid. Families share food, neighbors shelter displaced households, community organizations coordinate emergency assistance, and diaspora networks transfer resources to relatives and vulnerable populations. These forms of solidarity often begin operating before international agencies can establish a formal response.

Their effectiveness rests partly upon proximity and trust. Community organizations understand local languages, social relationships, transportation routes, and rapidly changing conditions. They may identify vulnerable households that centralized systems overlook. They can sometimes distribute resources through networks that remain functional despite broader institutional disruption.

Such advantages make local humanitarian initiatives indispensable, particularly when formal aid structures have weakened. However, recognizing their importance should not become an excuse for abandoning international responsibility.

Community solidarity cannot indefinitely compensate for destroyed hospitals, widespread food shortages, large-scale displacement, or sustained warfare. Mutual aid networks also face financial constraints, exhaustion, and unequal access to resources. Expecting vulnerable communities to absorb the consequences of international withdrawal would transform the language of local empowerment into a justification for neglect.

A more responsible approach would establish genuine partnerships between international donors, regional institutions, national governments, and community organizations. Funding should reach credible local responders through arrangements that respect their independence while supporting transparent financial management. Flexible grants can enable organizations to respond to changing conditions rather than forcing them to conform to narrowly predetermined activities.

Policies governing financial transfers also deserve attention. Diaspora remittances can provide essential support during emergencies, particularly where formal humanitarian operations have declined. Excessively restrictive banking procedures or poorly designed financial regulations may unintentionally obstruct these transfers. Improving access to secure and accountable financial channels can strengthen communities' capacity to respond without requiring entirely new humanitarian institutions.

Yet even the most effective local relief networks cannot fully protect civilians while armed violence continues to destroy livelihoods and obstruct assistance. Conflict prevention and accountability must therefore occupy a central position in any credible regional strategy.

This requires confronting the political choices that sustain humanitarian disasters. Armed groups and governments may restrict movement, interfere with food distribution, damage agricultural infrastructure, or deliberately deprive communities of essential resources. Where starvation is used as a method of warfare, the resulting suffering cannot be adequately explained as an unfortunate consequence of scarcity. It becomes a question of responsibility for actions that violate fundamental humanitarian principles.

International actors must consequently treat civilian access to food, water, medical services, and safe movement as matters of political accountability rather than optional elements of emergency relief. Diplomatic engagement, independent investigation, and appropriate legal mechanisms are necessary to address violations and discourage their recurrence.

External governments also bear responsibilities when their financial assistance, weapons transfers, or political support contribute to the continuation of violent conflict. Humanitarian assistance loses much of its preventive value when other policies simultaneously intensify the conditions producing displacement and hunger. A coherent international response must therefore examine the relationship between military support, diplomatic incentives, economic interests, and humanitarian consequences.

This does not mean that conflict resolution is straightforward. The region's wars involve complex political histories, competing interests, and deeply rooted grievances. Durable peace cannot be imposed through humanitarian declarations alone. Nevertheless, recognizing political complexity must not become a reason for accepting indefinite civilian suffering. Even when comprehensive peace agreements remain elusive, negotiated humanitarian access, protection of essential infrastructure, local ceasefires, and monitoring of violations can reduce immediate risks.

Reliable information is another indispensable requirement. Effective intervention depends upon understanding where food insecurity is worsening, which populations are being displaced, how disease risks are developing, and whether humanitarian assistance is reaching intended recipients. Monitoring systems allow governments and aid organizations to identify emerging threats before they escalate.

When these systems deteriorate, decision-makers become increasingly dependent upon incomplete reports, delayed assessments, and politically contested information. This uncertainty can result in misdirected resources, inadequate preparation, and delayed recognition of catastrophic conditions.

The problem becomes particularly serious in conflict zones, where access restrictions and deliberate misinformation may conceal the scale or causes of civilian suffering. Independent data collection can help distinguish between environmental shortages, market disruptions, and deliberate interference with food supplies. Such distinctions are essential because different causes require different forms of intervention and accountability.

Investing in credible monitoring should therefore be regarded as a form of humanitarian protection. Early warning has little value if the institutions receiving warnings lack the capacity or political willingness to act. Equally, emergency resources may be wasted when reliable information is unavailable. The effectiveness of humanitarian response depends upon maintaining the connection between evidence, decision-making, and timely intervention.

A possible objection to this comprehensive approach is that it demands more coordination and resources than governments and humanitarian organizations can realistically provide. The region's problems involve numerous countries, armed actors, international markets, public institutions, and environmental systems. Attempting to address all these dimensions simultaneously may appear administratively overwhelming.

Yet the alternative is not a simpler path to success. Fragmented responses may temporarily relieve individual symptoms while leaving the mechanisms generating repeated crises untouched. Food distributions may reduce immediate hunger, but their benefits can be undermined if conflict prevents agricultural recovery. Medical interventions may contain an outbreak, but future disease risks remain elevated if water systems and health infrastructure continue to deteriorate. Agricultural support may improve yields, but farmers may remain unable to cultivate land if insecurity forces them to flee.

An integrated strategy does not require every problem to be solved at once. It requires institutions to recognize how their actions influence interconnected risks and to prioritize interventions that reduce several vulnerabilities simultaneously.

Protecting transportation corridors, for example, can improve access to food markets, medical supplies, and humanitarian assistance. Strengthening local healthcare systems can enhance epidemic preparedness while improving routine treatment. Supporting water infrastructure can reduce disease risks, protect livelihoods, and limit displacement pressures. Conflict-sensitive agricultural assistance can help households recover productive capacity without intensifying competition over scarce resources.

Such interventions illustrate how coordination can improve efficiency rather than merely increase complexity. The objective is not to replace specialized expertise with an unrealistic universal program, but to ensure that specialized efforts reinforce one another.

The experience of the Greater Horn of Africa also raises a broader question about the meaning of international solidarity. Humanitarian emergencies are often portrayed as exceptional moments during which wealthier societies provide temporary assistance to less fortunate populations. This perspective obscures the structural relationships connecting regions through trade, climate impacts, financial policies, military involvement, and international political decisions.

Communities facing famine risk do not exist outside the global economy. Their vulnerabilities are shaped partly by conflicts, market disruptions, and policy choices that originate far beyond their borders. International responsibility should therefore be understood not merely as charitable generosity but as a recognition of shared consequences within an interconnected world.

At the same time, this recognition must avoid portraying African societies exclusively through the language of helplessness and catastrophe. The Greater Horn contains communities with extensive experience adapting to uncertainty, organizing mutual support, and sustaining livelihoods under difficult conditions. Their knowledge and initiative are essential resources for effective crisis prevention. A credible humanitarian framework must strengthen these capabilities rather than replace local decision-making with externally imposed priorities.

The fundamental challenge is to combine international responsibility with regional ownership and community agency. External actors can provide financial resources, technical support, diplomatic engagement, and mechanisms for accountability. National and regional institutions can coordinate public services, strengthen infrastructure, and develop cooperative approaches to shared risks. Local communities can contribute practical knowledge, trusted networks, and immediate response capabilities.

None of these levels can succeed sustainably in isolation.

Ultimately, the danger confronting the Greater Horn of Africa is not simply the prospect of another severe drought, another disease outbreak, or another period of economic instability. It is the possibility that multiple pressures will converge upon societies whose capacity to withstand further shocks has already been weakened by years of conflict and institutional disruption.

The moral urgency of this situation lies in the fact that much of the potential suffering is foreseeable. Climate indicators, food market disruptions, conflict patterns, and humanitarian capacity assessments can reveal mounting risks before their most devastating consequences occur. The existence of such knowledge creates an obligation to act before preventable deaths and displacement become widespread.

A world capable of anticipating complex humanitarian emergencies should not regard mass suffering as inevitable merely because the causes are interconnected. Complexity makes prevention more demanding, but it also makes coordination more necessary.

The future of humanitarian action must therefore be guided by a principle that extends beyond the Greater Horn of Africa: when crises reinforce one another, responses must be designed to reinforce resilience across the same interconnected systems. This means preserving preventive capacity, supporting local institutions, protecting civilian livelihoods, improving monitoring, and confronting the political decisions that sustain violent conflict.

The measure of international commitment should not be how dramatically the world responds after catastrophe becomes undeniable. It should be how effectively governments, institutions, and communities act when the warning signs are already visible.

Humanitarian success is not simply the ability to rescue people from the consequences of a collapsing system. It is the determination to prevent that collapse by recognizing that food security, public health, political stability, economic opportunity, and human dignity are inseparable foundations of collective survival.

1. Title of the Work

**The Multiplier of Ruin: Redefining Resilience in the Era of the Polycrisis**

2. Creative Work

Humanity has long been conditioned to conceptualize catastrophe in the singular. We mentally compartmentalize the world’s tragedies into neat, isolated categories: a sudden drought, a localized armed conflict, a volatile spike in market prices, or the sudden emergence of a virulent pathogen. This siloed view of disaster allows for a siloed response, where specialized agencies deploy targeted solutions to extinguish one fire at a time. However, this antiquated framework is collapsing under the weight of modern reality. In some of the globe’s most historically vulnerable regions, disaster is no longer a solitary event but an intricate, self-sustaining ecosystem. We have entered the era of the polycrisis—a devastating calculus where overlapping hazards do not merely add to one another, but multiply.

Consider the compounding alchemy of modern ruin. A climatic anomaly sweeping across an ocean does not merely wither crops; it forces desperate populations to migrate, straining the resources of neighboring regions and accelerating the spread of unpredictable epidemic variants. Simultaneously, a geopolitical conflict erupting thousands of miles away can choke off the global supply of essential agricultural inputs, meaning that even if the rains do eventually fall, the soil cannot yield enough to sustain the population. When these environmental and economic shocks collide with entrenched internal warfare, the result is an inescapable vortex of vulnerability. In this environment, a marginalized farmer is not just fighting the weather, but also hyper-inflation, border closures, and the looming specter of armed factions.

Compounding this multiplying threat is a profound structural abdication by the global north. For decades, vulnerable regions relied on a vast, albeit imperfect, scaffolding of international humanitarian aid to act as a backstop against mass mortality. Today, that scaffolding is being deliberately dismantled. Sweeping ideological shifts and aggressive budget cuts by major Western donors have not simply reduced available funds; they have gutted the very infrastructure—the personnel, the logistical networks, the monitoring systems—required to mount a coordinated response. The international community operates under the dangerous illusion that a sudden injection of emergency cash can magically revive a shattered system, ignoring the reality that once the infrastructure of aid is sold off or abandoned, it cannot be rebuilt overnight.

With the deliberate retreat of traditional global saviors, the architecture of survival must undergo a radical transformation. The burden of mitigation has fallen squarely onto the shoulders of local communities, forcing a shift from top-down dependency to grassroots resilience. In the absence of foreign aid workers, the true first responders are kin, neighbors, and decentralized mutual aid networks fueled by the lifelines of diaspora remittances. If the international community wishes to play a constructive role in this new reality, it must abandon its rigid, transactional models of charity and instead provide flexible, direct support that empowers these localized systems to function without friction.

Yet, no amount of mutual aid can overcome the darkest variable in this polycrisis: the intentional weaponization of human suffering. In the shadows of crippled monitoring systems and waning global attention, warring parties are increasingly exploiting environmental and economic chaos to utilize starvation as a calculated military tactic. Until the international community musters the political will to hold these actors—and their foreign enablers—accountable for engineering famine, all other interventions remain little more than temporary bandages.

The perfect storm is no longer a distant forecast; it has made landfall. To survive the polycrisis, we must stop viewing crises as isolated anomalies and recognize them as a devastating web of cause and effect. We must shift our faith from hollowed-out global institutions to the resilient networks of local communities, and demand uncompromising accountability for those who seek to turn a natural disaster into a man-made famine.

Border cooperation can become an instrument of diplomatic bargaining rather than a predictable mechanism of migration management. A government receiving financial or political benefits for restricting movement may recognize that temporarily relaxing enforcement can produce immediate pressure on European leaders.

If participating countries enjoy the advantages of integrated markets and shared mobility while refusing to cooperate over predictable challenges at external borders, the credibility of European integration is weakened. A union cannot consistently present freedom of movement as a collective achievement while treating the responsibilities necessary to sustain that freedom as exclusively national problems.

Repeated political confrontations reveal the limitations of an approach dominated by emergency meetings and short-term compromises. When migration becomes politically contentious, leaders often respond through temporary border checks, diplomatic accusations, or promises of stronger enforcement. Dramatic political language may create the impression that exceptional enforcement measures are necessary even when more careful analysis would reveal complex economic, legal, and diplomatic causes.

Fear-driven politics also encourages competition among governments seeking to demonstrate toughness. Instead of developing shared solutions, leaders may introduce unilateral restrictions designed to reassure domestic audiences. The danger is that migration governance becomes increasingly shaped by political performance rather than evidence of effectiveness.

Regularization can also serve important administrative and economic purposes. Individuals who already live and work within a country may remain vulnerable to exploitation when their legal status prevents them from asserting workplace rights or engaging fully with public institutions. Providing a regulated pathway to legal residence can improve labor protections, strengthen tax compliance, and reduce dependence upon informal employment arrangements.

This does not imply that every regularization program will achieve the same results or that governments should disregard eligibility requirements. Rather, it demonstrates why migration policy must be evaluated through evidence rather than assumptions shaped by political fear.

The same principle applies to border enforcement. Governments should assess whether specific measures reduce dangerous journeys, disrupt exploitative trafficking networks, improve administrative efficiency, and protect legitimate asylum claims. A reduction in recorded arrivals at one location may not indicate overall success if movement simply shifts toward more hazardous routes.

The objective should be effective governance rather than the production of politically convenient statistics.

Another essential component of reform is the preservation of meaningful access to asylum procedures. Their circumstances may require urgent movement, and they may lack the documents or resources typically necessary for lawful entry.

Consequently, the right to seek protection cannot be reduced to the physical design of a border barrier. When governments rely upon technical border arrangements to prevent individuals from accessing asylum procedures, legal form risks displacing humanitarian purpose. The central question should remain whether a person faces circumstances requiring protection and whether the relevant procedures provide a fair opportunity to establish that claim.

This principle does not require granting asylum to everyone who requests it. It requires a process capable of distinguishing eligible claims from those that do not meet the relevant legal standards, without exposing applicants to arbitrary treatment or dangerous removal.

The legitimacy of immigration control is strengthened, rather than weakened, when decisions are transparent, reviewable, and consistent with established legal obligations.

Economic differences, demographic changes, political instability, family relationships, and labor demand will continue to influence human mobility. Such a framework would require greater cooperation among European member states. Countries experiencing disproportionate pressure at external borders should receive reliable financial and administrative support. Responsibility-sharing mechanisms should reflect both the practical capacities of participating states and the need for fair treatment of migrants and asylum seekers.

Reception systems should be sufficiently prepared to manage fluctuations in arrivals without becoming overwhelmed. Expanding administrative capacity, improving coordination, and maintaining clear procedures would help prevent temporary increases in migration from developing into broader political emergencies.

Legal labor mobility could also play a constructive role where economic needs and appropriate safeguards justify it. Transparent recruitment arrangements can reduce dependence upon dangerous irregular routes while helping employers address legitimate labor shortages. Such programs must include protections against exploitation and should be designed with attention to the interests of both destination and origin countries.

Most importantly, partnerships with neighboring societies should move beyond the narrow objective of preventing departure. Economic development assistance should support productive employment, education, infrastructure, and accountable public institutions. Programs should be evaluated according to improvements in people's lives rather than solely according to the number of individuals prevented from reaching Europe.

This requires acknowledging that development and migration have a complicated relationship. Rising incomes and educational opportunities do not always immediately reduce migration. In some circumstances, improved resources may initially increase people's ability to move. Development policy should therefore not be treated as a simple instrument for suppressing mobility.

Its deeper purpose should be to expand meaningful choices.

A society in which individuals can pursue education, secure employment, participate politically, and support their families offers stronger foundations for stability than one in which movement is constrained while underlying grievances remain unresolved. People may still choose to migrate, but they are less likely to experience migration as their only realistic possibility for improving their circumstances.

This understanding challenges a fundamental assumption underlying much contemporary border politics: that stability can be achieved by controlling where people go without considering the conditions under which they live.

In reality, migration connects domestic governance to international inequality. Decisions made in European capitals influence relationships with neighboring states, while political and economic developments beyond Europe's borders shape the pressures experienced within Europe. Treating these processes as unrelated encourages ineffective policy and recurring diplomatic confrontation.

The humanitarian dimension of migration makes this failure particularly consequential. Individuals undertaking dangerous journeys are not merely numerical indicators of border pressure. They are people making decisions under conditions of uncertainty, hope, fear, and limited opportunity. Their experiences differ, and their legal claims must be assessed individually, but their basic dignity should not depend upon the political convenience of their arrival.

Recognizing that dignity does not require abandoning immigration law. It requires ensuring that the pursuit of effective borders remains compatible with the protection of human life and the fair application of legal standards.

Ultimately, Europe's repeated migration confrontations reveal the limits of a political strategy that prioritizes containment over cooperation and deterrence over structural understanding. Physical barriers can influence movement, and international agreements can assist border administration. Neither can substitute for coherent European institutions, accountable diplomatic partnerships, and policies responsive to economic and political realities.

The deeper danger is that Europe may continue investing resources in measures that provide the appearance of control while reproducing the conditions of instability. Dependence upon neighboring governments creates diplomatic vulnerability. Fragmented responsibility encourages disputes among member states. Fear-driven politics undermines reasoned debate. Restrictions unaccompanied by adequate legal alternatives can increase the risks associated with migration without eliminating its causes.

A different approach is possible, but it requires political leaders to measure success through sustainable outcomes rather than immediate demonstrations of toughness.

European migration governance should be judged by whether it reduces preventable deaths, maintains legitimate border procedures, protects those entitled to asylum, supports constructive regional partnerships, and preserves cooperation among member states. These objectives are demanding, but they provide a more credible foundation for stability than recurring cycles of enforcement and emergency diplomacy.

The most important border Europe must confront is therefore not simply the physical boundary separating its territory from neighboring countries. It is the conceptual boundary between treating migration as an external threat to be contained and recognizing it as a complex political reality requiring shared responsibility.

Until European governments cross that boundary in their own thinking, additional fences, financial agreements, and deportation measures are unlikely to resolve the contradictions at the heart of their migration policies.

A durable system cannot be built solely upon the capacity to keep people out. It must also rest upon the capacity to govern fairly, cooperate consistently, address underlying inequalities, and preserve human dignity when political pressures are greatest.

## 1. Title of the Work

**The Gatekeeper's Bargain: How Europe Keeps Building Its Own Border Crises**

## 2. Creative Work

Imagine a wealthy household that lives beside a struggling neighborhood. Instead of investing in the streets around it, the household builds a taller wall and hires a guard from next door to keep people out. The guard is paid well, but he soon realizes that his employer is completely dependent on him. Whenever he wants a favor, a larger fee, or silence about how he treats his own neighbors, he only has to step away from the gate for an afternoon. The crowd surges in, the household panics, and the family members inside turn on one another over who left the door unlocked. Then they pay the guard more and add another layer of bricks.

That parable captures Europe's approach to migration along its southern frontier. Every few years, a sudden wave of arrivals at a border fence or on a stretch of coastline sets off emergency meetings, angry accusations among member states, and promises of tougher controls. Each episode is treated as an unpredictable shock, as if it came from nowhere. It did not. Europe's recurring migration emergencies are largely the product of its own choices. By outsourcing border control to neighboring governments, many of them authoritarian, and by pouring resources into fortifications while neglecting the inequality and misrule that drive people to leave, the European Union has built a system that guarantees future crises. Breaking the cycle means changing the bargain itself.

The first problem is dependence. For decades, the EU has offered money, trade benefits, and diplomatic favor to countries on its borders in exchange for stopping migrants before they reach European soil. On paper, this looks pragmatic. In practice, it hands those governments a powerful lever. A state that can open or close the flow of people at will can turn that ability into a bargaining chip in disputes that have nothing to do with migration, whether over contested territory, trade terms, or criticism of its human rights record. Europe has repeatedly seen border guards look the other way at politically convenient moments, letting thousands cross in a matter of hours. When that happens, the crisis is not a failure of the arrangement. It is the arrangement working exactly as its partner intends.

The second problem is that this money often strengthens the very conditions that push people out. Funds labeled as tackling the "root causes" of migration frequently end up equipping police forces, financing surveillance, or propping up leaders who suppress protests about unemployment and corruption. Young people in regions marked by joblessness and heavy-handed policing can look across a short stretch of water or a fence line at a standard of living many times higher than their own. When peaceful demands for change are met with batons, and when the only visible path to a decent life runs north, it should surprise no one that rumors of an open border spread quickly on social media and that people will risk drowning to test them. A policy that makes neighboring regimes more repressive while leaving their economies stagnant is not addressing the causes of migration. It is feeding them.

The third problem lies within Europe itself. The union has never settled on a fair way to share responsibility among its members. Countries on the frontier receive the most arrivals, while others refuse to accept any share. Every surge revives the same quarrels: calls to suspend free movement, threats to expel a member from the passport-free zone, the reintroduction of internal checks that make little practical sense. Recent reforms have focused mainly on faster deportations and narrower rights of appeal, measures designed to signal toughness to voters more than to create a working system. Leaders also reach for convenient explanations, blaming a neighbor's decision to grant legal status to long-settled undocumented residents. Yet past regularization programs in Europe and elsewhere have not been shown to trigger new waves of irregular migration. Blaming them diverts attention from the deeper structural failures.

Defenders of the current approach raise legitimate concerns. States have a right to control their borders, and voters across Europe have made clear that they want orderly, managed migration. Sudden mass crossings can overwhelm local services, and smugglers who spread false promises put lives at risk. Cooperation with neighboring countries, critics argue, is unavoidable given geography. All of this is true, but none of it justifies the current bargain. Order is exactly what Europe's strategy fails to produce. A system that lets a foreign government trigger chaos whenever it chooses is the opposite of control. Real security comes from reducing the pressures that make people desperate and from building rules that work predictably, not from betting everything on the goodwill of a gatekeeper.

A better approach would shift Europe's investment from walls to opportunity. Aid to neighboring states should be tied to measurable improvements in jobs, education, and accountable government, not to how many people border guards turn back. Europe should expand legal routes for work and study, so that those who seek a better life have an alternative to the sea and to smugglers. Within the union, member states must accept a binding, fair system for sharing responsibility for asylum seekers, so that each new arrival does not become a test of European unity. And asylum procedures should be fast but fair, protecting those who genuinely need refuge while returning others humanely and lawfully.

The wealthy household in the parable will never be safe as long as its security depends on a guard who profits from its fear, and as long as the neighborhood beyond its wall stays poor and repressed. Europe faces the same choice. It can keep paying for higher barriers and hoping the gatekeeper stays loyal, or it can invest in a neighborhood where fewer people feel they have no option but to run. The first path promises control and delivers chaos. The second is harder and slower, but it is the only one that leads anywhere.

---

The essay argues one side, just as the original does. Supporters of stricter border policy would disagree with parts of it. They argue that firm deterrence and cooperation with transit countries do reduce dangerous crossings, that aid tied to development has a mixed track record, and that legal routes and regularization should only expand once governments can show they control their borders.

Scientific progress has always depended upon humanity's ability to expand the boundaries of what can be understood, manipulated, and created. From the development of microscopes to the discovery of DNA's molecular structure, advances in biological knowledge have transformed medicine, agriculture, and our understanding of living systems. The central challenge is therefore not whether artificial intelligence should participate in biological research, but whether societies can establish effective systems of oversight before the capacity to engineer living systems becomes more accessible, autonomous, and potentially dangerous than the institutions responsible for governing it.

These possibilities offer compelling reasons to encourage responsible innovation. However, the same characteristics that make automated biological research valuable also complicate its governance.

The fundamental difficulty is that biological capabilities are not inherently beneficial or harmful. Their consequences depend upon the purposes for which they are used, the circumstances of their deployment, and the safeguards surrounding them. Methods that improve the design of useful biological molecules may also provide knowledge relevant to manipulating dangerous biological agents. Systems capable of accelerating legitimate experiments may similarly accelerate research that creates unacceptable safety or security risks.

This is the dual-use dilemma at the heart of modern biotechnology.

The problem is not entirely new. Scientific knowledge has long been applicable to both constructive and destructive purposes. Advances in chemistry, nuclear physics, and microbiology have repeatedly demonstrated that powerful discoveries can improve human welfare while creating opportunities for misuse.

What distinguishes AI-driven biology is the possibility that computational intelligence and physical automation will combine to reduce barriers across several stages of biological research simultaneously.

Previously, obtaining scientific information did not necessarily provide the practical ability to conduct sophisticated experiments. A person might encounter detailed descriptions of biological methods yet lack the training, laboratory infrastructure, or experience necessary to implement them. These barriers have historically limited the number of individuals capable of translating complex biological knowledge into functioning experimental systems.

Artificial intelligence may gradually weaken some of these constraints by helping users understand scientific literature, plan research, interpret experimental results, and troubleshoot technical difficulties. Automated laboratories may further reduce the need for direct manual involvement.

The convergence of these technologies raises a consequential question: what happens when scientific capabilities that once required extensive specialized training become increasingly available through digital interfaces?

There is no justification for assuming that every inexperienced user will immediately acquire the ability to conduct dangerous biological research. Laboratory work involves practical difficulties that computational assistance may not resolve. Biological systems are often unpredictable, experimental materials require specialized handling, and successful outcomes depend upon conditions that cannot always be controlled through software.

Nevertheless, the absence of complete automation today does not guarantee the persistence of existing barriers tomorrow.

Research into AI-assisted biological tasks has produced mixed findings, suggesting that the effects of these systems depend upon the particular activity being studied. In some controlled evaluations, AI assistance has improved the ability of individuals with limited experience to address complex technical problems. Other investigations have found more modest effects when participants must complete demanding physical laboratory procedures.

These differences are important because they discourage both exaggerated alarm and premature reassurance. Current evidence does not support the simplistic claim that artificial intelligence has already eliminated the expertise required for dangerous biological experimentation. Equally, it would be irresponsible to conclude that the remaining difficulties provide permanent protection.

As automated equipment becomes more capable and accessible, practical barriers may decline. The relevant security question is therefore not restricted to what individual AI models can accomplish today. It concerns how their capabilities may interact with emerging laboratory infrastructure over time.

This distinction reveals a central weakness in conventional technology governance. Regulatory systems often evaluate individual products or activities within relatively separate categories. Software is assessed as software, biological materials are regulated as physical substances, and laboratory facilities are governed through established safety requirements.

AI-driven experimental systems cross these boundaries.

A computational model may generate biological designs in one jurisdiction, transmit instructions to an automated facility in another, and receive experimental information through remote networks. Different organizations may control the model, the laboratory equipment, the biological materials, and the underlying datasets.

Under these circumstances, responsibility becomes distributed across an interconnected technical system. Rules designed for a single laboratory or a single software provider may fail to address the combined risks.

Effective oversight must therefore examine the entire pathway through which computational suggestions become physical biological activity.

This requires a shift from regulating individual components in isolation toward assessing the capabilities and consequences of integrated systems. A model that generates theoretical biological predictions presents a different risk profile from one that can autonomously direct experiments using physical materials. Similarly, a research platform limited to low-risk applications requires different safeguards from a system capable of supporting work with biological agents that present serious security concerns.

A proportionate regulatory framework should recognize these distinctions rather than imposing identical restrictions on every use of artificial intelligence in biology.

Risk-based governance offers a particularly promising approach. Under such a framework, access to sensitive capabilities would depend upon the nature of the research, the potential severity of misuse, the reliability of safety controls, and the qualifications or institutional responsibilities of users.

Low-risk educational or research applications could remain broadly accessible, supporting scientific learning and legitimate innovation. More sensitive capabilities could require additional verification, institutional authorization, monitoring, or independent review.

The purpose of such distinctions would not be to preserve scientific knowledge exclusively for established elites. It would be to ensure that access to powerful capabilities is accompanied by responsibilities appropriate to their potential consequences.

This is a crucial ethical consideration. Excessive restrictions could reinforce global inequalities by concentrating advanced biological technologies within wealthy corporations and research institutions. Scientists in lower-income countries may already face substantial barriers involving funding, equipment, and access to specialized facilities. A poorly designed security framework could intensify these disparities while doing little to prevent determined misuse.

Responsible governance must therefore balance openness with safeguards. Security measures should be evidence-based, transparent where possible, and narrowly tailored to the risks they address.

The distinction between legitimate scientific accessibility and unrestricted operational capability is especially important. Broad access to biological education and foundational research can coexist with stronger controls over systems capable of enabling particularly hazardous experiments. Supporting scientific participation does not require treating every technical function as equally appropriate for public availability.

Another essential element is the evaluation of artificial intelligence systems before they are deployed.

In many technological fields, safety testing concentrates on whether a system performs its intended function reliably. Biological AI requires a broader approach because technical success may itself create additional risks. A model that becomes more effective at solving complex biological problems may simultaneously become more useful to individuals pursuing harmful objectives.

Consequently, evaluation must examine not only accuracy, scientific usefulness, and operational reliability, but also the ways in which a system could contribute to dangerous activities.

Such assessments should be grounded in realistic conditions. Evaluating isolated model responses may not reveal how the system behaves when connected to external tools, laboratory automation, or iterative experimental feedback. A model's capabilities can change substantially when it receives opportunities to interact with physical processes and incorporate observations into subsequent decisions.

Testing must therefore address the performance of the combined system, including its safeguards against unauthorized actions and its capacity to detect concerning patterns of use.

Independent scrutiny is particularly important because commercial incentives may not always align with public security. Companies developing advanced artificial intelligence have strong reasons to demonstrate technological progress, attract investment, and release competitive products. These incentives can coexist with sincere commitments to safety, but voluntary commitments alone cannot guarantee consistent standards across an industry.

A company that invests heavily in protective measures may face competitive pressure from organizations imposing fewer restrictions. If the benefits of rapid deployment are privately captured while the consequences of serious misuse are borne by society, market competition may encourage insufficient investment in prevention.

This problem provides a compelling justification for public regulation.

Governments should establish clear expectations for evaluating high-risk biological capabilities, documenting safety decisions, reporting significant incidents, and maintaining appropriate controls over access. Independent authorities should possess sufficient technical expertise to assess whether protective measures correspond to actual risks.

However, regulation must be adaptive rather than rigid. Artificial intelligence and biotechnology are developing rapidly, and highly prescriptive rules may become obsolete as new systems emerge. A framework focused on capabilities, operational contexts, and measurable risks is more likely to remain useful than one tied exclusively to particular algorithms or commercial products.

The governance of biological information also requires careful attention.

Artificial intelligence systems acquire many of their abilities through training on large scientific datasets. Genomic sequences, protein structures, research publications, and experimental records contain information that can support valuable discoveries. Yet particular categories of biological data may also contribute to capabilities that raise security concerns.

This creates difficult questions about how information should be collected, shared, and used in model development.

An approach based upon indiscriminate secrecy would be both impractical and harmful. Open scientific communication enables independent verification, international collaboration, and advances in public health. Restricting broad categories of legitimate research could slow medical progress without necessarily preventing misuse.

Nevertheless, the existence of these benefits does not eliminate the need to examine how specific datasets contribute to dangerous capabilities. Researchers and policymakers should investigate whether certain combinations of information, computational tools, and automated experimental access create risks that justify additional controls.

Data governance should therefore focus on demonstrable hazards rather than treating biological knowledge itself as inherently threatening.

The relationship between biological AI and commercial DNA synthesis presents another important area for oversight. Synthetic biological materials can support beneficial scientific applications, but their production also creates opportunities for misuse. Screening procedures are intended to identify concerning requests before physical materials are supplied.

As computational design becomes more sophisticated, screening systems must be capable of responding to biological designs that differ from familiar reference sequences. Traditional methods may be inadequate if they depend too heavily upon recognizing previously documented patterns.

This does not mean that screening can provide perfect protection. Biological risks are complex, and no single control can identify every potentially dangerous application. However, improving screening methods and coordinating standards among providers can reduce vulnerabilities within the broader research ecosystem.

Crucially, screening should be viewed as one element of a layered security framework. Access controls, laboratory safety procedures, independent evaluations, professional accountability, and effective incident reporting remain necessary even when material screening is in place.

A further challenge involves international coordination.

Biological threats do not respect national borders. The consequences of a serious biological incident can extend far beyond the country in which the underlying research occurred. Meanwhile, AI models, scientific data, and remote laboratory services may operate across multiple jurisdictions.

If governments develop incompatible regulations, organizations may relocate sensitive activities to jurisdictions with weaker requirements. This could undermine more stringent national safeguards while creating uneven conditions for legitimate research.

International cooperation is therefore not simply desirable but essential.

Existing agreements prohibiting biological weapons establish important principles concerning the unacceptable use of biology for hostile purposes. Yet international security arrangements developed before the emergence of autonomous AI-driven experimentation may not adequately address the new pathways through which dangerous capabilities can arise.

Modernizing these arrangements does not necessarily require replacing established treaties. It may involve developing supplementary standards, technical guidance, information-sharing mechanisms, and procedures for evaluating emerging forms of risk.

Scientific organizations, governments, technology companies, and public health institutions should collaborate on common approaches to system evaluation, laboratory oversight, and the responsible management of sensitive capabilities.

Such cooperation must also acknowledge that countries possess unequal resources for implementing safeguards. A regulatory framework that wealthy states can enforce but resource-constrained states cannot realistically maintain may create significant gaps. International capacity-building, technical assistance, and equitable access to safety infrastructure should therefore form part of any credible global strategy.

The same principle applies to public health preparedness. Preventing misuse is essential, but societies must also strengthen their ability to detect and respond to biological emergencies regardless of their origin.

Disease surveillance, diagnostic capacity, resilient healthcare systems, and effective communication networks provide protection against naturally emerging threats as well as deliberate incidents. Investments in these areas can generate immediate public benefits while reducing vulnerability to future technological risks.

This broader understanding of biosecurity is especially valuable because the distinction between accidental and intentional harm may not always be apparent during the early stages of an emergency. Public health institutions must be capable of responding effectively before the precise cause of an incident has been established.

Technical controls should also be complemented by ethical education and professional responsibility.

Scientific communities have long recognized that the ability to conduct an experiment does not automatically establish that the experiment should be conducted. Research involving human participants, animals, and hazardous materials is governed by ethical principles that reflect the relationship between scientific freedom and social responsibility.

AI-driven biology requires these principles to be extended into new forms of decision-making.

When computational systems participate in experimental design, responsibility cannot simply be transferred to the machine. Human institutions remain accountable for determining legitimate objectives, evaluating foreseeable risks, and deciding which forms of experimentation are appropriate.

The presence of autonomous technology should not become a means of obscuring accountability.

If a system produces an unexpected or harmful result, it may be necessary to examine the decisions of model developers, laboratory operators, research supervisors, and institutional authorities. Clear records of system behavior and human authorization can help establish responsibility and support improvements in safety.

This need for accountability challenges a popular assumption about technological autonomy. Greater machine independence does not eliminate the importance of human judgment. Instead, it increases the importance of deciding in advance when human oversight is required and which decisions should remain subject to explicit authorization.

One possible objection is that extensive oversight could slow scientific discovery at a time when humanity urgently needs better treatments, improved vaccines, and faster responses to emerging diseases. This concern is particularly significant when biological research offers the possibility of reducing suffering on a large scale.

However, the relationship between safety and innovation should not be understood as a simple competition in which every additional safeguard reduces progress. Well-designed standards can make technological development more sustainable by creating public confidence, clarifying institutional responsibilities, and reducing the likelihood of incidents that provoke severe restrictions.

The history of scientific regulation demonstrates that public trust is an important resource. When communities believe that powerful technologies are being developed without adequate consideration of their consequences, opposition may intensify and legitimate research may become politically vulnerable.

Responsible oversight can therefore protect the conditions necessary for continued innovation.

The more difficult problem is determining when precaution is proportionate. Demanding absolute proof of safety before any technological development would make meaningful progress impossible. Yet waiting until a catastrophic incident occurs before establishing safeguards would represent a profound failure of foresight.

A reasonable approach should therefore combine continuous evaluation, measured restrictions, independent review, and mechanisms for revising policy as evidence develops.

Regulatory decisions should acknowledge uncertainty rather than disguising it. Where evidence concerning a particular capability remains inconclusive, authorities should distinguish between demonstrated risks, plausible emerging hazards, and speculative scenarios. Transparency about these differences can support more rational public debate and discourage both exaggerated fear and unjustified confidence.

This principle is especially important because public discussions of artificial intelligence frequently alternate between promises of extraordinary transformation and warnings of imminent catastrophe. Neither narrative adequately captures the complexities of biological research.

AI systems can be exceptionally effective in some computational tasks while remaining limited in others. Automated laboratories can accelerate experimentation without eliminating every physical constraint. Security safeguards can reduce risks without guaranteeing perfect prevention.

A credible policy framework must be capable of accommodating these realities simultaneously.

The deeper philosophical issue concerns the changing nature of scientific agency.

Historically, the scientist has been understood as the central figure responsible for formulating questions, designing investigations, interpreting evidence, and deciding how knowledge should be applied. Instruments extended human perception and physical capability, but the direction of inquiry remained primarily human.

AI-driven experimentation complicates this arrangement by allowing machines to contribute increasingly substantial portions of the investigative process. Computational systems may identify research possibilities that humans did not explicitly anticipate, select experiments from enormous combinations of alternatives, and adapt subsequent actions in response to new findings.

This transformation does not necessarily diminish the value of human scientific intelligence. It may expand what researchers can accomplish and enable them to investigate problems previously beyond practical reach.

However, it requires a clearer distinction between the automation of scientific tasks and the delegation of ethical authority.

A machine may optimize an experimental outcome according to specified criteria, but those criteria do not automatically capture the broader consequences of success. An objective that appears technically desirable within a restricted computational system may conflict with public safety, environmental responsibility, or acceptable research practices.

Human institutions must therefore remain responsible for defining the limits within which automated optimization can occur.

Scientific progress has never been determined solely by what researchers are capable of discovering. It has also depended upon collective judgments about how knowledge should be pursued and used. The greater the potential consequences of experimentation, the more important these judgments become.

This understanding suggests that governing AI-driven biology is not merely a technical challenge. It is a test of society's capacity to coordinate innovation with responsibility.

The same technologies that could help accelerate medical discovery may create opportunities for harmful misuse if released without appropriate oversight. Restricting them too broadly could undermine beneficial research and reinforce inequalities. Regulating them too weakly could expose communities to risks they have little ability to anticipate or control.

The solution lies in constructing institutions capable of responding to this tension rather than denying its existence.

Such institutions must operate across the boundaries separating computer science, biology, public health, national security, and international law. They must encourage legitimate discovery while recognizing that automated biological experimentation changes the scale, speed, and accessibility of scientific capabilities.

They must also preserve accountability as machines take on more responsibilities within research processes.

Ultimately, artificial intelligence is not simply providing biology with a more efficient set of tools. It is changing the relationship between knowledge, experimentation, and action. Biological designs can increasingly move from computational representation toward physical implementation through systems requiring less continuous human involvement.

This capacity offers extraordinary promise, but it also narrows the distance between imagining a biological possibility and attempting to realize it.

The central responsibility of modern governance is to ensure that this narrowing distance does not become a widening gap between technological capability and collective control.

Humanity should neither reject the transformative potential of AI-assisted biology nor assume that scientific progress will automatically produce adequate safeguards. The benefits of programmable biological systems will be most durable when supported by transparent evaluations, proportionate access controls, accountable institutions, international cooperation, and strong public health infrastructure.

The future of biological innovation should not be measured solely by how many experiments machines can perform or how quickly they can generate useful discoveries. It should also be measured by whether human societies retain the ability to understand, supervise, and responsibly direct the consequences of those discoveries.

The most important achievement will not be creating laboratories that can operate with increasingly little human intervention. It will be building a system of scientific responsibility strong enough to ensure that greater automation serves human well-being rather than exposing it to preventable harm.

As artificial intelligence expands humanity's power to redesign aspects of the living world, the need for wisdom, restraint, and cooperation becomes more urgent, not less. The defining challenge of this new era is therefore to ensure that our capacity to create advances alongside our capacity to care for what we create.

**Topic:** AI combined with robotic labs can now design and run huge numbers of biological experiments with little human involvement. This promises faster drugs and vaccines, but the same tools could help people cause serious biological harm. Current laws and voluntary company safeguards have fallen far behind. **주제:** AI와 로봇 실험실이 결합하면서 이제 사람의 개입을 거의 받지 않고도 엄청난 수의 생물학 실험을 설계하고 수행할 수 있게 되었습니다. 이는 더 빠른 신약과 백신 개발을 약속하지만, 같은 도구가 심각한 생물학적 피해를 일으키는 데 쓰일 수도 있습니다. 현재의 법과 기업의 자발적 안전장치는 이를 따라가지 못하고 크게 뒤처져 있습니다. 각국 정부는 유익한 연구를 막지 않으면서 위험을 통제할 수 있도록 서로 조율된 구속력 있는 감독 체계를 마련해야 합니다.

---

## 1. Title of the Work

**Brakes Before Speed: Governing the Age of Self-Driving Biology**

## 2. Creative Work

When the first automobiles appeared on city streets, there were no traffic lights, no driving tests, and no speed limits. Early cars were slow and rare, so the absence of rules seemed harmless. Within a few decades, cars had become fast, cheap, and everywhere, and the death toll forced governments to invent, in a hurry, the system of licenses, signals, and safety standards we now take for granted. That system works so well that we rarely think about it. But it came late, and it was paid for in lives.

Biology is now approaching its own automobile moment. Artificial intelligence can propose biological designs, send them to robotic laboratories that carry out the work without human hands, and learn from the results to plan the next round, again and again, around the clock. Tasks that once took a team of scientists years can now be explored in days through thousands of parallel trials. This shift promises cheaper medicines and quicker responses to new diseases. It also creates a danger that our laws were never built to handle. The rules that govern biological research ignore AI, and the rules that govern AI largely ignore biology. Societies should not wait for a disaster to close that gap. Governments must build coordinated, binding oversight for AI-driven biology now, designed to manage serious risks while leaving room for the enormous good this technology can do.

The potential benefits deserve to be stated plainly, because they are the reason this technology should not simply be banned. Proteins carry out nearly every function in a living cell, and designing new ones has always been slow and uncertain, since tiny changes can reshape a molecule in unpredictable ways. AI models trained on vast libraries of natural sequences can now predict those effects and suggest promising designs. Paired with automated labs, they can test and refine candidates at a speed no human team could match. That could mean vaccines developed in weeks instead of months, drugs that cost a fraction of today's prices, and new enzymes for cleaner industry and agriculture. A world that turned its back on these gains would be poorer and less healthy.

Yet the same qualities that make AI-driven biology so powerful make it dangerous. The knowledge needed to cure a disease often sits very close to the knowledge needed to cause one. Researchers studying these systems have found that AI models can give useful guidance on sensitive laboratory techniques, and that safety filters meant to block such help can sometimes be worked around. Studies disagree about how much AI actually helps a person with little training carry out dangerous work. Some find a large boost, while others find a smaller one. But even the more reassuring results suggest some advantage, and the trend is moving in only one direction. For a long time, the hard physical skills of laboratory work served as a natural barrier: a clever plan still needed experienced hands to carry it out. As remote, automated laboratories become cheaper and easier to access, that barrier is wearing away.

Against this backdrop, today's safeguards look thin. In many countries, screening of synthetic DNA orders to catch dangerous sequences is still largely voluntary, and existing screening methods may miss sequences that AI designs specifically to look unfamiliar. The main international treaty banning biological weapons was written half a century ago and says nothing about AI. National policies have shifted with changes of government, with protections introduced by one administration withdrawn by the next. Meanwhile, AI companies run their own safety evaluations before releasing new models, but these tests are often private, vary from company to company, and may not reflect how tools behave in the real world. Some firms have adopted stricter internal safeguards, which is welcome. But voluntary measures are only as strong as the most careless company's commitment, and even industry leaders have admitted that the technology may soon advance faster than any single firm can assess.

Critics of regulation raise a serious objection. Heavy-handed rules, they warn, could drive talented researchers and investment to countries with looser standards, slowing beneficial science at home while doing little to stop the technology's spread abroad. Overreaction carries real costs, especially if it delays treatments that could save lives. This concern should shape how oversight is designed, but it is not an argument against oversight itself. Car makers did not abandon the industry when seatbelts and brake standards became mandatory. Clear, predictable rules can actually strengthen innovation by building public trust and giving responsible companies a level playing field. The real choice is not between regulation and progress. It is between thoughtful rules made now and panicked rules made after a catastrophe.

What would sensible governance look like? First, DNA synthesis screening should become mandatory and be updated to catch AI-designed sequences, since the moment a digital design becomes physical material is one of the clearest points for control. Second, access to the most capable biological AI tools should be matched to their level of risk, with verified researchers allowed to use powerful models under supervision and not every tool released to everyone without checks. Third, AI developers should be required to run independent, standardized safety evaluations before release, and to share the results with regulators. Fourth, the biological data used to train these systems, especially sensitive genomic information, needs its own rules on collection and sharing. Finally, because pathogens do not respect borders, nations must coordinate through international agreements that bring biosecurity into the age of AI.

The pioneers of the automobile did not set out to cause harm, and neither do the scientists building self-driving biology. But good intentions did not prevent traffic deaths, and they will not prevent misuse of powerful biological tools. Innovation alone has never made a technology safe. That comes from the rules, institutions, and shared expectations we build around it. This time, we have the chance to put the brakes and the traffic lights in place before the road fills up. We should take it.
