1. Title of the Work

**The Invisible Pipette: Surviving the Automation of Biological Engineering**

2. Creative Work

For millennia, biology was a discipline of humble observation. Humanity stood before the intricate tapestry of life and sought only to patiently trace its threads, eventually learning to splice and mend the fabric through genetic editing. Yet, even those revolutionary breakthroughs were fundamentally anchored by the physical limitations of the human scientist at the laboratory bench. Today, that paradigm has been violently overthrown. We have crossed the threshold into the era of programmable biology, where artificial intelligence has transformed the laboratory into a tireless, automated factory. By outsourcing the design, iteration, and execution of biological experiments to algorithmic minds and robotic appendages, we have unleashed an unprecedented engine of discovery. However, in our desperate rush to conquer disease, we have willfully ignored the existential peril of this acceleration. We are handing the profound power of genesis to autonomous systems while our geopolitical and regulatory frameworks remain disastrously rooted in the analog past.

The scale and speed of this new biological-industrial complex defy traditional scientific comprehension. Through remote cloud laboratories, an AI can now independently hypothesize, synthesize, execute, and evaluate tens of thousands of molecular variations in the time it takes a human researcher to design a single trial. The historical bottleneck of scientific progress—the absolute necessity for highly trained, physical hands to execute complex protocols—has completely evaporated. Algorithms now iterate through genetic codes exactly as software engineers refine a digital prototype, rapidly closing the loop between digital design and physical reality. While this velocity promises to deliver miraculous vaccines and radically cheaper therapeutics, it simultaneously masks a terrifying dual-use reality: the exact same digital architecture required to fold a life-saving protein can be effortlessly inverted to optimize the transmission and lethality of a pathogen.

What makes this convergence of artificial intelligence and synthetic biology uniquely dangerous is its sheer capacity to democratize catastrophic risk. Historically, the creation of biological weapons required not only malicious intent but also vast institutional resources, specialized knowledge, and decades of hands-on laboratory expertise. Artificial intelligence systematically dismantles every one of these barriers. Today, advanced language models can act as infinitely patient, omniscient mentors to absolute novices, bypassing safety filters to guide untrained individuals through the intricate, step-by-step processes of reviving or enhancing viral threats. When this unregulated intellectual access is coupled with automated, remote laboratories, an amateur with an internet connection could theoretically command a distant facility to manufacture a pandemic.

Against this hyper-accelerated threat, humanity’s defensive posture is terrifyingly fragile. We are attempting to govern a borderless, digital frontier using archaic international treaties drafted half a century ago, long before artificial intelligence was a viable concept. Our current oversight mechanisms are a perilous patchwork of voluntary corporate self-regulation and inconsistent governmental screening protocols that entirely fail to account for algorithms capable of designing sequences that evade traditional detection methods. Tech companies may periodically adjust their internal safety thresholds out of an abundance of caution, but relying on the profit-driven magnanimity and opaque evaluations of a few corporations to safeguard the global biological commons is an invitation to disaster.

If we are to survive this automated revolution, we must radically and urgently reinvent our approach to global biosecurity. We can no longer afford to treat genomic data and cloud-based biological synthesis as unregulated commodities. The international community must implement mandatory, dynamic oversight frameworks that rigidly control access to AI biological tools based on user risk, firmly severing the frictionless pipeline between algorithmic design and physical synthesis unless rigorous, standardized verifications are met. The automation of life holds the promise of a golden age for human health, but if we refuse to build the necessary guardrails now, our greatest technological triumph may very well engineer our final undoing.

## 1. Title of the Work

# The Algorithmic Evolution of Extremism: Why Counterterrorism Must Understand the Strategic Cultures Behind Artificial Intelligence

## 2. Creative Work

Artificial intelligence is transforming the relationship between technological capability and organized political violence. Tools originally developed to improve communication, automate complex tasks, and expand access to information can also be exploited by extremist organizations seeking to amplify their influence. Generative systems can accelerate the production of persuasive media, translate ideological messages across linguistic boundaries, and create synthetic content that complicates the distinction between authentic and fabricated information. These capabilities present serious challenges for governments, technology companies, and organizations responsible for public security. Yet the significance of artificial intelligence in terrorism cannot be understood simply by cataloging the tools that extremist networks acquire. Different organizations interpret technological innovation through distinct ideological assumptions, institutional habits, and strategic expectations. Consequently, effective counterterrorism policy must examine not only what artificial intelligence enables extremist movements to do, but also how their organizational cultures shape the purposes for which they adopt it.

The tendency to regard technological innovation as an independent force that automatically transforms political violence is misleading. Throughout history, new communication systems, transportation technologies, and military capabilities have influenced the activities of armed organizations. Nevertheless, these innovations have rarely produced identical outcomes across competing movements. Their effects depend upon the resources available to particular organizations, their internal structures, political ambitions, and willingness to experiment.

An organization seeking rapid public attention may prioritize technologies that increase the speed and visibility of its messaging. Another organization pursuing influence over extended periods may be more concerned with whether technological dependence strengthens or undermines its strategic independence. Both may adopt similar software, yet their decisions can reflect fundamentally different understandings of political struggle.

This distinction is especially important when examining extremist networks associated with the Islamic State and al-Qaida. Although both movements have employed violent extremist ideologies and have demonstrated interest in emerging digital technologies, their organizational histories reveal different strategic tendencies. Islamic State-linked networks have frequently emphasized highly visible communication, rapid mobilization, and the immediate projection of power. Al-Qaida-linked networks have often placed greater emphasis on organizational endurance, dispersed operations, and the belief that prolonged conflict can exhaust a more technologically advanced opponent.

These differences help explain why artificial intelligence may acquire distinct meanings within the two movements.

A relatively small network can use digital tools to create the appearance of extensive activity. Repeated synthetic publications may imply broad organizational coordination even when their production depends upon a limited number of individuals. Visually polished material may suggest institutional sophistication that does not correspond to real operational strength.

This distinction matters because terrorism often seeks psychological and political effects beyond the immediate consequences of violence. Extremist propaganda attempts to influence perceptions, attract attention, intimidate opponents, and encourage identification with a movement. Movements that associate success with rapid mobilization may reward experimentation before developing comprehensive internal guidance. Their supporters may adopt emerging platforms quickly because immediate communication advantages appear more valuable than prolonged doctrinal debate. This pattern illustrates a broader relationship between technological change and organizational legitimacy. Extremist groups cannot simply adopt every useful technology without considering how its use will be interpreted by supporters. They must also construct explanations that fit their ideological identities.

In movements where religious authority plays a central role, technological innovation may become the subject of arguments concerning obligation, legitimacy, and the acceptable boundaries of human knowledge. These debates should not be interpreted as evidence that the technologies themselves possess any particular religious meaning. Rather, they demonstrate how organizations reinterpret external developments through the concepts that structure their internal authority.

The Islamic State's interest in artificial intelligence can be understood partly through this interaction between immediate utility and ideological mobilization. Digital competence may be presented within associated extremist discourse as necessary for survival in an environment where opponents also possess advanced technological capabilities.

Such arguments transform technological adaptation into a matter of collective urgency. The perceived danger of falling behind becomes an incentive for experimentation, while the promise of improved communication offers an immediate organizational benefit.

This does not imply that every supporter or affiliate shares the same level of enthusiasm. Extremist movements are not perfectly unified systems, and disputes over technology can emerge between different media organizations, ideological authorities, and local networks. Nevertheless, the broader tendency toward rapid experimentation reflects a strategic culture that places considerable value on visible effects.

Al-Qaida-linked discourse reveals a different dimension of the relationship between artificial intelligence and extremist strategy. While affiliated networks have also explored digital tools for communication and other purposes, some associated ideological discussions have considered the deeper implications of technological change for prolonged warfare.

The central question in such discussions is not merely whether artificial intelligence can improve a particular task. It is whether advanced technology fundamentally changes the relationship between military power, political purpose, and strategic endurance.

This distinction is significant because technological superiority has not always translated into decisive political success in asymmetric conflicts. States may possess advanced surveillance capabilities, extensive financial resources, and highly sophisticated military equipment while confronting opponents capable of surviving through dispersion, adaptation, and prolonged resistance.

Al-Qaida's strategic narratives have historically emphasized the possibility that an organization with fewer material resources can survive against a stronger adversary by maintaining commitment over time. Within that worldview, technological innovation may be regarded as important without being considered decisive.

Artificial intelligence can therefore become part of a broader intellectual argument about the limits of military modernization.

Such arguments should not be confused with reliable predictions about the outcome of conflict. They represent the strategic assumptions of an extremist movement seeking to justify its own methods and expectations. The belief that endurance can overcome technological superiority does not establish that this outcome will occur.

Nevertheless, examining those assumptions is essential for understanding organizational behavior. A movement that sees technological advantage as temporary may be less inclined to reorganize its entire identity around new tools. It may instead adopt selected capabilities while continuing to prioritize dispersed networks, ideological continuity, and long-term survival.

The contrast illustrates an important principle: two organizations can acquire similar technologies without undergoing the same strategic transformation.

Artificial intelligence should therefore be understood as interacting with existing organizational structures rather than replacing them.

The consequences for counterterrorism are substantial. Security analysis often begins by identifying technological capabilities that could increase the effectiveness of extremist activity. Such assessments are necessary, especially when digital tools can facilitate propaganda distribution, deception, or other harmful conduct.

However, capability-centered analysis becomes incomplete when it assumes that all organizations will pursue the same opportunities or respond similarly to technological change.

An emerging tool may appear highly valuable to one movement because it supports immediate public visibility. Another movement may adopt it more selectively because the organization's priorities center on long-term continuity. A third network may reject or restrict its use because of internal distrust, ideological disagreement, or concerns about surveillance.

Understanding these differences can improve assessments of likely behavior and reduce the risk of treating extremist organizations as interchangeable.

This approach also discourages technological determinism: the belief that the arrival of a new tool inevitably produces a predictable social or political outcome.

Artificial intelligence does not possess an independent political agenda. Its consequences emerge through the decisions of users, developers, institutions, and governing authorities. In extremist contexts, those decisions are shaped by organizational beliefs and political objectives that predate the technology.

The existence of an advanced language model does not automatically create a sophisticated extremist movement. Nor does access to image generation transform a fragmented network into a coherent organization. Technological tools may enhance particular activities, but organizational effectiveness still depends upon leadership, resources, relationships, social conditions, and the ability to maintain support.

This distinction is essential for avoiding exaggerated assessments of emerging threats.

Public discussions of artificial intelligence and terrorism can sometimes portray the technology as an unprecedented force that will fundamentally reinvent extremist violence. Such claims may generate attention, but they risk obscuring the continuity between established extremist practices and their newer technological forms.

Propaganda, recruitment, ideological justification, and the exploitation of public fear existed long before generative artificial intelligence. New systems may accelerate or complicate these activities, yet the underlying political purposes often remain recognizable.

Acknowledging this continuity does not minimize the danger. On the contrary, it helps identify where artificial intelligence creates genuinely important changes.

One such change concerns the economics of extremist communication.

Producing high-quality multilingual material has traditionally required considerable human labor. Translation, editing, graphic design, and audiovisual production depend upon skills that may not be widely distributed across a decentralized organization. Artificial intelligence can reduce some of these costs.

As a result, extremist communication may become more frequent, more linguistically diverse, and easier to adapt to specific audiences. The reduced cost of production can increase the amount of material circulating online, potentially complicating efforts to identify and respond to harmful content.

Yet the relationship between increased production and successful persuasion remains uncertain. Greater quantities of propaganda do not necessarily produce greater ideological influence. Audiences may recognize manipulation, reject the underlying message, or become less responsive to repetitive content.

Counterterrorism research must therefore distinguish between what extremist networks can produce and what their communications actually accomplish.

A second important change concerns the credibility of digital information.

Synthetic video, manipulated audio, and fabricated imagery can complicate public understanding of violent events. Extremist supporters may circulate material that falsely suggests organizational achievements, misrepresents statements by public figures, or creates misleading impressions of events.

Such manipulation can impose costs on journalists, investigators, and public institutions required to verify information rapidly. It may also undermine confidence in authentic evidence when audiences become increasingly aware that convincing media can be fabricated.

However, the problem extends beyond the deliberate spread of false information. The widespread availability of synthetic media can enable individuals to dismiss genuine documentation as artificial. This creates an environment in which both deception and unjustified denial become easier.

The preservation of reliable information therefore becomes an important component of public security.

Media organizations, technology platforms, and independent verification groups need methods for establishing provenance, identifying manipulation, and communicating uncertainty without amplifying extremist narratives. These efforts should focus on credible evidence rather than sensational claims concerning technological sophistication.

A third concern involves the relationship between artificial intelligence and organizational learning.

Extremist groups, like other organizations, adjust their practices in response to changing environments. They observe countermeasures, evaluate communication methods, and interpret political developments. Artificial intelligence may assist some forms of information processing, potentially accelerating the circulation and interpretation of material available to supporters.

Yet organizational learning is not equivalent to the possession of computational tools.

A group must still decide which information to trust, how to resolve internal disagreements, and whether to act upon particular conclusions. In ideologically rigid organizations, these decisions may be strongly influenced by established beliefs that limit the practical value of new information.

This suggests that the consequences of artificial intelligence will depend partly upon whether extremist movements possess institutional structures capable of translating technical outputs into meaningful organizational adaptation.

The distinction also highlights the importance of understanding decentralization.

Modern extremist networks may include formal leadership structures, regional affiliates, loosely connected media organizations, and individuals acting without direct operational supervision. These participants do not necessarily possess identical resources or follow uniform technological policies.

Some supporters may experiment with new digital tools independently of central leadership. Their activities may attract considerable public attention even when they do not represent an officially coordinated strategy.

Consequently, analysts should avoid treating every technological experiment by a supporter as evidence of a movement-wide transformation. Careful distinctions between official organizations, affiliated networks, ideological sympathizers, and independent actors are necessary for accurate threat assessment.

These distinctions can also reduce the risk of exaggerating the organizational coherence of extremist movements.

A fourth dimension concerns the relationship between artificial intelligence and ideological authority.

When digital systems generate information or interpret complex texts, they may challenge established methods through which organizations determine what constitutes acceptable knowledge. Extremist movements that place great importance on doctrinal consistency may face internal disagreements over whether computational outputs can be trusted.

Some participants may view automated systems as useful aids to communication or research. Others may regard dependence upon them as intellectually unreliable or ideologically inappropriate.

These disagreements reveal that technological adoption is also a cultural negotiation. Organizations must determine how new capabilities fit within existing hierarchies of expertise, authority, and legitimacy.

For counterterrorism researchers, such debates offer valuable evidence about internal organizational priorities. They may reveal tensions between younger digitally engaged supporters and more cautious ideological authorities, or between immediate operational convenience and established strategic assumptions.

However, these internal debates should not be romanticized as signs of intellectual sophistication or ideological legitimacy. Violent extremist movements may engage in extensive strategic reasoning while pursuing objectives that fundamentally violate human rights and civilian security.

Understanding their arguments is an analytical necessity, not an endorsement of their purposes.

This distinction becomes especially important when examining how extremist organizations interpret the writings of external military theorists or technology researchers.

The use of academic or strategic literature does not necessarily demonstrate agreement with the political values of its authors. Organizations may selectively extract ideas that appear consistent with existing assumptions while ignoring broader ethical or historical contexts.

A movement committed to prolonged conflict may emphasize arguments questioning the decisiveness of technological superiority because those arguments reinforce its preferred understanding of warfare.

Such selective interpretation illustrates how ideology influences the reception of knowledge. New information is often evaluated not only according to its accuracy but also according to its compatibility with established beliefs.

Counterterrorism analysis must therefore consider the interpretive framework through which technological developments are understood.

This perspective has practical implications for public policy.

Governments confronting AI-enabled extremist activity need coordinated responses involving security agencies, technology companies, civil society organizations, and independent researchers. Yet those responses should remain proportionate to demonstrated risks.

Broad restrictions on digital technology may create substantial costs for legitimate users without effectively preventing determined extremist actors from obtaining comparable capabilities elsewhere. Excessively expansive surveillance measures may also threaten privacy, freedom of expression, and public trust.

Such consequences are particularly troubling when security policies disproportionately affect communities already exposed to suspicion or discrimination.

A legitimate counterterrorism strategy must therefore combine targeted interventions with strong protections for civil liberties.

Technology companies can contribute by evaluating how their systems might facilitate serious misuse, improving responses to clearly identifiable terrorist propaganda, and strengthening mechanisms for reporting dangerous activity. At the same time, content moderation should distinguish between the promotion of violence and legitimate activities such as journalism, academic research, historical documentation, and criticism of extremist organizations.

The distinction is necessary because understanding violent movements often requires examining the materials they produce. Overly broad removal policies can unintentionally restrict the evidence available to investigators and researchers.

Responsible governance must protect the public without undermining the informational foundations of accountability.

International coordination is also essential because extremist networks and digital platforms operate across national boundaries.

Propaganda may be produced in one country, distributed through services based in another, and consumed by audiences across multiple regions. National governments cannot address these problems effectively through isolated action.

Cooperation on digital investigations, information integrity, and the identification of serious threats can improve collective responses. However, international arrangements should incorporate clear legal standards and safeguards against political abuse.

Governments must not use the language of counterterrorism to suppress legitimate dissent or criminalize peaceful political expression. The existence of genuine security threats does not justify abandoning the legal distinctions that separate violent extremism from lawful disagreement.

A further limitation of technology-centered counterterrorism is its tendency to overlook the social and political circumstances that make extremist recruitment possible.

Artificial intelligence may improve the production or circulation of ideological material, but technological sophistication does not explain why individuals become receptive to violent extremist narratives.

Political grievances, armed conflict, social exclusion, identity struggles, institutional distrust, and local conditions may influence recruitment and support. Their relative importance varies across societies and individuals, and no single explanation applies universally.

Nevertheless, these underlying conditions cannot be resolved through content moderation or technical restrictions alone.

An effective prevention strategy must address the broader environments in which extremist movements attempt to gain influence. This can include strengthening trustworthy public institutions, protecting communities affected by violence, supporting educational opportunities, and ensuring that legitimate political grievances can be expressed without coercion.

Such measures do not replace immediate security responses. They complement them by reducing vulnerabilities that technological interventions alone cannot address.

The distinction is particularly important because extremist organizations may interpret artificial intelligence as evidence that the technological balance of conflict is changing. Yet the political outcomes of violent movements remain dependent upon far more than communication tools or computational capabilities.

A movement may produce sophisticated digital material while failing to achieve durable political support. Another may possess limited technological resources but remain difficult to eliminate because of unresolved local conflicts or weak governing institutions.

This demonstrates why the effectiveness of counterterrorism cannot be measured solely through technological superiority.

The history of asymmetric conflict repeatedly shows that advanced capabilities can coexist with persistent insecurity. Governments may successfully disrupt communications, capture leaders, or weaken organizational infrastructure without resolving the conditions that permit extremist networks to regenerate.

Artificial intelligence may alter the methods through which these struggles unfold, but it does not abolish the relationship between political legitimacy, social institutions, and security.

This leads to a broader philosophical question about the significance of technology in organized human conflict.

Technological change is often described as though it follows an autonomous trajectory, transforming societies regardless of the intentions of those who adopt it. In reality, technologies acquire political meaning through human decisions.

The same computational system can support medical research, language education, emergency response, or harmful propaganda. Its technical capabilities may be similar across these contexts, but its social consequences differ because the purposes guiding its use differ.

The significance of artificial intelligence in extremism therefore lies partly in what it reveals about the persistence of organizational identity.

Movements do not encounter new technologies as neutral collections of individuals. They interpret them through shared narratives about history, power, vulnerability, and success.

An organization emphasizing immediate influence may regard artificial intelligence primarily as an opportunity for rapid communication and mobilization. A movement focused on long-term endurance may also ask whether the technology changes deeper assumptions about political struggle.

Neither interpretation guarantees strategic success. Both demonstrate that technological adoption is shaped by beliefs about how the world works and how political objectives might be achieved.

For policymakers, the lesson is clear: understanding an adversary requires more than measuring its tools.

Counterterrorism institutions should investigate the organizational incentives that guide technological experimentation, the internal debates surrounding new capabilities, and the practical evidence of their effects. This approach can help distinguish emerging threats from speculative possibilities and prevent responses driven primarily by technological fear.

It also offers a more realistic understanding of innovation. Artificial intelligence may make certain extremist activities less expensive and more accessible, but it cannot automatically create effective leadership, popular legitimacy, or strategic coherence.

The danger should neither be exaggerated nor dismissed.

Overestimating AI-enabled extremist capabilities risks encouraging disproportionate policies, unnecessary public anxiety, and the inadvertent amplification of terrorist narratives. Underestimating them risks leaving institutions unprepared for increasingly convincing deception, faster propaganda production, and new forms of organizational experimentation.

A responsible approach must occupy the difficult space between these extremes.

This requires continuous research, careful assessment of evidence, collaboration across institutions, and the willingness to revise assumptions as technological capabilities evolve.

Ultimately, the relationship between artificial intelligence and violent extremism reveals a broader truth about technological power. Innovation changes the opportunities available to organizations, but those opportunities are filtered through existing political aims, institutional habits, and interpretations of conflict.

The emergence of powerful digital tools does not erase the historical differences between extremist movements. It may instead make those differences more consequential by providing new means through which established strategies can be pursued.

Effective counterterrorism must therefore look beyond the surface of technological adoption. The central questions are not merely which organizations possess artificial intelligence, how frequently they use it, or how sophisticated their digital material appears. More important are the purposes those systems serve, the assumptions guiding their deployment, and the real-world consequences that follow.

The future of security will depend partly upon governments' ability to regulate emerging technologies responsibly. But it will also depend upon their willingness to recognize that the deepest drivers of extremist violence remain political, organizational, and human.

Artificial intelligence may transform the instruments through which violent movements communicate and adapt. It does not remove the need to understand the beliefs and structures that give those instruments direction.

The most durable defense against technologically enabled extremism will therefore combine technical vigilance with historical understanding, institutional resilience, democratic accountability, and careful attention to the social conditions that sustain violent political movements.

In an age increasingly fascinated by intelligent machines, the greatest analytical mistake may be to forget that human organizations still determine what those machines are asked to accomplish.

**Topic:** Terrorist groups don't all use AI the same way. Each group's organizational culture, and especially its sense of time, shapes how it takes up the technology. The Islamic State moves fast and wants visible results now, while al-Qaida plans for a long war and asks whether AI really changes the nature of conflict. **주제:** 테러 조직이 모두 같은 방식으로 AI를 쓰는 것은 아닙니다. 각 조직의 문화, 특히 시간을 바라보는 관점이 기술을 받아들이는 방식을 결정합니다. 이슬람국가(IS)는 빠르게 움직이며 당장 눈에 보이는 성과를 원하고, 알카에다는 장기전을 내다보며 AI가 정말로 전쟁의 본질을 바꾸는지 묻습니다. 따라서 대테러 전략은 그들이 쓰는 도구만이 아니라 각 조직의 사고방식을 연구해야 합니다.

---

## 1. Title of the Work

**The Same Machine, Two Clocks: Why Counterterrorism Must Read Culture, Not Just Code**

## 2. Creative Work

In the years between the two world wars, France and Germany owned roughly the same new weapon: the tank. France had more of them, and many were better armored. Yet when war came in 1940, German forces cut through French defenses in a matter of weeks. The difference lay not in the machines but in the minds behind them. French commanders treated tanks as support for slow-moving infantry and spread them thinly along the front. German planners saw them as the spearhead of fast, concentrated attacks. The same technology, filtered through two different military cultures, produced two very different wars.

That lesson matters again as violent extremist movements begin to adopt artificial intelligence. Much public discussion treats AI as a single, uniform threat: a tool that makes propaganda cheaper, translation faster, and planning easier for anyone who wants to cause harm. That picture is accurate as far as it goes, but it is incomplete. Extremist groups do not take up technology in a vacuum. Each absorbs new tools through its own habits, priorities, and above all its sense of time. The two most influential jihadi movements of this century, al-Qaida and the Islamic State group, show this clearly. Both use AI for many of the same practical purposes, but they think about it in fundamentally different ways. Governments and technology companies that want to counter them must learn to read those differences, or they will keep preparing for the wrong fight.

Consider the movement built around urgency. The Islamic State rose to prominence by claiming territory and displaying it to the world in real time, through a media machine famous for speed, polish, and shock. Its project depended on proving, again and again, that it was acting now. That instinct has carried into the age of AI. Networks linked to the group have embraced synthetic images, machine translation, and artificially generated presenters, often driven by younger supporters who experiment eagerly with new tools. At one point, an affiliate's publication went so far as to declare learning about AI a religious obligation, then quietly dropped that claim after mockery from rival militants while keeping its practical advice. The pattern is revealing: adopt first, rationalize later. For this culture, the question is never whether a new technology transforms war. The question is how quickly it can be mastered, and how to avoid falling behind enemies who are already using it.

Now consider the movement built around patience. Al-Qaida has long framed its struggle as a war spanning generations, one it believes it can win by surviving, absorbing losses, and outlasting opponents with far greater resources. It endured the arrival of armed drones, mass surveillance, and precision strikes not by matching them but by dispersing and waiting. Its supporters also use AI tools, for chatbot guides, translation, and research. But parts of its media ecosystem do something the Islamic State's rarely does: they stop to ask what the technology means. Pro-al-Qaida outlets have translated serious Western writing on AI and the future of war, staging an extended debate about whether machines can replace human judgment and whether technological superiority can ever substitute for willpower and endurance. The answer these texts keep circling back to fits the movement's founding bet: tools may change how wars are fought, but not who ultimately prevails.

Why should this distinction matter to those trying to stop political violence? Because each mindset produces a different kind of danger and calls for a different response. A movement that prizes immediate spectacle is likely to flood online spaces with high volumes of AI-generated content, exploit breaking news within hours, and seize on every new tool the moment it becomes available. Countering it demands speed: rapid detection of synthetic media, quick cooperation between platforms, and moderation systems that can keep up with a constant stream of fresh material. A movement that thinks in decades is less likely to chase novelty but more likely to fold technology into a durable strategy and a persuasive story about why its cause will endure. Countering it demands patience of a different kind: long-term intelligence work, attention to its strategic writings, and efforts to undermine the narrative that it can simply wait out its enemies.

Some will argue that these distinctions are academic. Both groups use AI to spread propaganda and recruit followers, so a single set of defenses, they say, should be enough. Others might worry that studying how extremists think gives their ideas undeserved attention. These objections deserve a hearing, but they miss the point. Shared tools do not mean shared intentions, and defenses designed for one style of threat may leave gaps against another. A system tuned to catch floods of flashy synthetic videos may overlook a slower, more careful effort to adapt technology for planning. Meanwhile, understanding an adversary's assumptions is not the same as endorsing them. Every effective security strategy in history has depended on grasping how the opponent sees the world.

The practical implications are clear. Analysts assessing AI-related risks should look beyond lists of tools and ask how each movement's culture shapes what it will do with them. Technology companies should share information about patterns of misuse while recognizing that different groups leave different fingerprints. Policymakers should resist the temptation to treat AI misuse as one generic problem and instead fund research into how particular organizations learn, adapt, and justify their choices. And counter-messaging efforts should aim at the specific stories each group tells, whether that is the thrill of instant impact or the comfort of inevitable victory.

French generals in 1940 were not defeated because they lacked tanks. They were defeated because they misjudged how their opponent would use the same technology. The contest with violent extremism in the age of AI will turn on a similar point. Machines can be bought, copied, and downloaded by anyone. Ideas about time, patience, and purpose are harder to see, and they determine how those machines are used. Whoever understands the culture behind the code will hold a decisive advantage.

1. Title of the Work

**The Calculus of Eternity and the Microsecond: AI on the Asymmetric Battlefield**

2. Creative Work

There is a pervasive, almost superstitious dread that artificial intelligence will soon engineer an entirely unprecedented breed of terrorism. The collective imagination conjures visions of algorithmic masterminds devising novel, inescapable methods of destruction. Yet, the history of warfare suggests that technology rarely rewrites the fundamental nature of an insurgency; rather, it acts as a hyper-efficient mirror. When radical networks encounter a disruptive tool like generative AI, the technology does not overwrite their dogma. Instead, it is seamlessly bent to serve the disparate organizational cultures of the militants who wield it, revealing profound differences in how these groups perceive time, endurance, and the nature of war itself.

On one side of the ideological divide exists the vanguard of the spectacle, an archetype perfected by the Islamic State. This is an organizational culture built upon the frantic urgency of the immediate, heavily reliant on younger, digitally native recruits who view technological experimentation as second nature. For a movement that predicates its legitimacy on the visible domination of the present moment, AI is a tool of sheer acceleration. It is the engine behind instant, multilingual propaganda and synthetic, AI-generated news anchors rapidly deployed to capitalize on the shockwaves of recent massacres. In this hyper-reactive ecosystem, algorithmic fluency is elevated beyond mere utility into a doctrinal mandate, framing the mastery of AI as a strict religious duty required to defend the faith against technologically advanced adversaries. This approach treats artificial intelligence as a blunt, tactical instrument meant to overwhelm the digital landscape, trading deep strategic patience for the immediate, viral impact of the microsecond.

Conversely, the traditionalists of the militant underground, exemplified by al-Qaida, approach the exact same technology through the lens of a generational war of attrition. Where the spectacle-driven networks seek the immediate psychological strike of a deepfake, the architects of the long war pause to interrogate the philosophical boundaries of the machine. They dedicate considerable effort to translating and scrutinizing foreign strategic doctrines regarding cyberwarfare, actively debating whether artificial intelligence could ever genuinely alter the fundamental nature of human conflict. While they undeniably utilize AI for practical logistics—such as researching explosives or automating translations—their internal discourse frequently questions whether an over-reliance on digital tools signifies a fatal erosion of ideological conviction and human agency.

This divergence reveals a profound schism regarding how to defeat a technologically superior adversary. The patient insurgency operates on the bedrock wager that no algorithm, drone swarm, or surveillance network can ultimately outlast raw human endurance and political will. Having survived decades of precision airstrikes by dispersing and waiting, they view AI not as a magical key to immediate victory, but as merely another variable to be absorbed and outlasted in a century-long equation.

Ultimately, the advent of artificial intelligence is not flattening the strategic landscape of global extremism; it is bifurcating it. The true danger of generative AI in the hands of non-state actors does not lie in the sudden invention of a synthetic, machine-led terror. The danger lies in how perfectly the technology accommodates both the frenetic, dopamine-driven opportunist and the patient, calculating zealot, allowing each to wage their distinct version of war faster, cheaper, and with chilling efficiency.

## 1. Title of the Work

# The Illusion of Consumer Choice: Why Digital Subscription Contracts Must Protect the Promises They Sell

## 2. Creative Work

The digital economy has transformed the way people purchase and experience services. Instead of acquiring products through individual transactions, consumers increasingly pay recurring fees for access to entertainment, software, cloud storage, and other digital platforms. Subscription arrangements promise convenience, continuity, and predictable costs, allowing customers to enjoy services without repeatedly negotiating the conditions of access. Yet this apparent simplicity conceals an increasingly important problem: the companies providing these services often retain extensive contractual powers to change what customers receive after payment has already been made. When a platform introduces advertising into a previously advertising-free service or demands additional payment to preserve existing features, the transaction raises questions extending far beyond customer dissatisfaction. It challenges the meaning of contractual consent, the fairness of unequal bargaining power, and the responsibilities of corporations operating at enormous scale. Consumer protection in the subscription economy must therefore rest on a straightforward principle: businesses should not be able to substantially reduce the value of prepaid services without providing affected customers with meaningful remedies.

The foundation of any legitimate commercial agreement is the exchange of promises. A customer agrees to pay a specified amount, and a business undertakes to supply goods or services according to established conditions. Although contracts cannot eliminate every uncertainty, they create reasonable expectations about what each party will receive. These expectations are particularly important when customers make payments in advance, because they surrender immediate control over their money in exchange for a commitment concerning future performance.

Digital subscriptions complicate this relationship. Unlike the purchase of a physical product, which generally transfers possession of an identifiable item, a subscription grants continuing access to a service controlled by the provider. The company may alter its interface, modify its content library, introduce new technical requirements, or change the features included in particular pricing tiers.

Some degree of flexibility is necessary. Streaming services must update software, negotiate licensing agreements, maintain technical infrastructure, and adapt to changing commercial conditions. A contract that prevented every operational adjustment would be impractical and could ultimately harm consumers by obstructing improvements.

However, the need for operational flexibility does not justify unrestricted authority to alter the essential value of an agreement. There is an important difference between modifying a service to maintain its functionality and reducing a benefit that materially influenced the customer's purchasing decision.

Advertising illustrates this distinction particularly clearly.

For viewers, the absence of advertising is not merely an incidental technical feature. It can be a significant component of the entertainment experience. Advertising interrupts narrative continuity, consumes time, and influences how audiences engage with films and television programs. Some consumers may tolerate these interruptions in exchange for lower subscription prices, while others deliberately select services that offer uninterrupted viewing.

Neither preference is inherently unreasonable. The problem arises when a company changes the relationship between price and service quality after consumers have already committed to a particular arrangement.

If a customer purchases a year of access under one set of conditions and the provider subsequently introduces advertisements, the customer may receive a materially different experience for the remainder of the subscription. If the provider then offers to restore the previous experience through an additional monthly payment, the customer faces a difficult choice: accept a reduction in service quality or spend more money to preserve what was originally expected.

This arrangement raises a fundamental issue of fairness. The consumer has already fulfilled the principal financial obligation by paying the subscription fee. The provider, however, may attempt to redefine the benefits associated with that payment.

A system that permits substantial unilateral reductions in service value risks undermining the reciprocal nature of contractual commitments.

The underlying difficulty is the unequal bargaining power characteristic of many digital markets. Consumers rarely negotiate the terms of streaming subscriptions individually. Instead, they encounter standardized agreements drafted by corporate legal departments and presented on a take-it-or-leave-it basis.

Such contracts frequently contain provisions allowing providers to modify services, prices, or other conditions. These clauses may appear reasonable when described as mechanisms for managing technological change. Yet their practical significance can be much greater than consumers anticipate.

The fact that a contractual provision is disclosed does not necessarily establish that it is substantively fair.

Customers may technically agree to extensive modification clauses without understanding how dramatically those clauses could affect the services they purchase. Even careful readers may struggle to anticipate the consequences of broadly worded provisions that permit companies to make changes at their discretion.

This creates a distinction between formal consent and meaningful consent.

Formal consent occurs when a person accepts the written conditions of an agreement. Meaningful consent requires that the agreement provide a reasonably balanced arrangement in which the consequences of important commitments can be understood and evaluated.

In mass-market digital services, the existence of standardized contractual language may satisfy certain procedural expectations while leaving consumers exposed to substantial disadvantages.

For this reason, consumer protection law cannot rely exclusively upon whether a disputed term appeared somewhere in an agreement. It must also examine whether that term creates an unjustified imbalance between the rights and obligations of the parties.

A particularly troubling imbalance occurs when one side is bound by its promise while the other retains broad discretion to change its performance.

Consider the position of an annual subscriber. The customer has paid for a defined period of service and cannot ordinarily recover that payment merely because personal preferences have changed. The provider, meanwhile, may reserve the ability to alter important features during the same period.

If the agreement allows the business to modify essential benefits while retaining the full subscription payment, the distribution of risk becomes highly unequal. The consumer bears the consequences of changes that the company controls.

Such an arrangement conflicts with the ordinary expectation that a prepaid contract provides a degree of stability.

It is sometimes argued that customers remain protected because they can cancel their subscriptions whenever the company introduces an unfavorable change. At first glance, this appears to preserve consumer choice. A dissatisfied subscriber can simply terminate the relationship.

However, the effectiveness of this remedy depends upon what cancellation actually provides.

If a person has paid for twelve months of service and decides to leave after a substantial change during the subscription period, cancellation without reimbursement may offer little meaningful protection. The customer can stop using the service, but the provider may retain payment for benefits the customer no longer wishes to receive.

The freedom to abandon a prepaid service is not equivalent to the freedom to recover the value of an unfulfilled agreement.

This distinction is essential because cancellation rights can appear generous while leaving the underlying economic disadvantage unchanged.

A genuine remedy should place consumers in a reasonable position following a material contractual change. Depending on the circumstances, this might involve maintaining previously agreed service conditions for existing subscribers, allowing customers to reject the modification, or providing an appropriate refund for the unused portion of a prepaid period.

The purpose is not to prevent businesses from adjusting their products indefinitely. It is to ensure that consumers do not bear the entire financial cost of corporate decisions made after payment.

Proportional refunds are particularly important because they connect the customer's remedy to the remaining value of the contract.

If a company substantially changes a prepaid service, returning payment attributable to the unused period can help restore the balance between the parties. Consumers would then have a meaningful opportunity to compare alternatives rather than being financially pressured to accept a diminished service.

Such protections also improve commercial incentives.

When providers are permitted to retain prepaid fees regardless of unfavorable changes, they may have insufficient financial motivation to preserve the original value of their offerings. The company can introduce adjustments that increase revenue or reduce costs while transferring much of the resulting inconvenience to consumers.

By contrast, requiring meaningful remedies makes the financial consequences of substantial changes more visible to the business itself. Management must consider not only the additional revenue associated with a new pricing model but also the possibility that customers will reject the change and recover unused payments.

This encourages businesses to evaluate consumer welfare as part of commercial decision-making rather than treating it as an external concern.

Nevertheless, the question of contractual fairness cannot be resolved through a simplistic assumption that every unilateral modification is unlawful. Digital services operate in changing technological and commercial environments, and some contractual flexibility is necessary to preserve functionality.

The challenge is to distinguish legitimate operational adjustments from changes that undermine essential features of the bargain.

A minor interface update, security improvement, or adjustment necessary to comply with legal obligations may not warrant the same response as the introduction of advertising, the removal of a major service category, or a substantial reduction in previously included functionality.

A reasonable legal framework should examine the nature of the change, its significance to consumers, the clarity of the original agreement, the notice provided, and the availability of effective remedies.

Such an approach recognizes that contractual fairness is not determined solely by the existence of a modification clause. It depends upon how that clause operates in practice.

The legal assessment also becomes more complicated when businesses have relied upon regulatory guidance that does not expressly require every remedy later sought by enforcement authorities.

Companies should be able to consult official guidance when designing contractual arrangements. If regulators identify specific factors associated with fair terms, businesses may reasonably use those factors to assess their compliance.

However, regulatory guidance and the ultimate requirements of consumer protection law are not necessarily identical. General advice cannot always anticipate every contractual arrangement or every consequence of a disputed practice.

This creates a legitimate tension between legal certainty for businesses and meaningful protection for consumers.

On one hand, enforcement should be predictable enough that companies can understand their obligations. Retrospectively imposing requirements that were not clearly communicated may raise concerns about fairness in regulatory administration.

On the other hand, an incomplete explanation of consumer rights should not automatically justify contractual practices that create substantial disadvantages.

Courts may therefore need to determine whether the substantive imbalance of a contractual term outweighs the procedural steps a company took to notify customers and permit termination.

The significance of such decisions can extend beyond the particular parties involved.

Large digital platforms operate across numerous countries, often using similar subscription structures and commercial strategies in different markets. A legal dispute in one jurisdiction can attract international attention because its reasoning may influence regulators, consumer organizations, and businesses elsewhere.

This is particularly important where different legal systems share principles concerning unfair contractual terms, transparency, and consumer remedies.

Although legal outcomes cannot automatically be transferred between jurisdictions, judicial interpretations can shape broader expectations about responsible commercial conduct.

A ruling that clarifies the importance of effective remedies for prepaid subscribers may encourage companies to reconsider how they introduce changes to subscription services internationally.

The issue therefore concerns not only one company's pricing decisions but also the standards governing an increasingly important model of digital commerce.

Another central consideration is the cumulative impact of relatively small losses.

A modest additional monthly charge may appear insignificant when considered as a single consumer complaint. Companies may argue that the amount involved is too small to justify extensive regulatory attention or costly litigation.

Yet the scale of digital platforms transforms small individual disadvantages into substantial collective consequences.

When hundreds of thousands of customers experience the same contractual change, even minor financial effects can produce considerable aggregate gains for the provider and correspondingly widespread losses or inconvenience for consumers.

This reveals a persistent weakness in market-based consumer protection. Individuals may have little incentive to challenge small losses because the cost of seeking redress exceeds the value of the claim.

A customer who believes a streaming subscription has become unfair may simply express dissatisfaction, cancel future payments, or accept the change rather than pursue a formal complaint.

From the perspective of the business, this reluctance can reduce the practical consequences of questionable contractual practices.

Regulatory enforcement helps address the imbalance by considering the collective effects of conduct that individual consumers are unlikely to challenge through litigation.

The importance of such enforcement cannot be measured solely by the amount of money at stake for each subscriber. It also concerns whether standardized contracts can be used to impose widespread disadvantages without effective accountability.

This principle applies across many sectors beyond entertainment.

Cloud storage companies may alter the capacity included in a plan. Software providers may move previously available features into more expensive subscription tiers. Digital publications may introduce new restrictions on access. Online services may modify privacy settings, usage limits, or customer support arrangements after users have committed to recurring payments.

These changes differ in their commercial justification and legal implications, but they raise a shared question: how much control should a provider possess over the substance of an agreement once consumers have already paid?

The answer must account for the distinctive structure of subscription markets.

Digital businesses often benefit from recurring revenue, predictable customer relationships, and the convenience associated with automatic renewal. Consumers, meanwhile, may develop substantial dependence upon particular services through accumulated preferences, stored information, integrated devices, or established habits.

This dependence can make switching more difficult than the apparent availability of competitors suggests.

A consumer may technically have access to several alternative streaming platforms, yet those services may offer different libraries and content rights. Switching may therefore involve giving up entertainment that cannot easily be obtained elsewhere.

In other digital sectors, switching costs may be even greater. Customers may have stored extensive files, learned specialized software, or integrated a platform into professional workflows.

Such dependencies strengthen the argument for contractual protections that operate independently of consumers' ability to leave.

Competition is important, but it does not eliminate every imbalance within an existing contractual relationship.

A market containing multiple providers can still permit unfair practices if consumers lack effective rights when terms change after payment.

For this reason, consumer law should complement competition policy by ensuring that individual agreements remain substantively fair.

The broader ethical significance of the issue lies in the meaning of corporate promises.

Businesses frequently emphasize trust, convenience, and customer satisfaction in their marketing. Subscription services invite users to establish continuing relationships based upon the expectation that advertised benefits will remain available according to the agreed conditions.

When providers substantially change those benefits without offering adequate remedies, they risk converting trust into a form of commercial vulnerability.

Consumers may begin to suspect that any favorable feature is temporary and that companies can gradually transfer existing benefits into higher-priced tiers.

This expectation can weaken confidence in subscription arrangements more generally.

The resulting harm is not confined to immediate financial losses. It also affects the credibility of commercial commitments in digital markets.

Contracts serve an important social function because they allow people to plan their activities and allocate resources with reasonable confidence. If one party can redefine important obligations whenever doing so becomes profitable, the stability that contracts are supposed to provide is weakened.

Some defenders of flexible subscription agreements may argue that consumers understand digital services are continuously evolving and should therefore anticipate changes. They may also contend that advertising helps finance content production, maintain affordable entry-level pricing, and support long-term investment.

These arguments have merit within appropriate limits.

Advertising-supported services can provide legitimate alternatives for consumers who prefer lower fees. Businesses must be able to develop sustainable revenue models, particularly in competitive industries where production and licensing costs are substantial.

However, the commercial justification for introducing advertising does not settle the contractual question.

A company may have sound business reasons to establish a new advertising-supported tier while still owing existing prepaid subscribers the benefits associated with their original agreement.

The issue is not whether advertising is inherently unacceptable. It is whether consumers should be required to accept an unfavorable change during a period for which they have already paid.

This distinction permits commercial innovation without treating contractual commitments as disposable.

A provider could introduce new pricing structures for future subscribers while preserving existing conditions until current prepaid periods expire. Alternatively, it could offer meaningful refunds to customers unwilling to accept the revised service.

Both approaches recognize the company's freedom to evolve while respecting consumers' legitimate expectations.

The question of notice is similarly important but insufficient on its own.

Businesses should clearly communicate changes before they take effect, allowing customers time to understand their options. Information should be accessible, specific, and presented in language that ordinary consumers can reasonably interpret.

Yet transparency does not automatically produce fairness.

A company may openly announce that it intends to reduce the quality of a prepaid service, but the clarity of that announcement does not eliminate the disadvantage imposed upon customers.

This demonstrates why meaningful consumer protection requires both procedural and substantive standards.

Procedural protections ensure that customers receive adequate information and opportunities to respond. Substantive protections address whether the underlying allocation of contractual rights and obligations is reasonable.

A system focused exclusively on disclosure risks legitimizing unfavorable practices merely because they are announced in advance.

Conversely, a system that disregards transparency may prevent consumers from making informed decisions even when remedies are available.

Both dimensions are necessary.

The role of multinational corporations adds another layer of complexity.

Large digital platforms may develop pricing strategies centrally while implementing contractual arrangements through subsidiaries operating under different national legal systems. Decisions concerning advertising, subscription tiers, or service features can therefore originate beyond the jurisdiction in which consumers experience their effects.

This corporate structure can complicate accountability.

If a local subsidiary implements a policy designed and authorized by a parent company, regulators may need to examine how responsibility should be distributed among the entities involved.

The issue is not whether every participant in a multinational business should automatically face identical legal consequences. Liability must be established according to applicable law and evidence.

Rather, effective consumer protection should prevent corporate complexity from becoming a means of avoiding responsibility for decisions that produce widespread local harm.

A global company should not be able to treat consumer rights as an afterthought simply because commercial policy is established elsewhere.

The possibility of significant financial penalties is relevant in this context.

For very large corporations, modest fines may be insufficient to discourage conduct that generates substantial revenue across enormous customer bases. If the anticipated financial gain from a practice exceeds the likely cost of enforcement, penalties may become a predictable business expense rather than an effective deterrent.

Regulatory systems therefore need consequences proportionate to the scale and seriousness of unlawful conduct.

However, penalties should serve identifiable public purposes. Their legitimacy depends upon fair procedures, evidence of violations, and consistency with legal standards.

Financial sanctions should not replace meaningful remedies for affected consumers. A penalty paid to public authorities may discourage future misconduct, but it does not necessarily compensate subscribers who experienced the disputed change.

Effective enforcement should consider both deterrence and redress.

The relationship between these goals illustrates a broader principle of commercial accountability: protecting consumers requires addressing the consequences of past conduct while improving incentives for future behavior.

The most constructive response to unfair subscription practices would therefore combine clear contractual standards, accessible remedies, proportionate enforcement, and improved transparency.

Companies should identify essential features of prepaid services and explain the circumstances under which those features may change. Material reductions should trigger clearly defined consumer options, including appropriate reimbursement where justified.

Regulators should provide sufficiently detailed guidance to help businesses distinguish acceptable operational changes from potentially unfair contractual modifications.

Consumer organizations should also make information about subscription rights accessible, particularly because digital contracts often involve complex provisions that ordinary users are unlikely to study extensively.

Courts, meanwhile, have an important role in clarifying how general principles of fairness apply to evolving commercial models.

These reforms would not eliminate every dispute. Reasonable disagreement may remain concerning whether a particular change is sufficiently significant to justify a remedy or whether a proposed refund adequately reflects the value of the affected service.

Nevertheless, clearer standards can reduce uncertainty and encourage companies to consider consumer interests before implementing substantial changes.

The deeper significance of this debate is that the subscription economy has altered the practical relationship between ownership, access, and control.

Consumers increasingly pay not for permanent possession but for conditional participation in services managed by private companies. Their entertainment libraries, software tools, information storage, and digital experiences may depend upon terms that the provider retains some authority to revise.

As this model expands, the importance of enforceable promises becomes greater rather than smaller.

A society in which access replaces ownership must ensure that access rights possess meaningful substance. Otherwise, consumers may find themselves paying continuously for benefits that remain subject to unilateral redefinition.

This is not an argument against subscriptions as a commercial model. Recurring services can provide flexibility, convenience, and economic value. The concern is that these advantages should not depend upon an imbalance that leaves consumers financially committed while providers remain free to reduce essential benefits.

The legitimacy of digital commerce ultimately depends upon the credibility of the agreements through which it operates.

Businesses should be free to innovate, adjust pricing strategies, and respond to changing market conditions. Consumers should be equally entitled to expect that prepaid commitments will be honored or that meaningful remedies will be available when essential conditions are altered.

These principles are not mutually exclusive. They establish the reciprocal obligations necessary for sustainable commercial relationships.

The central question in disputes over digital subscription changes is therefore not whether companies possess the technological ability to modify their services. They clearly do. Nor is it simply whether the terms of a contract mention that modifications may occur.

The more important question is whether the contractual structure gives consumers a fair share of protection when the company exercises that power.

A subscription agreement should not function as a one-sided arrangement in which payment creates a firm obligation for the customer but only a flexible aspiration for the provider.

The future of consumer protection in digital markets will depend upon preserving this distinction. As subscriptions become increasingly central to everyday life, legal institutions must ensure that convenience does not come at the expense of enforceable rights and that commercial flexibility does not dissolve the meaning of consent.

Ultimately, a fair digital marketplace requires more than competitive prices and attractive services. It requires confidence that the promises attached to those prices will retain their value after payment.

When businesses substantially alter what customers have already purchased, meaningful choice must include more than the option to accept disappointment or walk away from prepaid benefits.

The defining principle should be simple: a company may change its future commercial offerings, but it should not be able to rewrite the economic substance of an existing agreement without accepting corresponding responsibility.

That principle protects not only individual subscribers but also the trust upon which the entire subscription economy depends.

## 1. Title of the Work

**A Promise With an Escape Hatch Is No Promise at All: Why Subscribers Deserve Fair Contracts**

## 2. Creative Work

Imagine buying a year's pass to a swimming pool. You pay up front, glad to lock in a good price. A few months later, the pool announces that the water will no longer be heated, unless you pay a small monthly fee on top of what you already paid. You complain, and the manager points to a line buried in the terms: the pool may change its services at any time, as long as members are told. You may leave if you wish, he adds, but the rest of your yearly fee will not be returned. You have done nothing wrong. You simply trusted that the deal you paid for would be the deal you got.

That scenario is no longer imaginary for millions of people who subscribe to digital services. Streaming platforms, software providers, and online retailers increasingly write contracts that let them reshape what they sell after customers have paid, whether by adding advertising, removing features, or moving once-included benefits behind extra fees. These "unilateral variation" clauses are often defended as necessary flexibility in a fast-changing market. They are not. A clause that allows one party to rewrite a deal at will empties the contract of its purpose. When a company makes its service worse during a period a customer has already paid for, fairness requires more than a notice and an exit door. It requires a refund for what was taken away, and regulators are right to insist on it.

Start with what a contract is for. People sign agreements to gain certainty. The buyer gets a promise about what they will receive, and the seller gets a promise of payment. That exchange is especially important for prepaid subscriptions, where customers hand over months of fees in advance, often in return for a discount. If the seller can change the terms whenever it likes, the buyer's side of the bargain disappears while the seller keeps the money. The buyer is left holding a promise that binds only one party. No one would accept such a deal if it were stated openly. Its acceptability depends on the clause being hidden in fine print that few customers read and none can negotiate.

Defenders of these clauses point to the right to cancel. If customers dislike a change, they argue, they can simply walk away, so no one is forced to accept a worse service. But this freedom is hollow when cancelling means forfeiting money already paid. A subscriber halfway through an annual plan faces a choice between two losses: accept a degraded service, or give up the unused portion of their fee. Either way, the company keeps the benefit of the original price while delivering less than it promised. A genuine choice would let the customer leave without penalty, which means returning the value of the remaining period. Anything less turns the right to cancel into a polite name for a one-sided price increase.

The scale of these practices also matters. For any single customer, the loss from an unwanted change may look trivial: a few dollars a month, a few minutes of advertising per evening. Few people will spend hours fighting a corporation over such sums, and companies know it. But multiplied across hundreds of thousands or millions of subscribers, those small losses add up to very large gains for the business. This is exactly the kind of harm consumer protection authorities exist to address. Individual customers lack the time and resources to challenge powerful firms, but a regulator acting on behalf of all of them can. When watchdogs take such cases to court, they are not interfering with business. They are restoring balance to relationships that were lopsided from the start.

Companies may respond that they followed the rules as written, giving notice of changes and allowing customers to leave, in line with official guidance that did not explicitly require refunds. That defense deserves to be taken seriously, and it exposes a real weakness. If regulators expect pro-rata refunds, they should say so clearly, so that businesses know where the line lies. But the absence of a precise instruction does not make an unfair practice fair. Consumer law in many countries rests on broad principles of fairness precisely because no list of rules can anticipate every trick. A company with large legal teams and global operations hardly needs a checklist to recognize that taking money for a service and then shrinking that service is not a fair exchange. Tellingly, some firms have quietly begun offering refunds after such disputes arise, a change that suggests they understand what fairness requires.

The way forward is straightforward. Laws and official guidance should state plainly that when a supplier makes an adverse change during a prepaid term, customers who cancel must receive a proportional refund. Contracts should spell out in clear language what can and cannot be changed, instead of granting open-ended discretion. Regulators should continue pursuing cases where many people suffer small losses, since no individual consumer can do so alone. And because digital services cross borders, authorities in different countries should share their findings, so that a fair standard in one market becomes the expectation everywhere.

The swimmer who paid for a year of warm water did not ask for anything unusual. They asked only that a promise be kept, or, if it could not be, that their money be returned. That simple principle has guided fair dealing for centuries. It should not be dissolved by a few lines of fine print in the digital age. A contract that one side can rewrite at will is not really a contract. It is a gamble the customer was never told they were making.
