14. Claude Mythos and Project Glasswing: why an AI superhacker has the tech world on alert

## 1. Title of the Work

# The Age of Automated Vulnerability: Why Superhuman AI Hacking Demands a New Global Cybersecurity Order

## 2. Creative Work

The security of modern civilization depends upon an extraordinary collection of invisible technological systems. Operating systems, communication networks, financial platforms, transportation infrastructure, and countless software applications support everyday life so thoroughly that their existence is often noticed only when something goes wrong. For decades, cybersecurity has relied upon a difficult balance between those who discover vulnerabilities and those who attempt to repair them before malicious actors can exploit them. This balance has been shaped by the limited availability of highly specialized expertise, the considerable time required to investigate complicated software, and the practical difficulties of turning technical weaknesses into successful attacks. Advanced artificial intelligence threatens to transform these conditions. Emerging systems capable of discovering obscure software vulnerabilities and developing sophisticated exploitation methods could dramatically accelerate both defensive security research and malicious cyber operations. The challenge is therefore no longer simply how to make software more secure, but how to govern a technological capability that could alter the speed, accessibility, and consequences of cybersecurity itself. Society must respond through coordinated vulnerability management, responsible access controls, independent evaluation, and stronger public accountability rather than assuming that technological progress will automatically favor defenders.

The significance of advanced AI-assisted cybersecurity becomes clearer when examining the foundations of the digital systems upon which societies depend. Modern computing environments are not constructed from isolated programs developed entirely by individual organizations. They consist of extensive layers of interacting components, including operating systems, libraries, communication protocols, drivers, applications, and shared open-source software.

A single widely used software component may appear in thousands of products, often performing essential functions without being visible to ordinary users. Developers depend upon these components because rebuilding every function independently would be inefficient and expensive. Their reuse accelerates innovation and allows complex systems to operate through established technical standards.

However, this interconnected structure also creates shared vulnerabilities.

A defect within a widely distributed library may affect numerous unrelated organizations. A weakness in an operating system component can expose applications that depend upon its protections. An overlooked configuration problem may become dangerous when combined with vulnerabilities elsewhere in the system.

The consequences of such weaknesses depend partly upon whether anyone discovers them and how that knowledge is used.

Historically, many software vulnerabilities have remained undiscovered for extended periods. This does not necessarily indicate that the affected software was well designed or that the weakness was impossible to exploit. It may simply reflect the difficulty of identifying the relevant conditions.

Complex programs contain enormous numbers of possible interactions. Finding a security flaw may require understanding unfamiliar source code, tracing complicated execution paths, or recognizing unusual relationships between seemingly unrelated components.

Even experienced security researchers cannot examine every possible behavior within a large software ecosystem.

Human attention, time, and expertise have therefore acted as practical constraints upon vulnerability discovery.

Artificial intelligence threatens to weaken these constraints substantially.

A sufficiently capable computational system may analyze large quantities of code, generate hypotheses concerning unexpected behavior, and evaluate promising weaknesses at a scale that individual researchers cannot easily match.

When such systems can also reason across different software components, their capabilities may extend beyond identifying isolated programming mistakes. They may recognize how several weaknesses interact and whether their combined effects undermine protections that appear effective when examined individually.

This possibility represents a significant development because cybersecurity failures frequently emerge from interactions rather than single catastrophic defects.

A minor vulnerability may provide limited access, while a separate weakness may permit an unauthorized process to acquire additional privileges. Another flaw may allow the resulting access to affect more sensitive components.

The ability to connect these opportunities can transform individually constrained weaknesses into a more serious compromise.

Advanced AI systems capable of identifying such relationships could therefore alter the practical accessibility of sophisticated cyber operations.

Yet the existence of these capabilities should not automatically be interpreted as evidence that artificial intelligence has developed independent hostile intentions.

There is an important distinction between technical competence and autonomous malice.

A system may discover vulnerabilities because researchers have instructed it to investigate software weaknesses. It may produce technically significant results through processes intended to improve cybersecurity.

The same general capability could nevertheless be misused by an actor seeking unauthorized access.

The danger lies primarily in the interaction between a powerful technical tool and the objectives of those who control it.

This distinction matters because public discussions often describe increasingly capable AI systems through the language of rebellion, escape, or machine hostility.

Such descriptions can create the misleading impression that the greatest threat comes from artificial intelligence spontaneously deciding to attack humanity.

In reality, a more immediate concern is that advanced models may make dangerous capabilities available to individuals or organizations that previously lacked the necessary expertise or resources.

The technology does not need to possess malicious intentions to facilitate harmful conduct.

It only needs to provide useful capabilities to someone who intends to misuse them.

This is the fundamental dual-use problem confronting AI-enabled cybersecurity.

The same technology that helps a security team discover vulnerabilities before attackers exploit them may also allow malicious actors to identify weaknesses more efficiently.

A defensive researcher may use an AI system to examine legacy software, recognize errors, and help prioritize repairs. A criminal organization might seek comparable analytical capabilities for unauthorized purposes.

The technical foundation can be similar even though the objectives and consequences differ radically.

Consequently, the central policy question is not whether powerful cybersecurity AI should be considered beneficial or dangerous in absolute terms.

It is how society can preserve its defensive benefits while reducing the probability and severity of misuse.

This question becomes especially urgent when advanced capabilities are concentrated within a small number of private technology companies.

Organizations developing frontier AI models may possess substantial computational resources, specialized researchers, and access to sophisticated evaluation infrastructure.

They may discover that a model demonstrates capabilities whose broad release could create significant security concerns.

Restricting access under such circumstances can be a reasonable precaution.

However, selective availability creates its own difficulties.

When a company controls a tool capable of identifying serious vulnerabilities across widely used digital infrastructure, its decisions can affect organizations far beyond its direct customers.

The company may determine which researchers receive access, which institutions benefit first, and which discoveries are communicated to software maintainers.

These decisions have consequences for public security, economic competition, and the distribution of technological power.

Private organizations can make valuable contributions to cybersecurity, but their commercial authority does not automatically confer democratic legitimacy over matters affecting critical infrastructure.

A responsible framework must therefore distinguish between the necessity of controlled access and the risks of concentrating security capabilities within a limited group of institutions.

Access restrictions may reduce immediate misuse, but they should be accompanied by transparent principles, independent oversight, and mechanisms ensuring that important defensive benefits reach organizations with legitimate security needs.

This is particularly important because the world's digital infrastructure extends far beyond major technology companies.

Hospitals, municipal governments, educational institutions, small businesses, nonprofit organizations, and public utilities all depend upon software that may contain serious vulnerabilities.

Many of these organizations lack the resources required to conduct sophisticated security research independently.

If advanced defensive AI becomes available primarily to wealthy corporations, existing inequalities in cybersecurity preparedness may deepen.

Large organizations could identify and repair vulnerabilities more rapidly while smaller institutions remain exposed to similar weaknesses.

The result could be a digital security environment in which protection increasingly depends upon financial resources and institutional influence.

Such an outcome would be especially troubling because cybersecurity is not purely a private benefit.

The failure of a hospital's information systems can disrupt patient care. An attack on a water utility may affect public services. Compromised transportation infrastructure can create consequences for people who have no contractual relationship with the software provider.

Digital insecurity produces social costs that extend well beyond the organization directly attacked.

For this reason, defensive access to advanced cybersecurity tools should be treated partly as a public-interest concern.

A coordinated approach could provide appropriately controlled access to researchers, public institutions, and software maintainers responsible for widely used infrastructure.

The objective would not be unrestricted distribution of sensitive capabilities.

It would be to ensure that the benefits of technological progress are not confined to organizations already possessing the strongest defenses.

A further challenge concerns the reliability of claims about advanced AI capabilities.

Technology companies operate in competitive markets where demonstrations of extraordinary performance can attract investment, customers, and public attention.

Announcements that a model has discovered long-hidden vulnerabilities or substantially outperformed earlier systems can carry considerable commercial value.

Such findings may be genuine and important, but their significance depends upon the methods used to evaluate them.

A system that performs exceptionally well under a particular benchmark may not demonstrate equivalent reliability across every real-world environment.

Claims concerning vulnerability discovery should therefore be distinguished from evidence that the reported weaknesses were independently confirmed and that the model's performance generalizes beyond the tested conditions.

This distinction is particularly important when most technical details cannot immediately be released.

Responsible vulnerability disclosure often requires withholding information that would enable exploitation before affected software has been repaired.

Public transparency and immediate security can therefore come into tension.

Publishing every detail may help independent researchers assess the credibility of a claim, but it could also provide useful information to malicious actors.

Concealing all relevant evidence, however, requires outsiders to accept corporate assertions without meaningful verification.

Neither extreme provides an adequate foundation for public trust.

A better approach would involve independent evaluation under controlled conditions.

Qualified external researchers could assess important findings while respecting confidentiality requirements. Independent bodies could verify whether reported vulnerabilities exist, whether proposed exploitation methods are effective, and whether the claimed performance advantages are supported by reliable evidence.

Public reports could then communicate conclusions, limitations, and methodological information without exposing dangerous technical details.

Such arrangements would allow society to distinguish demonstrated capabilities from promotional narratives while preserving responsible disclosure.

The need for credible evaluation also highlights the importance of avoiding exaggerated interpretations of AI autonomy.

A model that discovers complex software vulnerabilities may demonstrate remarkable reasoning and technical competence.

However, these abilities do not necessarily establish that it possesses independent strategic goals or a general desire to evade human control.

Capability assessments should distinguish between following instructions, acting within delegated authority, encountering unexpected opportunities, and deliberately pursuing goals contrary to those assigned.

These categories have different implications for safety.

A system that helps researchers identify vulnerabilities requires safeguards appropriate to sensitive technical assistance.

An autonomous agent capable of independently executing consequential actions may require additional controls over permissions, network access, and operational authority.

Treating all these cases as identical can produce poorly targeted policy.

Effective governance depends upon understanding what the system can actually do, under what conditions it can do it, and which human or institutional decisions make those actions possible.

The deeper significance of AI-assisted vulnerability discovery lies in its potential to change the economics of cybersecurity.

Traditionally, sophisticated security research has involved high costs.

Researchers require specialized training, computational infrastructure, familiarity with complex systems, and substantial time.

These costs have limited the number of individuals and organizations able to conduct advanced vulnerability investigations.

If AI substantially reduces the expertise or time required to identify weaknesses, the cost of discovering vulnerabilities could decline.

This creates two opposing possibilities.

Defenders may become capable of examining software more comprehensively and repairing problems that would otherwise remain hidden.

Attackers may also gain access to capabilities that allow them to identify targets more efficiently.

The resulting outcome depends upon which side can translate technological capability into effective action more quickly.

It is therefore misleading to assume that better vulnerability discovery automatically produces better cybersecurity.

Discovering a weakness is only the beginning of the defensive process.

Software maintainers must understand the flaw, develop a reliable correction, evaluate whether the correction creates additional problems, and distribute the update.

Organizations must then install the update across their systems.

In many environments, this final stage can be slow and difficult.

Critical services may rely upon legacy software that cannot easily be replaced. Systems may require extensive testing before updates can be deployed. Smaller organizations may lack dedicated security personnel.

Even when a vulnerability has been identified and corrected by its developer, users may remain exposed because the relevant patch has not been installed.

Advanced AI could therefore accelerate vulnerability discovery faster than institutions can accelerate remediation.

This possibility creates a serious strategic problem.

If thousands of previously unknown weaknesses become identifiable within a relatively short period, software maintainers may struggle to prioritize and repair them.

A growing inventory of known vulnerabilities could increase risk rather than reduce it if attackers gain access to the information before defensive updates are widely implemented.

The challenge is not simply to discover more weaknesses.

It is to increase the entire system's capacity to repair them.

This requires a broader approach to cybersecurity infrastructure.

Software developers need effective methods for receiving vulnerability reports, evaluating severity, coordinating disclosure, and distributing reliable patches.

Organizations responsible for deploying software need accurate inventories of their systems and clear procedures for installing important updates.

Public institutions may need additional resources to maintain essential technologies that are no longer adequately supported by vendors.

Open-source projects deserve particular attention.

Much of the internet depends upon software maintained by communities of developers, sometimes with limited financial resources.

These projects provide enormous public value by enabling shared innovation and supporting widely used technical infrastructure.

However, their maintainers may lack the time, equipment, or institutional support required to respond rapidly to large numbers of sophisticated vulnerability reports.

If AI systems begin identifying weaknesses throughout widely used open-source components, the burden of remediation could fall disproportionately upon developers who already face substantial demands.

This raises an important question of fairness.

Organizations that benefit commercially from shared software should not assume that volunteer maintainers will absorb the full cost of securing it against increasingly advanced threats.

Financial support, technical assistance, and coordinated security programs may be necessary to ensure that open-source infrastructure remains resilient.

The benefits of automated vulnerability discovery will be limited if the institutions responsible for repairing software cannot keep pace.

A coordinated defensive initiative should therefore include resources for remediation rather than concentrating exclusively upon the prestige of discovering impressive flaws.

The importance of coordinated disclosure also increases as AI accelerates security research.

When a previously unknown vulnerability is discovered, immediate public release can create opportunities for exploitation before affected organizations have time to respond.

However, withholding information indefinitely can leave users unaware of continuing risks.

Responsible disclosure requires balancing these competing concerns through communication between researchers, software maintainers, and relevant security organizations.

Advanced AI may increase both the volume and complexity of discoveries entering this process.

Consequently, disclosure procedures may need to become more standardized, efficient, and capable of managing large quantities of information.

Automation could assist with identifying affected components, organizing reports, and supporting developers as they investigate possible corrections.

Nevertheless, important decisions concerning disclosure timing and public risk should remain subject to accountable human judgment.

A system that identifies vulnerabilities does not automatically possess the institutional authority to determine when sensitive information should become public.

This distinction reflects a broader principle: technical capability should not be confused with legitimate decision-making authority.

Artificial intelligence may provide information that improves cybersecurity decisions, but the social consequences of those decisions require human responsibility.

This becomes especially important when vulnerabilities affect essential infrastructure.

The software supporting electricity networks, hospitals, transportation systems, and financial institutions can be deeply interconnected.

A weakness within a widely used component may have consequences far beyond ordinary data theft.

Disruption to essential services can affect public health, economic activity, and physical safety.

Therefore, the discovery of serious vulnerabilities in critical infrastructure should trigger carefully coordinated responses involving relevant operators, government agencies, and software providers.

Such coordination must protect sensitive information while enabling timely defensive action.

It also requires recognizing that cybersecurity cannot be delegated entirely to individual organizations.

When the failure of one system can disrupt services used by millions of people, the public has a legitimate interest in minimum security standards and reliable incident-response capacity.

Governments consequently have a role in establishing expectations for critical infrastructure protection.

However, regulation should not rely exclusively upon fixed technical requirements that become obsolete as threats evolve.

A more adaptable framework would emphasize risk assessment, secure development practices, vulnerability management, incident reporting, and independent evaluation.

Organizations should be expected to demonstrate that they can identify important weaknesses and respond within timeframes appropriate to their potential consequences.

The increasing capabilities of AI-assisted security tools may justify revisiting what constitutes reasonable defensive practice.

A standard considered adequate when vulnerability discovery required extensive manual effort may become insufficient when more advanced techniques are widely available.

This does not mean that every organization should be required to deploy the most expensive technologies.

It means that security expectations must evolve alongside the capabilities available to potential attackers.

The emergence of powerful cybersecurity AI also raises difficult questions about international cooperation.

Digital infrastructure crosses national borders, and vulnerabilities in widely used software can affect organizations in numerous countries simultaneously.

A weakness discovered by researchers in one jurisdiction may threaten systems operating under entirely different legal and political conditions.

Uncoordinated national responses can create delays, conflicting disclosure requirements, or unequal access to protective information.

International mechanisms for sharing verified vulnerability information could therefore become increasingly important.

Such cooperation should include technical standards, secure communication channels, and procedures for assisting institutions with limited defensive capacity.

However, international cybersecurity cooperation is complicated by geopolitical competition.

Governments may regard advanced vulnerability discovery as a strategic capability with intelligence or military implications.

A state possessing technology that can identify weaknesses in foreign systems may be reluctant to share its most powerful tools or findings.

The same capabilities useful for protecting domestic infrastructure could also become valuable for offensive cyber operations.

This creates a tension between national security incentives and the collective interest in secure digital systems.

A country may benefit in the short term from retaining knowledge of vulnerabilities in another country's infrastructure, even though the widespread persistence of such weaknesses increases global insecurity.

The challenge resembles other problems involving dual-use technologies: states must establish sufficient cooperation to reduce shared risks without ignoring legitimate security concerns.

A comprehensive solution may be difficult, but the absence of perfect international agreement should not prevent narrower forms of collaboration.

Countries and technical organizations can cooperate on protecting widely used software, strengthening vulnerability reporting, and improving defensive capabilities in sectors where disruption would have severe humanitarian consequences.

Such initiatives could help establish cybersecurity as a shared component of international stability.

The question of who should receive access to highly capable security AI remains particularly contentious.

Unrestricted public release could support research and democratize technical knowledge, but it may also increase the accessibility of capabilities that facilitate serious misuse.

Restricting access to a small group of corporations and government agencies may reduce some immediate risks while creating concerns about unequal power and insufficient accountability.

Neither approach is universally appropriate.

A more defensible model would match access permissions to the risks associated with particular capabilities.

Lower-risk analytical tools could be made widely available for education and defensive research.

Capabilities with greater potential for harmful application could be provided through controlled environments, verified institutional access, or supervised research partnerships.

Such arrangements should be regularly reviewed as evidence develops.

Access controls should not become permanent mechanisms for protecting commercial monopolies or excluding legitimate researchers.

Their purpose should be to manage demonstrable security risks while supporting beneficial use.

Independent oversight could help evaluate whether restrictions remain proportionate and whether defensive opportunities are being distributed fairly.

This approach recognizes that technological power and public responsibility must develop together.

An additional concern is the possibility that AI-assisted security research may create an escalating competition between attackers and defenders.

As defensive tools become more capable, malicious actors may adopt similar technologies to search for weaknesses that remain unresolved.

Defenders may respond by deploying more sophisticated automated monitoring and vulnerability analysis.

This cycle could increase the speed at which both attacks and protective measures evolve.

Such competition is not entirely new. Cybersecurity has long involved continuous adaptation between competing capabilities.

However, artificial intelligence may compress the time available for human response.

Organizations accustomed to addressing vulnerabilities over weeks or months may face greater pressure to identify and repair serious weaknesses rapidly.

This possibility reinforces the importance of preventive security architecture.

Systems should not depend upon every vulnerability being discovered and corrected before exploitation becomes possible.

Layered defenses, restricted permissions, network segmentation, and resilient recovery procedures can reduce the consequences of individual failures.

The objective should be to make compromise more difficult and limit its impact even when software defects remain undiscovered.

This principle also challenges the assumption that AI-driven vulnerability discovery will eventually eliminate cybersecurity problems.

Software systems are continuously changing.

Developers release new applications, update existing components, and connect technologies in unfamiliar ways. Every significant change can introduce new interactions and potential weaknesses.

Even if AI becomes exceptionally effective at examining software, security will remain an ongoing process rather than a final condition.

Furthermore, vulnerabilities do not arise exclusively from programming errors.

Misconfigured systems, stolen credentials, inadequate access controls, social engineering, and organizational failures can all undermine security.

Advanced code analysis may improve one important dimension of defense without resolving every source of cyber risk.

A comprehensive strategy must therefore combine automated analysis with secure organizational practices and human judgment.

For ordinary users, this broader understanding has practical implications.

Individuals cannot independently inspect the operating systems and applications they use, nor can they reasonably be expected to understand the technical details of newly discovered vulnerabilities.

Their security depends partly upon the quality of software development and the responsiveness of institutions providing digital services.

Nevertheless, personal security practices remain important.

Keeping devices and applications updated can reduce exposure to known weaknesses. Strong authentication practices can limit unauthorized access to accounts. Replacing unsupported equipment can prevent continued dependence upon systems that no longer receive essential security corrections.

These measures do not guarantee protection against sophisticated threats.

Their value lies in reducing common vulnerabilities and limiting the consequences of preventable failures.

The increasing sophistication of AI-assisted attacks should therefore encourage ordinary users to maintain sound security habits rather than conclude that personal precautions have become meaningless.

However, placing the burden entirely upon individuals would be unjustified.

Users should not be expected to compensate for insecure product design or inadequate vendor support.

Companies providing digital services have responsibilities to develop secure products, communicate important risks, and distribute timely updates.

Governments and regulators have responsibilities to establish appropriate standards where failures can cause substantial public harm.

The growth of advanced cybersecurity AI makes these institutional duties more urgent.

Another important question concerns the relationship between cybersecurity and public trust.

Digital services function because users believe that their personal information, financial transactions, and essential communications will receive reasonable protection.

Major security incidents can damage this confidence.

When personal records are exposed or essential services disrupted, the consequences may include financial loss, identity misuse, emotional distress, and reduced willingness to rely upon digital institutions.

These harms cannot be understood solely through technical descriptions of compromised systems.

A stolen database may contain information about people's private lives, medical histories, or financial circumstances.

An interrupted service may affect individuals who depend upon it for employment, healthcare, or basic daily activities.

Cybersecurity is therefore not simply a contest between technical specialists.

It is a matter of human welfare.

The potential of advanced AI to identify long-hidden weaknesses should be evaluated partly according to whether it helps prevent these real-world harms.

A technological demonstration may be impressive, but its public value depends upon whether discoveries lead to stronger protections.

This distinction is especially important when companies announce extraordinary capabilities.

The number of vulnerabilities discovered does not by itself measure the success of a defensive initiative.

A more meaningful assessment would consider how many serious weaknesses were responsibly reported, how effectively they were corrected, and whether affected organizations were able to deploy protections.

It would also examine whether security improvements reached public institutions and smaller organizations rather than remaining concentrated among influential partners.

These measures connect technical achievement to social benefit.

The ultimate purpose of defensive cybersecurity is not to produce an impressive inventory of vulnerabilities.

It is to reduce the likelihood and severity of harmful incidents.

This emphasis on outcomes should guide both public policy and corporate responsibility.

The philosophical implications of AI-assisted cybersecurity are also significant.

For much of computing history, technological security has depended upon a relationship between human intelligence and the complexity of engineered systems.

Humans create software, but the interactions within large programs can become too complicated for any individual to understand completely.

Security researchers attempt to identify the consequences of this complexity, while attackers search for opportunities hidden within it.

Artificial intelligence introduces a new form of analytical capability into this relationship.

Machines may become increasingly effective at examining complexity generated by human engineering.

This could strengthen security by revealing weaknesses that would otherwise remain invisible.

Yet it also means that the obscurity of a vulnerability may no longer provide the same practical protection against discovery.

A defect that previously remained hidden because it required decades of accumulated human investigation might become identifiable through sufficiently capable automated analysis.

The significance is not that secrecy or complexity ever constituted reliable security.

It is that technological limitations have sometimes delayed the discovery of weaknesses, even when those weaknesses were theoretically accessible.

As these limitations diminish, software systems may face more intensive scrutiny from both authorized researchers and malicious actors.

This development could encourage a beneficial transformation in engineering culture.

Developers may place greater emphasis on designing systems that remain secure under sustained examination rather than relying upon the assumption that obscure weaknesses will go unnoticed.

Security testing could become more continuous, and vulnerability discovery could become integrated more closely into software development.

However, achieving this transformation requires investment.

Organizations must possess the resources to analyze findings, repair defects, and verify that corrections are effective.

Without that institutional capacity, accelerated discovery may simply expose the depth of existing technical debt.

The broader lesson is that intelligence alone cannot guarantee security.

A highly capable AI model may reveal weaknesses, but it cannot ensure that organizations have the authority, resources, or willingness to repair them.

Technological progress must therefore be accompanied by improvements in governance and organizational preparedness.

This is particularly important because the private sector controls much of the infrastructure upon which public institutions depend.

Major technology companies develop operating systems, cloud platforms, communication services, and software components used throughout society.

Their security decisions have consequences for governments, businesses, and individuals who may possess limited ability to influence those decisions.

When advanced AI becomes capable of examining this infrastructure at extraordinary scale, the governance of that capability becomes a public concern.

The legitimacy of access decisions should not depend exclusively upon corporate discretion.

Companies possess valuable technical expertise and may act responsibly, but they should remain subject to appropriate scrutiny when their decisions affect widespread digital security.

Independent evaluation, structured cooperation, and clear accountability can help align private innovation with public protection.

At the same time, policymakers must avoid responding to advanced AI capabilities through indiscriminate restrictions.

Cybersecurity research depends upon the ability to investigate vulnerabilities, reproduce failures, and communicate findings.

Excessively broad rules could discourage legitimate researchers and reduce opportunities for discovering weaknesses before attackers exploit them.

Responsible regulation should therefore distinguish authorized security research from malicious activity.

It should also encourage controlled experimentation, ethical disclosure, and cooperation with affected software providers.

The objective is to strengthen defensive capacity rather than suppress technical inquiry.

A balanced framework must acknowledge that the same capability can be beneficial or harmful depending upon how it is governed.

This principle extends to the broader development of artificial intelligence.

Powerful AI systems are increasingly capable of performing tasks once associated with highly trained professionals.

Their benefits may include accelerated scientific research, improved engineering, and more effective public services.

However, the reduction of expertise barriers can also make specialized harmful activities more accessible.

The resulting risks cannot always be addressed through the model's behavior alone.

They may require controls over tools, permissions, infrastructure, and access to sensitive capabilities.

Cybersecurity offers a particularly clear illustration because the consequences of technical assistance can be immediate and substantial.

A model capable of identifying serious software weaknesses is not necessarily dangerous in isolation.

Its impact depends upon the surrounding environment, the objectives of users, and the safeguards governing what can be done with its outputs.

This systems-based understanding should become central to AI governance.

The most important question is not simply how intelligent a model becomes.

It is how that intelligence interacts with institutional authority and real-world capabilities.

As these interactions become more powerful, accountability must become more precise.

Organizations developing advanced AI should be able to explain the capabilities they have evaluated, the safeguards they have established, and the procedures used to manage significant risks.

Institutions deploying such systems should understand the permissions granted to them and the potential consequences of their actions.

Regulators should possess sufficient expertise to assess whether these arrangements are credible.

Public communication should distinguish verified findings from uncertain claims and avoid sensational narratives that obscure practical responsibilities.

Together, these measures can help create an environment in which technological progress supports security rather than undermining it.

Ultimately, the emergence of advanced AI systems capable of sophisticated vulnerability discovery represents a turning point in the history of cybersecurity.

The significance of this development lies not merely in the technical sophistication of individual models, but in the possibility that highly specialized security analysis could become faster, cheaper, and more widely accessible.

This transformation creates extraordinary defensive opportunities.

Weaknesses that have remained hidden for years may be identified and corrected. Software developers may gain access to forms of analysis previously beyond their resources. Critical infrastructure may become more resilient through earlier recognition of serious defects.

Yet the same capabilities could increase the efficiency of malicious activity if access is poorly governed or defensive institutions fail to respond.

The outcome will not be determined by technological capability alone.

It will depend upon the relationship between discovery and repair, commercial innovation and public accountability, national security and international cooperation, and restricted access and equitable defensive benefit.

A future in which advanced AI continuously reveals software weaknesses does not necessarily have to be a future of greater insecurity.

It could instead encourage a more rigorous and transparent culture of software engineering.

But achieving that outcome requires society to recognize that the ability to discover vulnerabilities is not the same as the capacity to eliminate them.

The hardest task may be institutional rather than computational.

Governments, technology companies, researchers, and infrastructure operators must develop systems capable of responding to discoveries at a pace comparable to the technologies producing them.

They must also ensure that powerful capabilities are governed through legitimate rules rather than concentrated discretion.

The central ethical principle should be that technologies capable of transforming collective security must be managed according to responsibilities proportionate to their consequences.

Advanced cybersecurity AI should not be treated simply as a commercial product whose distribution is determined by market opportunity.

Nor should it be treated as an uncontrollable force whose emergence makes human governance irrelevant.

It is a powerful technological capability whose effects will depend upon deliberate choices.

The future of digital security will be shaped by whether those choices encourage cooperation, accountability, and practical resilience.

The most important achievement will not be creating an AI system capable of finding every hidden weakness in the world's software.

It will be building a cybersecurity order capable of ensuring that such discoveries make society safer rather than more vulnerable.

As artificial intelligence expands the power to uncover the hidden defects of modern technology, it also exposes a deeper truth: the greatest weakness in digital civilization may not be a particular line of software code, but the failure of institutions to coordinate the protection of systems upon which everyone depends.

The age of automated vulnerability discovery therefore demands more than stronger machines. It demands stronger public institutions, clearer responsibilities, and a shared commitment to protecting the digital foundations of everyday life.

Only when the capacity to repair and defend advances alongside the capacity to discover and exploit will artificial intelligence fulfill its promise as an instrument of collective cybersecurity rather than a source of expanding systemic risk.

14. Claude Mythos and Project Glasswing: why an AI superhacker has the tech world on alert

1. Title of the Work

The Locksmith Who Knows Every Lock: Who Should Hold AI’s Master Keys?

2. Creative Work

Picture a locksmith of almost supernatural talent. Shown any door in the city, whether a bank vault, a hospital pharmacy, or the back entrance of a power station, she can find within minutes the tiny flaw that will let it swing open. Some of those flaws have gone unnoticed for decades, hidden in locks that millions of people trusted every day. Now imagine that this locksmith’s skill can be copied and handed to anyone. Whether the city becomes safer or more dangerous depends entirely on whose hands receive it first, and on whether someone is watching how it is used.

That is no longer a fantasy. AI developers now report models able to search the vast, hidden layers of software that run the modern world, including operating systems, web browsers, network equipment, and shared open-source code, and to uncover serious security flaws at a speed and scale no human team could match. One company recently announced such a model and then declined to release it to the public, sharing it instead with a group of major technology firms, open-source organizations, and financial institutions so they could find and fix weaknesses before attackers gained similar tools. This approach is a reasonable first step. But it cannot be the last. When a private company alone decides who may use a tool that could expose the foundations of global infrastructure, society is relying too heavily on trust. We need independent verification, public oversight, and shared rules for how such capabilities are governed, while every organization and individual takes their own security far more seriously.

The first point to grasp is how deeply these tools could change the economics of cybersecurity. Until now, many dangerous flaws have stayed hidden simply because finding them was difficult. It required rare expertise, patience, and long hours spent examining obscure code. That difficulty acted as an invisible shield. If AI can perform the same work automatically and at enormous scale, the shield disappears. What was once the craft of a few elite specialists could become a routine process available to anyone with access to the right system. The software involved is not limited to computers and phones. It quietly supports electricity grids, water systems, hospitals, airlines, banks, and shops. A flaw in a widely shared piece of code can ripple outward into countless services people never realize depend on it.

The consequences of such failures are not abstract. Large data breaches have already exposed the personal details, and in some cases the medical histories, of millions of people at a time, leaving them vulnerable to fraud and humiliation. Those incidents turned technical weaknesses into crises of privacy and public trust. A world where vulnerabilities can be discovered faster than they can be repaired would make such crises more frequent and more severe.

Seen in that light, keeping a powerful model away from the public and giving defenders a head start makes sense. If the capability is coming regardless, it is better for software makers to patch their systems before criminals and hostile states acquire comparable tools. Responsible disclosure, which means quietly informing developers of a flaw before announcing it, is a long-standing principle of security research, and applying it at this scale is sensible.

Yet the same arrangement raises uncomfortable questions. Most of the evidence supporting the company’s claims cannot be examined by outsiders, partly because unpatched flaws must remain secret. The public is being asked to accept, largely on faith, both that the model is as capable as described and that the safeguards around it are adequate. History offers reasons for caution. AI companies have announced before that a model was too dangerous to release, and such announcements can serve marketing goals as well as safety ones, signaling power while projecting responsibility. Neither motive makes the claims false, but both mean they deserve independent scrutiny.

A deeper problem concerns who decides. Today, decisions about which organizations count as trustworthy recipients of such tools are made by the companies that build them. A small circle of large firms and financial institutions may gain early protection, while smaller businesses, public agencies, hospitals, and organizations in poorer countries wait their turn, even though they often run the most fragile systems. Defining the “right hands” for a technology with such broad public consequences should not be a private choice.

Some will argue that government involvement would slow down urgent defensive work, and that companies understand their own technology far better than regulators do. Speed and expertise matter, but oversight need not mean bureaucracy. Independent technical bodies can be given confidential access to verify capabilities and audit safeguards, much as aviation and nuclear regulators examine sensitive systems without publishing every detail. Clear public criteria for access, mandatory reporting of serious incidents, and international cooperation on handling discovered flaws would strengthen trust without paralyzing progress.

There is also a role for everyone else. Organizations that have long treated security as an afterthought must now treat it as a core duty, investing in rapid patching, replacing outdated systems, and testing their own defenses. Individuals can do their part through simple habits: keeping devices and software updated, retiring unsupported equipment, using password managers, turning on multi-factor authentication, and never ignoring security updates. These steps will not stop a determined state-sponsored attacker, but they close many of the easy doors through which most attacks enter.

The gifted locksmith in our imagined city is now real, and her skills will not stay rare for long. The question is not whether such tools will exist, but who will hold them, under what rules, and with whose oversight. Leaving that answer entirely to the companies that build them would be a gamble with the infrastructure we all share. A safer future depends on opening the decision to public scrutiny while there is still time to set the terms.

Anthropic, the company that built the model in this article, is also the company that made me. I tried to keep the essay as balanced as the original, which is why it argues for independent scrutiny of the company’s claims.

1. Title of the Work

**The Algorithmic Locksmith: Surviving the Industrialization of Cyber-Exploitation**

2. Creative Work

Modern civilization rests upon an invisible, precarious foundation. The global economy, our critical infrastructure, and our most intimate personal data are all supported by an underlying architecture of ancient, deeply layered code. For decades, we have implicitly trusted this digital concrete, largely because the effort required to find its structural fractures was immense. Discovering a zero-day vulnerability in the internet’s plumbing demanded rare human genius, relentless patience, and significant time. However, the emergence of hyper-capable artificial intelligence has violently inverted this dynamic. We are no longer defending against the artisanal hacker; we are facing the industrialization of cyber-exploitation, and our foundational security paradigms are entirely obsolete.

The sheer scale of this new algorithmic capability defies traditional containment. Recent developments have proven that advanced AI models can systematically scan and dismantle the hidden plumbing of the digital world with terrifying efficiency. In a stark demonstration of this power, an AI recently unearthed a 27-year-old flaw in a security-focused operating system and a 16-year-old vulnerability in a ubiquitous multimedia framework, while also proving capable of chaining together obscure kernel bugs to seize complete control of a machine. By automating the discovery of foundational flaws at an unprecedented scale, these algorithmic locksmiths have fundamentally changed the economics of cybersecurity. What was once a slow, methodical search for weaknesses is now a frictionless, automated sweep.

Faced with the apocalyptic potential of a truly autonomous superhacker, the architects of this technology have predictably opted for a fortress mentality. By restricting public access and forming elite, closed-door coalitions with major tech and financial conglomerates, they aim to preemptively patch these newly discovered vulnerabilities before malicious actors can acquire similar capabilities. While this defensive mobilization is a necessary triage, it is not a permanent solution. It forces the global public into a deeply uncomfortable position of blind trust, as the vast majority of these uncovered software flaws remain fiercely guarded secrets pending their repair. We are now entirely dependent on the benevolence and efficiency of corporate titans to shield us from the very digital weapons they willed into existence.

We must recognize that the stakes of this new arms race are profoundly human. A vulnerability in an operating system is never merely a technical abstraction; it is the open door through which our lives are plundered. The recent history of massive cyberattacks—where the theft of millions of personal databases and sensitive health records resulted in the devastating extortion of private citizens—demonstrates that software failures inevitably metastasize into crises of identity, privacy, and safety. When the invisible software that underpins our hospitals, electrical grids, and banking systems is subjected to algorithmic scrutiny, the potential for catastrophic real-world harm is limitless.

The era of passive digital tenancy is over. The automated locksmith has arrived, and it is only a matter of time before its capabilities are replicated by those who wish to do us harm. Cybersecurity can no longer be outsourced as "someone else’s problem." The immediate defense requires militant, uncompromising cyber hygiene from every individual—relentlessly updating devices, replacing unsupported hardware, and universally adopting multi-factor authentication. But beyond the firewall, we must aggressively demand structural oversight. The future of our digital safety depends entirely on how society chooses to govern these algorithmic weapons, and who we ultimately trust to hold the keys.
