21. Featuring Trump on US coins and bills would put America in rare company

1. Title of the Work

The Face in Your Pocket: Why Republics Keep Living Leaders Off Their Money

2. Creative Work

In the 1860s, an official in charge of the United States’ currency office made a decision that would echo for more than a century and a half. When the government issued a new five-cent paper note, the portrait that appeared on it was his own. Lawmakers were furious. A mid-level bureaucrat had quietly placed his face on money that passed through millions of American hands. In response, Congress passed a law banning the portraits of living persons from the nation’s paper currency. The episode is often remembered as a historical curiosity, but the principle behind it runs much deeper than one man’s vanity.

Money is among the most intimate and universal symbols a state produces. Citizens carry it in their wallets, exchange it at markets, and hand it to their children. The images it bears quietly tell a story about who the nation is and whom it honors. That is why the choice of whose face appears on currency matters far more than it might seem. Around the world, the practice of putting a sitting leader on national money is overwhelmingly the habit of hereditary monarchies, where the ruler embodies the state. Republics, by contrast, have long resisted it, honoring founders, artists, scientists, and the departed instead. That restraint is not an accident or mere tradition. It expresses a core republican principle: power belongs to the people and is only lent to those who temporarily hold office. Republics should keep that line firmly in place.

History shows how closely the portrait of a living ruler has been tied to the idea of personal power. In ancient Rome, the republic’s coins traditionally depicted gods, symbols, or long-dead ancestors. Julius Caesar is widely recognized as the first living Roman to appear on the city’s coins, an innovation that alarmed many who feared he was becoming a king in all but name. Within months he was assassinated, and the emperors who followed made their own faces a permanent feature of Roman money. The image on the coin became a declaration that the state and the ruler were one.

Modern patterns follow a similar logic. Surveys of the world’s coins and banknotes show that sitting heads of state appear on currency in only a small minority of countries, and nearly all of those are hereditary monarchies. In kingdoms both democratic and authoritarian, it is common to see the reigning monarch on coins and notes, because the crown is meant to represent the continuity of the nation itself. In republics, the sitting president or prime minister almost never appears. The rare exceptions tend to be countries whose political culture retains strong elements of hereditary or traditional authority. The global consensus is striking: where leaders are chosen by citizens and expected to leave office, their faces stay off the money while they hold power.

Why should that consensus matter? Because symbols shape expectations. When a sitting leader’s face appears on the currency that every citizen uses daily, the message is that this person is not merely an official carrying out a temporary job but a figure whose identity is fused with the nation. That message sits uneasily with the basic promise of a republic, which is that leaders are servants of the public, accountable to voters and to the law, and replaceable through peaceful elections. Founding generations in several republics were acutely aware of this. In the early United States, lawmakers debated whether to put the president’s portrait on coins and rejected the idea in favor of an allegorical figure of Liberty, partly because the practice was associated with European monarchies they had just broken away from.

Supporters of honoring a sitting leader on currency make several arguments. They may say that the leader has achieved something historic, that voters freely elected the person and so honoring them reflects the public will, or that commemorative coins are harmless souvenirs with little political meaning. Others point out that democracies such as the United Kingdom place their monarch on money without any threat to their freedoms. These points deserve a fair hearing. Achievements can be real, and commemorations can be harmless. But the timing matters. A republic can honor its leaders generously after they leave office, when history has had time to judge their record and when the honor no longer reinforces their current power. The British example actually supports the principle, because the monarch’s portrait reflects a hereditary role that is deliberately separate from the elected government. In a republic, there is no such separation. The person in office is the political leader, and placing their image on money blurs the distinction between holding power and personifying the state.

Laws and norms that keep living leaders off currency also protect against a quieter danger: the gradual drift from respect for an office toward devotion to an individual. Few people would mistake a single coin for the end of democracy. But political cultures change through many small steps, each defended as harmless. Names on buildings, portraits in public spaces, branding on official documents, and finally faces on money can together create an atmosphere in which loyalty to the leader begins to replace loyalty to the constitution. Guardrails are most valuable when they are maintained before anyone feels threatened.

The practical course is simple. Republics should keep and respect laws that prohibit the portraits of living people on circulating currency. Commemorations of leaders should wait until their time in office has ended, and ideally until history has had a chance to weigh their legacy. And citizens should treat currency design not as a trivial matter of taste but as part of the shared symbolic language of self-government.

The official who put his own face on a nineteenth-century banknote probably saw his decision as a minor indulgence. Lawmakers saw something more important at stake. Money belongs to the public, and the faces it carries should remind citizens of the nation they share, not the person who governs them for a season. A republic that keeps its living leaders off its money is making a quiet but powerful statement: in this country, no one owns the state, and every officeholder will someday hand it back.

The original is about a current debate over a sitting U.S. president, so I based the essay on the general principle and history and didn’t argue about him directly. Supporters of the proposal would say an elected leader’s historic achievements deserve recognition, that commemorative coins are symbolic and not a threat, and that the choice should be left to Congress and voters.

1. Title of the Work

**The Sovereign's Canvas: Minting the Monarch in a Modern Republic**

2. Creative Work

National currency is arguably the most pervasive public monument a society can build. Every coin and banknote circulating through the veins of an economy acts as a miniature, tactile ambassador of a nation's values, history, and collective identity. For this reason, modern democracies have overwhelmingly adopted a steadfast rule: the faces that adorn their physical wealth belong strictly to the dead. By reserving these honors for historical figures, a republic ensures that its money celebrates enduring national ideals rather than the fleeting, partisan ambitions of the present. When a sitting leader attempts to shatter this convention by stamping their own visage onto public tender, it is not merely a breach of aesthetic tradition; it is a profound and deliberate subversion of the democratic ethos, signaling an ambition that aligns far more closely with autocracy than with public service.

The ongoing campaign to etch a sitting American president onto the nation’s currency—specifically through proposed $1 coins, a new $250 bill, and grandiose gold commemoratives—represents a chilling departure from the foundational principles of the republic. This is not a passive evolution of design, but a forceful political maneuver that requires the dismantling of institutional safeguards. The sheer aggression of this vanity project is evidenced by the punitive reassignment of federal treasury officials who dared to resist the creation of a $250 banknote, citing the 160-year-old legal prohibition against depicting living individuals on paper money. When the machinery of the state is weaponized to bypass historical constraints for the sake of a leader's self-aggrandizement, the currency ceases to belong to the people and becomes the exclusive propaganda of the executive.

To understand the gravity of this transgression, one must look at the global context of numismatic iconography. A comprehensive survey of the world’s circulating coins and banknotes reveals a stark and undeniable reality: the practice of featuring a sitting head of state on active currency is almost entirely the exclusive domain of hereditary monarchies. From absolute kingdoms to constitutional crowns, placing the sovereign on the coin is a declaration of divine or lifelong right. Conversely, among nations that do not possess a hereditary monarchy, the practice is virtually non-existent, with only the rarest of culturally specific exceptions. Therefore, for a constitutional republic to suddenly adopt this visual language is to deliberately embrace the aesthetics of a king.

This visual shift carries profound philosophical weight. A republic is built on the premise that its leaders are temporary stewards of power, subject to the will of the electorate and bound by the limits of time. When a living politician demands to be immortalized on the almighty dollar, they are attempting to cement a cult of personality into the bedrock of the economy itself. It is an act of psychological dominance, forcing every citizen—regardless of their political affiliation—to physically handle and trade the leader's image in order to survive in the marketplace.

Ultimately, the fierce public backlash against these numismatic ambitions, manifesting in nationwide protests against perceived monarchical overreach, is entirely justified. The face on a nation's currency tells the story of who holds the true power. If a democracy allows its money to become a mirror for the ego of a sitting ruler, it concedes the fundamental principle that no individual is larger than the state. A true republic must guard its mint as fiercely as it guards its ballot boxes, ensuring that the wealth of the nation never becomes the personal canvas of a would-be sovereign.

22. Five hidden pitfalls of fitness tracking

## 1. Title of the Work

# When Health Becomes a Score: Why Fitness Technology Must Serve Human Wellbeing Rather Than Control It

## 2. Creative Work

Modern society has become increasingly fascinated with the possibility of measuring human health. Smartwatches, mobile applications, and wearable sensors promise to transform everyday experiences into meaningful information about physical activity, sleep, energy expenditure, and personal fitness. What was once assessed through bodily sensations, habits, and occasional medical consultations can now be represented through continuously updated charts, numerical scores, and automated recommendations. These technologies offer genuine opportunities to improve health. They can help individuals recognize patterns of inactivity, establish exercise routines, and develop greater awareness of their physical behavior. Yet their growing influence also raises a fundamental question: does measuring health necessarily make people healthier? When devices convert complex human experiences into simplified targets, they can encourage users to treat numerical achievement as more important than physical wellbeing itself. A missed target may become a source of guilt, rest may be interpreted as failure, and movement may lose its intrinsic pleasure. The central challenge is therefore not whether fitness tracking should exist, but whether its design supports human autonomy, realistic health goals, and sustainable habits. Fitness technology should function as a flexible instrument of self-understanding rather than an authority that dictates how every body must behave.

The appeal of fitness tracking begins with a reasonable desire for greater knowledge. Many aspects of physical health are difficult to evaluate through immediate experience alone. People may underestimate how much time they spend sitting, overestimate the intensity of their exercise, or struggle to recognize patterns across busy weeks.

Wearable devices offer a convenient way to observe certain aspects of these behaviors.

A daily activity record can reveal periods of prolonged inactivity. A reminder can encourage someone to leave a desk and move briefly. A record of walking or cycling may help a beginner recognize improvements that would otherwise seem insignificant.

Such information can contribute to motivation and support healthier routines.

However, the benefits of measurement depend upon how information is presented and interpreted.

A device that simply records movement differs from one that continually evaluates the user against predefined standards. The latter does not merely describe behavior; it attempts to influence it.

Notifications, progress rings, achievement badges, streaks, and daily targets are designed to shape decisions. They encourage individuals to repeat certain activities and avoid others.

These features can be helpful when they support appropriate goals.

They become problematic when they treat the device's numerical objectives as universally desirable, regardless of the user's circumstances.

This distinction reveals why fitness trackers are not neutral observers of human behavior.

Their interfaces contain assumptions about what constitutes progress, which activities deserve recognition, and how users should respond when expectations are not met.

A device that celebrates increasing step counts may encourage walking.

It may also imply that more steps are always preferable, even when an individual needs rest or would benefit more from a different form of exercise.

The problem is not measurement itself.

It is the transformation of a limited measurement into an apparently comprehensive judgment about health.

A step count can describe a particular kind of movement.

It cannot determine whether a person's overall activity pattern is appropriate, whether their muscles have recovered, or whether they are experiencing excessive physical strain.

When users forget this limitation, a convenient number can acquire authority beyond its actual meaning.

The widespread influence of daily step targets illustrates the problem.

A numerical goal that originated from commercial promotion has become deeply embedded in contemporary fitness culture. Many people treat it as a standard that responsible individuals should satisfy, despite the absence of a universal biological threshold separating adequate from inadequate movement.

Research suggests that meaningful health benefits can occur at different activity levels, including amounts below commonly promoted targets.

The relationship between physical activity and wellbeing is gradual and influenced by individual circumstances.

A person who increases daily walking from a very low level may experience valuable improvements without reaching a conventional benchmark.

Conversely, someone who already exercises regularly may derive limited additional benefit from accumulating steps merely to satisfy a device.

A rigid target can therefore distort the meaning of progress.

It may encourage users to overlook improvements because they remain below the prescribed number.

Someone recovering from a period of inactivity might walk substantially more than before and still receive a notification indicating failure.

The device reports the shortfall accurately according to its chosen target, but the resulting judgment may be misleading.

From the perspective of the individual's health, the day may represent genuine progress.

This reveals a fundamental distinction between numerical compliance and meaningful improvement.

Health technologies should help users recognize changes that matter within their personal circumstances rather than measuring everyone against identical expectations.

The issue becomes even clearer when considering the diversity of physical activities.

Walking is valuable, but it is only one form of movement.

Swimming, cycling, resistance training, stretching, rehabilitation exercises, and activities requiring balance or coordination can contribute to physical wellbeing in different ways.

Some of these activities are not accurately represented by conventional step counting.

A person may complete a demanding strength-training session while recording relatively few steps. Another may spend considerable time swimming or cycling without producing a movement pattern that a particular device recognizes reliably.

If the interface rewards step accumulation more visibly than other activities, users may begin to prioritize what the technology measures most easily.

This is a form of measurement bias.

The device makes certain behaviors more visible and therefore more psychologically rewarding, even though less visible activities may be equally important or more appropriate.

Over time, users may adjust their exercise choices to satisfy the tracker rather than to meet their actual fitness needs.

This reverses the intended relationship between technology and health.

Instead of using measurement to support a sensible activity plan, the individual begins organizing activity around the limitations of the measurement system.

The danger is especially pronounced when the device provides a single summary score that appears to represent overall success.

Complex health outcomes cannot be reduced reliably to one number.

Cardiovascular endurance, muscular strength, mobility, balance, psychological wellbeing, and recovery are distinct dimensions of physical capacity.

An individual can perform well in one area while needing improvement in another.

A high daily step count does not necessarily demonstrate adequate muscular strength.

A low step count does not automatically indicate an unhealthy day.

The interpretation depends upon the full context.

A person recovering from illness may benefit more from carefully controlled movement and rest than from prolonged exercise.

Someone training for a physically demanding activity may need to alternate intense sessions with recovery periods.

A person with mobility limitations may achieve important health gains through activities that produce few measurable steps.

Fitness tracking becomes misleading when such distinctions disappear behind standardized indicators.

The broader lesson is that convenient measurements should not determine which aspects of health deserve attention.

Technology should reflect the diversity of human physical needs rather than encouraging people to narrow those needs to the quantities it can record.

The psychological consequences of numerical targets deserve equal consideration.

Regular physical activity is more likely to become sustainable when individuals find reasons to enjoy it.

Some people appreciate the feeling of moving outdoors. Others value social interaction, improved strength, relaxation, or the satisfaction of developing a skill.

These experiences create forms of motivation that do not depend entirely upon external rewards.

Fitness trackers can support motivation by providing evidence of progress.

However, they can also transform movement into a task performed primarily to obtain digital approval.

A walk becomes a method of completing a progress ring.

A workout becomes an opportunity to maintain a streak.

An ordinary rest day becomes a threat to a record of consecutive achievements.

The activity's value is increasingly determined by the device's response rather than the person's experience.

This can undermine intrinsic motivation.

When exercise is enjoyable, individuals may continue participating because the experience itself is rewarding.

When movement becomes associated primarily with obligation, the activity may begin to feel burdensome.

A person may continue exercising despite fatigue because they fear losing a digital achievement.

Another may stop using the device entirely after repeated failures to reach an unrealistic target.

In both cases, a tool intended to support sustainable health behavior can produce the opposite effect.

The problem reflects a familiar tension within motivational psychology.

External rewards can encourage participation, particularly during the early stages of establishing a habit.

However, excessive dependence upon those rewards can weaken the enjoyment and personal meaning associated with the activity.

The challenge is to design encouragement without making the reward system more important than the behavior it is intended to support.

A fitness tracker should help someone appreciate progress, not persuade them that movement has no value unless the device recognizes it.

This distinction becomes particularly important when examining the emotional language of fitness interfaces.

Many devices use positive reinforcement when users achieve goals. They display celebratory graphics, congratulate successful activity, and encourage continued participation.

Such feedback can be motivating.

However, reminders concerning missed targets may create feelings of inadequacy, especially when they occur repeatedly.

A person who has been caring for a family member, recovering from an exhausting workday, or managing health difficulties may receive a message suggesting that more effort is required.

The device may not understand the circumstances that made additional activity impractical.

Its feedback can therefore appear judgmental even when the designers intended it as encouragement.

This demonstrates why automated health communication must be sensitive to context.

A notification that motivates one user may discourage another.

The same numerical target may represent a reasonable challenge for one person and an unsafe expectation for someone else.

Personalization should therefore extend beyond allowing users to enter their age, height, or weight.

It should account for different goals, abilities, experiences, and circumstances.

A person who wants to improve cardiovascular fitness may require different guidance from someone focused on rehabilitation, strength, or maintaining mobility.

A universal interface cannot fully accommodate these differences through a single default target.

The concept of a standard fitness user is itself problematic.

Human bodies vary considerably in physical capacity, health history, biological characteristics, and response to exercise.

Age, disability, pregnancy, illness, and previous activity levels can influence what forms of movement are appropriate.

Lifestyle circumstances also matter.

Some people possess flexible schedules and access to exercise facilities. Others work long hours, care for dependents, or live in environments where outdoor activity is difficult.

Treating these individuals as though they possess identical opportunities for exercise can create unrealistic expectations.

The resulting design problem is not merely technical.

It reflects assumptions about whose body and lifestyle the technology considers normal.

A tracker designed primarily around an active, able-bodied consumer may provide less useful feedback to someone whose movement patterns differ substantially.

A device that automatically emphasizes weight reduction may be inappropriate for a person whose goal is strength, recovery, or general wellbeing.

Such defaults can shape behavior even when users do not consciously choose them.

This is why apparently minor design decisions deserve ethical attention.

The first target displayed, the metrics emphasized on the home screen, and the language used in notifications all influence how users interpret their health.

A system that repeatedly rewards weight loss or increasing exercise volume may reinforce narrow assumptions about what a healthy body should look like.

For some users, these messages can encourage excessive exercise, restrictive eating, or an unhealthy preoccupation with measurements.

It is important not to assume that every fitness tracker causes such harms.

Many users benefit from tracking, and the effects depend upon personal circumstances and patterns of use.

Nevertheless, the possibility of harm should be taken seriously when designing technologies intended for widespread daily use.

The existence of potential psychological risks means that developers should evaluate more than whether a device increases measurable activity.

They should also investigate how it affects motivation, body image, emotional wellbeing, and long-term behavior.

A product that increases step counts while contributing to harmful anxiety cannot automatically be considered an unqualified success.

Health technologies should be assessed according to broader outcomes than the metrics they are designed to maximize.

This principle becomes especially important when devices incorporate measurements associated with body size.

Body mass index, for example, is a widely used population-level indicator derived from height and weight.

It can provide useful information in certain contexts, but it does not directly measure body composition or the distribution of muscle and fat.

Its interpretation may therefore be limited for particular individuals.

When fitness applications treat such indicators as complete judgments about personal health, they risk encouraging simplistic or misleading conclusions.

A muscular person may receive feedback that fails to reflect their body composition.

Someone with a medical condition affecting weight may be encouraged toward an objective that does not correspond to their immediate health priorities.

The problem arises when a general measurement is presented as an individualized diagnosis.

Fitness trackers are not inherently equipped to evaluate every aspect of medical risk.

Their sensors and algorithms operate within specific technical limits.

Users should therefore understand the difference between a device's measurement and a professional assessment of health.

A watch may estimate energy expenditure or aerobic fitness using available data, but those estimates involve assumptions.

Their accuracy can vary according to the device, the activity, and the characteristics of the user.

An algorithmic estimate should not automatically override bodily symptoms or individualized medical advice.

This is especially important when people encounter unfamiliar fitness indicators.

Terms such as maximal oxygen uptake, recovery score, or training readiness may appear scientifically authoritative.

However, understanding their relevance requires some knowledge of physiology and measurement limitations.

Without appropriate explanation, users may interpret ordinary fluctuations as evidence of serious problems.

A lower score may produce anxiety even when the change reflects measurement variability or temporary circumstances.

Conversely, a reassuring score may encourage excessive confidence despite symptoms requiring attention.

The appropriate response is to improve health literacy rather than assume that more data always produces better decisions.

Devices should explain what their measurements mean, how reliable they are, and which conclusions cannot safely be drawn from them.

Users should be encouraged to interpret trends in context rather than react automatically to individual numbers.

This would help preserve the value of tracking while reducing the risk of misplaced confidence.

A further challenge concerns the relationship between automated recommendations and personal judgment.

Fitness trackers frequently suggest increasing activity, maintaining routines, or pursuing particular goals.

These recommendations can be useful when they reflect realistic needs.

However, the device may possess incomplete information about the user.

It may not know that someone slept poorly because of caregiving responsibilities, experienced unusual fatigue after illness, or developed pain during a previous workout.

It may not understand the emotional significance of a particular exercise goal or the practical constraints surrounding an individual's day.

When users treat the device's recommendation as an instruction that must be obeyed, they may surrender too much authority over their bodies.

This is a broader problem associated with automated decision support.

Technology can provide information that helps people make choices, but the presentation of algorithmic outputs can create an impression of objective superiority.

Users may assume that a computational recommendation is more reliable than their own understanding because it appears to be based upon precise measurements.

Yet precision in measurement does not guarantee completeness of judgment.

A device may accurately count an activity while remaining unable to determine whether that activity is appropriate at a particular moment.

The ability to measure behavior should not be confused with the authority to prescribe it.

Human wellbeing involves considerations that cannot always be captured through sensors.

Pain, fatigue, enjoyment, stress, recovery, personal obligations, and medical context may all influence what an individual needs.

Some of these factors can be recorded through self-reports or additional measurements, but no ordinary consumer device possesses complete knowledge of a person's circumstances.

Responsible fitness technology should acknowledge this limitation.

It should support reflection and informed choice rather than demanding automatic compliance.

This approach would also reduce the risk of overexertion.

Physical training involves both activity and recovery.

Exercise creates demands upon the body, while adaptation occurs through processes that require adequate rest and appropriate nutrition.

A routine that continually increases activity without allowing sufficient recovery may become counterproductive.

Yet many tracking interfaces emphasize uninterrupted achievement.

Daily streaks and escalating targets can make rest appear inconsistent with progress.

This framing misunderstands the relationship between effort and adaptation.

Recovery is not the absence of health-promoting behavior.

It is part of the process through which physical capacity is maintained and developed.

A person who rests appropriately after demanding activity may be acting responsibly, even if the device records fewer steps or a lower activity score.

Fitness technology should therefore recognize recovery as a legitimate component of healthy behavior.

Instead of treating reduced activity as automatic failure, systems could provide neutral feedback and allow users to adjust goals according to circumstances.

Such changes would help distinguish productive consistency from compulsive repetition.

The deeper challenge is to redefine success.

A successful fitness routine should not be measured solely by whether activity increases every day.

It should be evaluated according to whether the individual develops sustainable habits, maintains physical capacity, and experiences improvements appropriate to their goals.

In some circumstances, success may involve increasing movement.

In others, it may involve learning to rest without guilt.

The meaning of progress must remain connected to the person's actual needs.

This is particularly relevant for individuals beginning exercise after prolonged inactivity.

A new user may experience rapid improvements initially, followed by periods in which progress becomes slower.

If the tracker continually raises expectations, the user may interpret normal fluctuations as failure.

An adaptive system would recognize that sustainable improvement is rarely linear.

It would encourage manageable changes and allow periods of consolidation.

This could help users maintain motivation without developing unrealistic expectations of constant advancement.

The importance of sustainability also raises questions about commercial incentives.

Fitness technology companies operate within markets where continued engagement can contribute to business success.

Notifications, achievements, and personalized recommendations may encourage users to interact frequently with applications and devices.

These features can support healthy habits, but they can also create pressure to maintain continuous attention.

A person may feel compelled to check activity scores repeatedly or reorganize daily routines around maintaining achievements.

This creates a potential conflict between maximizing engagement and supporting wellbeing.

A product that keeps users constantly focused on its metrics may appear successful according to commercial measures, even when that attention becomes psychologically burdensome.

Developers therefore have responsibilities extending beyond user engagement.

They should consider whether design features encourage appropriate activity or create patterns of unnecessary dependence.

The ethical challenge is similar to that faced by other digital platforms.

Technology can capture attention through rewards and reminders, but the ability to maintain engagement does not establish that the resulting behavior benefits users.

A responsible design philosophy should distinguish between meaningful support and excessive behavioral pressure.

Fitness applications should ideally help people become healthier without requiring constant attention to the application itself.

This suggests that the best technology may sometimes be technology that encourages users to put the device aside.

An individual who has developed a satisfying walking routine may no longer need frequent notifications.

Someone who has learned to recognize appropriate activity and recovery patterns may benefit from less intensive monitoring.

The purpose of tracking should be to strengthen self-understanding, not create permanent dependence upon external approval.

This principle challenges a common assumption within digital consumer culture: that more interaction with a product necessarily indicates greater value.

For health technologies, success may instead involve enabling users to make confident choices independently.

An application that helps someone establish a sustainable habit and then becomes less central to daily life may have fulfilled its purpose exceptionally well.

The relationship between fitness tracking and individual responsibility also deserves critical attention.

Many health campaigns emphasize personal behavior because exercise, nutrition, and other habits influence wellbeing.

Encouraging individuals to move more can be valuable.

However, the ability to remain physically active depends upon circumstances beyond personal motivation.

People need time, safe environments, accessible facilities, and physical opportunities for movement.

A person working multiple jobs may have less time for recreational exercise than someone with a flexible schedule.

A caregiver may face responsibilities that make structured activity difficult.

A person with a disability may encounter inaccessible infrastructure or limited opportunities for appropriate exercise.

Residents of neighborhoods without safe sidewalks or public spaces may find outdoor movement challenging.

These conditions shape activity levels independently of individual willpower.

When fitness trackers present inactivity primarily as a failure of personal discipline, they risk ignoring these structural constraints.

A notification telling someone to move more does not create additional leisure time.

A progress ring cannot make an unsafe street suitable for walking.

An achievement badge cannot remove barriers created by inaccessible transport or unaffordable exercise facilities.

This demonstrates why health technology should not be treated as a substitute for public health policy.

Individual tools can support behavior, but they cannot independently resolve the social conditions that influence it.

Governments, employers, and communities have responsibilities to create environments that make movement possible.

Safe pedestrian infrastructure, accessible public spaces, appropriate workplace conditions, and inclusive recreational facilities can support physical activity across diverse populations.

Such investments may benefit people regardless of whether they use digital trackers.

The broader lesson is that health cannot be reduced to individual compliance with technological goals.

It is influenced by relationships between personal behavior and social opportunity.

This perspective also challenges the moral language sometimes attached to fitness.

Activity is frequently associated with discipline, responsibility, and self-control.

Inactivity may be interpreted as laziness or personal failure.

Such judgments can be especially harmful when they ignore disability, illness, economic hardship, or caregiving obligations.

A person who does not meet a device's target is not necessarily neglecting their health.

They may be navigating constraints that the device cannot observe.

The moral evaluation of individuals through fitness scores is therefore unjustified.

Health data should provide information about behavior, not determine personal worth.

This distinction is essential because technology can transform quantitative differences into social hierarchies.

People may compare activity levels and regard higher scores as evidence of superior discipline or character.

Yet those scores reflect a mixture of behavior, opportunity, physical ability, and measurement design.

They cannot support broad judgments about virtue.

A more humane approach would recognize that healthy behavior is influenced by unequal circumstances and that meaningful progress looks different across individuals.

This does not mean abandoning personal responsibility.

Individuals can often make choices that support their wellbeing within their circumstances.

However, responsibility should be understood as realistic agency rather than unlimited control.

People should be encouraged to pursue appropriate activity without being blamed for conditions they cannot easily change.

Fitness technology should reinforce this distinction through supportive and flexible design.

The need for inclusivity extends to how devices define bodies and goals.

Some users seek improved endurance. Others want greater strength, better mobility, reduced pain, or the ability to participate in everyday activities.

Still others may use trackers primarily to understand their routines rather than pursue major physical changes.

A system that assumes every user wants to lose weight or maximize daily activity fails to recognize this diversity.

Default settings should therefore avoid imposing narrow goals without user input.

A person should be able to choose objectives that reflect personal priorities and relevant health guidance.

The application should also make it easy to modify those objectives as circumstances change.

Such flexibility would support autonomy and reduce the risk of unsuitable recommendations.

Importantly, personalization should not require users to disclose more sensitive information than necessary.

Health data can be intimate, revealing patterns of movement, sleep, and daily routines.

Developers should therefore consider privacy and data protection alongside motivational design.

A device that provides useful feedback while collecting excessive personal information may introduce risks unrelated to exercise itself.

Users should understand what information is recorded, how it is used, and whether it is shared with other organizations.

Responsible design should support clear choices concerning data collection and access.

Although privacy is a distinct issue from numerical pressure, both reflect the broader principle that technology should serve users rather than treat them primarily as sources of data or engagement.

A person should retain meaningful control over the information their device collects and the influence its recommendations exert.

This principle is particularly important as wearable technologies incorporate increasingly sophisticated forms of automated analysis.

Future devices may provide more detailed assessments of activity, sleep, and recovery patterns.

Artificial intelligence may allow applications to identify complex trends and generate more personalized recommendations.

These developments could improve the usefulness of tracking.

However, greater analytical capability does not eliminate the need for appropriate boundaries.

A sophisticated algorithm can still operate upon incomplete information.

It may produce recommendations that appear authoritative without possessing sufficient context to determine whether they are appropriate.

As automated health guidance becomes more advanced, developers should become more transparent about its limitations.

Users should be able to distinguish between direct measurements, estimated indicators, general recommendations, and advice requiring professional interpretation.

This distinction would help prevent the transformation of consumer devices into unqualified substitutes for healthcare professionals.

The ethical value of technological progress depends not only upon what devices can calculate, but also upon how responsibly they communicate uncertainty.

The importance of uncertainty is often overlooked in fitness interfaces.

A daily score is typically presented as a definite number, even when it is derived from estimates and assumptions.

The display may appear precise while concealing the variability of the underlying measurement.

Users may then react strongly to small changes that are not clinically meaningful.

A more transparent system could explain that certain estimates vary in reliability and should be interpreted primarily as trends.

It could also avoid assigning excessive significance to isolated daily fluctuations.

This would support a more realistic understanding of personal health data.

The goal should be informed interpretation rather than blind confidence in numerical outputs.

Another potential objection is that strong goals and persistent reminders are necessary because many people struggle to maintain physical activity.

Without clear targets, some users may become less motivated.

This concern deserves consideration.

Behavioral prompts can help individuals remember intentions and overcome periods of inactivity.

Achievement systems may provide a sense of accomplishment, particularly when users are establishing new habits.

For people who respond positively to numerical challenges, these features can be genuinely useful.

However, the effectiveness of a particular motivational strategy for some users does not justify imposing it upon everyone.

A well-designed system can offer optional challenges while allowing others to choose less intensive forms of feedback.

Users should be able to reduce notifications, adjust targets, or suspend achievement streaks without being made to feel that they have failed.

Such flexibility would preserve the benefits of goal setting while reducing the risk of pressure.

The central question is not whether goals should exist.

It is whether individuals can control the role those goals play in their lives.

A target should support a person's intentions rather than become an independent demand.

Another objection is that fitness trackers cannot reasonably account for every individual circumstance.

Developers may argue that consumer devices require standardized defaults to remain affordable and usable.

This is partly true.

No device can perfectly understand the physical, psychological, and social circumstances of every user.

However, the impossibility of complete personalization does not justify ignoring predictable sources of harm.

Developers can implement safer defaults, provide clear explanations, and allow users to adjust goals.

They can avoid presenting rising activity levels as universally desirable.

They can recognize rest and recovery without treating them as failures.

They can provide more balanced recognition of different exercise types.

These improvements do not require perfect knowledge of every individual.

They require a design philosophy that treats human diversity as normal rather than exceptional.

The distinction is significant.

A system built around one imagined average user may require everyone else to adapt.

A system designed for diversity begins by recognizing that people have different abilities and priorities.

This approach can make technology more useful for a wider population.

It also reduces the tendency to interpret deviations from the default as evidence of personal inadequacy.

The philosophy of inclusive design therefore contributes directly to safer health technology.

The relationship between fitness tracking and medical care provides another important boundary.

Consumer devices may encourage activity and help individuals notice changes in behavior, but they do not replace individualized assessment when health concerns arise.

A person with persistent pain, unusual fatigue, or other concerning symptoms should not rely solely upon automated activity recommendations.

Similarly, a person recovering from injury or managing a significant medical condition may require guidance concerning appropriate exercise.

The tracker can provide supplementary information, but its outputs should be considered within the broader context of professional care and personal experience.

This distinction protects users from both excessive confidence and unnecessary alarm.

The broader objective is to create an appropriate relationship between data and judgment.

Measurements should inform decisions without determining them mechanically.

Users should remain able to question recommendations, recognize limitations, and adapt behavior when circumstances change.

Such autonomy is especially valuable because sustainable health habits require ongoing self-understanding.

A person who learns to recognize signs of fatigue, enjoyment, improvement, and discomfort may become better equipped to manage activity than someone who relies exclusively upon daily numerical commands.

Technology should support the development of this practical knowledge.

It should not discourage users from paying attention to their own experiences.

This leads to a deeper philosophical question concerning the meaning of health.

Modern measurement systems often assume that improvement can be represented through increasing quantities.

More steps, more exercise minutes, higher scores, and longer achievement streaks become symbols of progress.

Yet human wellbeing is not an unlimited accumulation problem.

Physical activity is valuable because it supports the capacity to live, work, participate, and enjoy life.

Beyond an appropriate level, additional activity may offer diminishing benefits or introduce unnecessary strain.

Rest can be beneficial.

Enjoyment can be important.

Maintaining function may matter more than maximizing performance.

A person who can move comfortably, participate in meaningful activities, and sustain an appropriate routine may be healthier in practical terms than someone who continually pursues higher numbers at the expense of recovery or peace of mind.

This challenges the assumption that the best health technology is the one that encourages the greatest measurable output.

The proper objective is not maximum activity.

It is appropriate activity.

Determining what is appropriate requires attention to individual goals, physical circumstances, and the balance among different aspects of wellbeing.

Numerical information can assist with this determination, but it cannot replace it.

The philosophical problem is closely related to the broader influence of quantification in modern society.

Schools, workplaces, financial systems, and digital platforms increasingly evaluate complex activities through standardized indicators.

Measurements can improve accountability and make patterns visible.

However, they can also encourage people to optimize what is counted while neglecting qualities that are difficult to measure.

In education, performance scores may receive more attention than curiosity or understanding.

In workplaces, productivity indicators may overshadow creativity or cooperation.

In fitness, daily activity metrics may displace enjoyment, recovery, and functional capacity.

The underlying danger is the same: a measurement designed to represent one aspect of reality becomes mistaken for reality itself.

This process can alter behavior because people respond to the standards by which they are evaluated.

When a device rewards steps, users may prioritize steps.

When an application celebrates uninterrupted streaks, users may avoid necessary rest.

When a dashboard emphasizes weight reduction, users may interpret other forms of progress as less important.

The problem lies not merely in inaccurate measurement but in the social influence of measurement systems.

Developers should therefore consider how metrics shape users' values and decisions.

A responsible fitness interface should avoid encouraging behaviors simply because they produce easily displayed numbers.

Instead, it should help users understand the relationship between different activities and their broader wellbeing.

This would require more nuanced feedback.

For example, a system could recognize consistency over time without implying that every day must involve identical activity.

It could allow recovery periods to coexist with progress.

It could encourage users to explore different types of movement and reflect upon which activities they find sustainable.

It could also provide opportunities to record personal achievements that are not reducible to step counts.

Someone might value being able to climb stairs more comfortably, return to a favorite activity, or complete rehabilitation exercises.

These accomplishments may be more meaningful than an arbitrary numerical target.

Allowing users to identify such goals would make tracking more closely aligned with real life.

The central design principle should be flexibility.

Health changes across the lifespan, and the value of different activities changes with it.

A young adult developing fitness, a parent managing limited time, an older person maintaining mobility, and someone recovering from illness may all benefit from movement.

However, their objectives and constraints differ.

A technology intended for broad use should accommodate those differences rather than impose one model of success.

This also suggests that users should be involved in the development and evaluation of fitness technology.

Designers may overlook harmful assumptions when they rely upon narrow groups of test participants.

Consulting people with different abilities, health histories, and experiences can reveal how features operate outside idealized conditions.

A reminder intended as encouragement may feel intrusive to someone managing chronic fatigue.

A default weight-loss objective may be inappropriate for a person recovering from disordered eating.

A step-focused interface may provide limited value to someone whose preferred activities involve swimming or wheelchair-based movement.

Such feedback can help developers recognize problems before they become widespread.

The purpose of inclusive evaluation is not to eliminate every possible negative experience.

It is to identify foreseeable risks and design systems that respond to them responsibly.

This should become a standard expectation for technologies that seek to influence health-related behavior.

The evaluation of fitness trackers should also extend beyond short-term changes in activity.

A device may encourage users to move more during the first several weeks after purchase.

However, sustainable benefits depend upon whether those habits continue.

If users become discouraged, anxious, or overly dependent upon the device, initial improvements may not translate into lasting wellbeing.

Longer-term research should therefore examine adherence, motivation, psychological effects, and the ability to maintain activity after intensive tracking ends.

Such evidence would help distinguish features that produce temporary compliance from those that support durable habits.

The difference is important because public health benefits depend upon sustained behavior.

A technology that increases activity briefly but creates negative associations with exercise may offer less long-term value than one that supports gradual, enjoyable change.

The same principle applies to commercial claims.

Manufacturers should avoid implying that their products can guarantee health simply by increasing measurable activity.

Users deserve accurate information about what devices can and cannot establish.

Promotional messages should not treat every numerical achievement as evidence of comprehensive wellbeing.

Greater transparency would help consumers make informed decisions and reduce unrealistic expectations.

It would also support a healthier relationship between technology and self-care.

Instead of promising that a device will transform users into ideal versions of themselves, companies could emphasize its role as a tool for understanding habits and supporting appropriate choices.

Such a shift may appear less dramatic from a marketing perspective, but it would more accurately reflect the technology's capabilities.

It would also reduce the moral pressure often attached to self-improvement.

People do not need to become continuously optimized versions of themselves to deserve health, respect, or dignity.

Exercise can improve wellbeing without becoming a permanent project of numerical perfection.

The ethical goal of fitness technology should be to support people's lives, not persuade them that their lives are inadequate whenever a target remains incomplete.

This understanding is especially important for those who have experienced shame or anxiety through tracking.

A person who repeatedly fails to meet a goal may begin to associate movement with disappointment.

Reducing pressure can help restore the enjoyment that makes physical activity sustainable.

The ability to walk without checking a device, exercise without recording every detail, or rest without losing a sense of accomplishment can be valuable.

These experiences remind users that the benefits of movement exist independently of digital recognition.

The body responds to appropriate activity whether or not a smartwatch records it accurately.

A person can improve strength without receiving a badge.

A short walk can provide relief from stress even if it does not complete a daily ring.

Rest can contribute to recovery even when it produces no visible achievement.

Recognizing these truths helps restore the proper relationship between technology and physical experience.

The device should record selected aspects of activity.

It should not determine whether the activity mattered.

This distinction may seem simple, but it challenges an increasingly influential assumption within digital health culture.

When numbers are always available, people may begin trusting them more than their own experiences.

They may feel successful when a device congratulates them and unsuccessful when it remains silent.

Over time, the external feedback can become a dominant measure of satisfaction.

A healthier relationship with tracking requires remembering that numerical information is incomplete.

It can reveal certain patterns, but it cannot capture every meaningful dimension of wellbeing.

The individual's experience remains relevant.

This does not require rejecting scientific evidence or relying exclusively upon intuition.

Human perception can also be inaccurate.

People may underestimate inactivity, overlook gradual changes, or misjudge their exertion.

The most productive approach combines measurement with contextual understanding.

Data can provide useful information, while personal judgment and appropriate professional guidance help determine what the information means.

Neither should be treated as universally sufficient on its own.

The broader ethical principle is that technology should expand human agency rather than replace it.

A device supports agency when it helps users understand options, recognize patterns, and make informed choices.

It weakens agency when it encourages unquestioning obedience to recommendations that may not reflect personal circumstances.

This distinction should guide the future development of consumer health technologies.

As wearable devices become more sophisticated, their capacity to influence behavior will likely increase.

Designers will have greater opportunities to personalize feedback and identify patterns.

These advances could make tracking more helpful.

However, they also increase the responsibility to prevent excessive pressure, misleading certainty, and harmful assumptions about bodies and health.

The success of future devices should therefore be measured according to whether they improve meaningful wellbeing rather than merely increasing recorded activity.

Ultimately, fitness tracking illustrates a broader tension between technological measurement and human complexity.

Wearable devices can make aspects of physical behavior visible, support motivation, and help individuals develop healthier routines.

These benefits are real and worth preserving.

However, the same technologies can encourage rigid numerical goals, displace enjoyment, reinforce narrow ideals of fitness, overlook individual differences, and assign personal blame for circumstances shaped by wider social conditions.

These harms are not inevitable consequences of measurement.

They arise partly from design choices that prioritize simplified targets and continuous achievement over contextual understanding.

A more responsible approach would treat health as multidimensional, recognize the importance of rest and recovery, and allow users to determine which forms of progress matter to them.

Developers should provide flexible goals, balanced recognition of different activities, and feedback that respects individual circumstances.

Public health institutions should address the environmental and economic conditions that influence physical activity rather than assuming that personal technology can overcome every barrier.

Users should approach tracking as a source of information rather than an unquestionable authority.

The deeper lesson is that measuring a behavior does not automatically reveal its value.

A step count can describe movement, but it cannot determine whether that movement was enjoyable, appropriate, or sufficient for an individual's needs.

A score can summarize selected measurements, but it cannot fully represent health.

A streak can demonstrate consistency, but it cannot establish that uninterrupted activity is always desirable.

Human wellbeing involves relationships among effort, recovery, physical capacity, psychological experience, and social opportunity.

No single number can capture all these dimensions.

The future of fitness technology should therefore move away from defining success through universal targets and toward supporting informed, sustainable choices.

The purpose of a smartwatch should not be to make users feel constantly accountable to an algorithm.

It should be to provide information that helps them care for themselves more effectively.

The most successful device may be one that encourages movement while preserving enjoyment, recognizes progress without demanding perfection, and allows rest without judgment.

When technology serves these purposes, measurement can become a valuable partner in health.

When it treats numbers as superior to lived experience, it risks transforming self-care into continuous self-surveillance.

The essential responsibility is to preserve the difference.

Health cannot be reduced to a completed ring, a daily score, or a sequence of digital rewards.

Its meaning lies in the ability to live with greater physical capacity, confidence, and wellbeing.

Fitness technology fulfills its promise only when it helps people pursue those outcomes without making the measurements themselves the ultimate goal.

The measure of a healthy life is not how consistently a device congratulates its wearer, but how effectively the person can move, recover, participate, and enjoy the activities that make life meaningful.

That is the standard fitness technology should be designed to serve.
texts.Claude:
22. Five hidden pitfalls of fitness tracking

1. Title of the Work

A Compass, Not a Leash: Why Fitness Trackers Should Serve Our Bodies Instead of Ruling Them

2. Creative Work

Economists have a principle known as Goodhart’s law, often summarized this way: when a measure becomes a target, it stops being a good measure. A factory judged only by how many nails it produces may churn out tiny, useless nails. A school judged only by test scores may teach students to pass tests instead of to think. The number was meant to reflect something valuable, but once people chase the number itself, the connection breaks.

Few modern devices illustrate this law more vividly than the fitness tracker on millions of wrists. Smartwatches, apps, and wearable sensors promise to help us become healthier by counting our steps, measuring our heart rates, and rewarding our progress with badges, streaks, and closing rings. For many people, they genuinely help, offering a gentle reminder to get up from a desk or a way to notice daily patterns. But these devices do more than observe. Through their targets, prompts, and default settings, they shape what people do and how they feel about it. When their design turns movement into a scoreboard, trackers can produce anxiety, shame, and even harmful behavior. These outcomes are not random accidents. They follow from choices made by the people who build the devices. Users should treat tracker data as information, not instruction, and designers must take responsibility for creating tools that serve real human needs.

The first problem is what trackers choose to count. Devices are best at measuring things that leave a clear signal, such as the rhythmic swing of an arm during walking. Activities that do not look like stepping, including cycling, swimming, strength training, stretching, yoga, and rehabilitation exercises, are often poorly captured or not captured at all. As a result, a person who spends an hour lifting weights or recovering from an injury may see a disappointing number at the end of the day, while someone who paces aimlessly around a room earns praise. Over time, this quietly teaches users that only countable movement matters. The activities many people most need, especially as they age or recover from illness, can seem worthless simply because a sensor cannot see them.

The second problem is that scorekeeping can drain movement of its pleasure. The most important factor in staying active over a lifetime is building habits that people actually enjoy. When the goal becomes hitting a daily number or keeping a streak alive, exercise can start to feel like an obligation imposed from outside. Missing a target can trigger guilt instead of curiosity, and repeated failure can lead people to abandon not only the device but the habit they were trying to build. A walk taken with a friend, a dance in the kitchen, or a bike ride to explore a new neighborhood has value whether or not it registers on a screen. When numbers become the only measure of success, the joy that keeps people moving can quietly disappear.

The third problem is the assumption that more is always better. Many trackers present higher numbers as the obvious goal, with persistent prompts and summaries that read like mild scolding when a day falls short. But healthy activity depends on context. A person recovering from illness, short on sleep, newly pregnant, injured, or just starting to exercise may need less today, not more. Devices rarely have enough information to judge this, yet they speak with the confidence of authority. Users who lack the training to interpret data such as heart rate variability or fitness scores may simply defer to whatever the screen suggests. That handing over of judgment leaves people vulnerable to pushing too hard or misunderstanding their own bodies.

The fourth problem is that trackers are often built for a person who does not exist. Their default settings tend to assume an able-bodied, non-pregnant adult who is already comfortable with exercise and has time to prioritize it daily. Some defaults reflect narrow ideas about bodies and health, nudging users toward weight loss even when that is not their goal, or relying on simplistic measures that misjudge muscular or naturally larger bodies. For people with a history of unhealthy relationships with food or exercise, such nudges can be genuinely dangerous, encouraging overexertion or restriction. A device that treats every user the same way will inevitably fail many of them.

The fifth problem is how trackers frame failure. Physical inactivity is shaped by many forces beyond individual willpower: long working hours, caring responsibilities, disability, unsafe streets, limited money, and lack of parks or affordable facilities. Yet trackers typically present the daily number as a personal achievement or a personal shortfall. When life gets in the way, users may feel they have simply not tried hard enough. This shifts responsibility away from the social conditions that make movement easier or harder, and onto individuals who may already be struggling.

Some will argue that these concerns are exaggerated. Trackers motivate countless people, they say, and anyone who feels pressured can switch off notifications or stop wearing the device. It is true that many users benefit, and that personal choice matters. But design is not neutral. Defaults, prompts, and reward systems are carefully engineered to influence behavior, and most people never change the settings they are given. When predictable harms arise from those defaults, the responsibility cannot rest solely with users.

The path forward involves both users and designers. Users can treat their devices like a compass instead of a leash: a source of useful information that they interpret in light of how they feel, what they need, and what they enjoy. Some days, the wisest choice is to rest, and no badge should make that feel like failure. Developers, meanwhile, should place less emphasis on fixed universal targets, make strength training and non-step activities visible and valued, build in rest and recovery as normal parts of health, and offer flexible goals suited to different bodies, abilities, and life circumstances. Safer defaults, especially around weight and calorie targets, should be standard.

Goodhart’s law warns that when we chase a number, we can lose sight of what it was meant to represent. Fitness trackers were created to help people live healthier lives, not to turn movement into an endless test. Used wisely and designed responsibly, they can still fulfil that promise. The measure of a good day of movement should never be a number on a wrist, but whether we cared for the body we live in.
