37. Return of the Red Scare: how the US right is weaponising the word ‘communism’

1. Title of the Work

Unpacking the Loaded Word: How Political Labels Shut Down Democratic Debate

2. Creative Work

Imagine buying a suitcase at a flea market because the seller says it contains a winter coat. When you get home and open it, you find the coat, but also a broken umbrella, a cracked mirror, and a bundle of someone else’s old letters. You agreed to take one thing, and you ended up carrying a whole collection of items you never wanted. Political language often works like that suitcase. A single word is offered to the public as a description of one idea, but packed inside it are many others, some frightening, some false, all carried along by the same label.

Few words carry heavier baggage than “communist.” In recent political debate in the United States, some leaders have used it with growing frequency against opponents who favor expanded public services or stronger regulation, warning of godless revolutionaries and enemies within. Yet the same pattern appears across the political spectrum and in many countries. Labels such as “communist,” “fascist,” “traitor,” or “extremist” are often used not to describe opponents accurately, but to attach to them the worst crimes of history. Linguists call such terms dysphemisms: deliberately negative labels chosen in place of more accurate or neutral ones. A healthy democracy depends on refusing to let these loaded words do our thinking for us. Citizens should unpack them, examine what is actually being proposed, and treat political opponents as fellow citizens with whom they disagree, not as monsters in disguise.

Consider what a word like “communist” actually bundles together. Historically, it can refer to at least four different things. There is an economic dimension, concerning how much of an economy should be publicly owned or regulated. There is a political dimension, concerning who rules and whether leaders can be removed peacefully. There is a religious dimension, since many twentieth-century communist regimes promoted official atheism and persecuted believers. And there is the question of means, since many of those regimes seized power through violent revolution and maintained it through repression. When a politician calls an opponent a communist simply because that opponent supports, say, publicly funded health care or a higher minimum wage, a limited economic resemblance is used to smuggle in all the other dimensions: dictatorship, persecution, and violence. The listener is invited to fear far more than the policy itself.

Context makes the distortion clearer. In much of Europe, Australia, and New Zealand, universal health coverage, public education, strong labor protections, and government pensions are ordinary features of mixed economies, supported by parties across the mainstream spectrum. The Nordic countries often admired by democratic socialists combine extensive public services with private enterprise, competitive elections, and protected civil liberties. Such systems are not one-party dictatorships. Meanwhile, governments of many political stripes intervene in markets in different ways, from subsidies and tariffs to public ownership stakes in companies. Disagreements about how much and what kind of intervention are legitimate and important. They are not evidence that one side secretly seeks revolution.

The same logic applies in reverse. Critics on the left sometimes describe conservative opponents as fascists or Nazis because those opponents support strict immigration controls, strong policing, or nationalist rhetoric. Here too, a partial resemblance is used to import an entire historical horror, including genocide, the abolition of elections, and total war. The internet even produced a well-known observation, often called Godwin’s law, noting how quickly online arguments reach comparisons with Hitler. Such comparisons can sometimes be illuminating when the specific parallels are real and carefully argued. Used casually, they end conversation instead of advancing it.

History shows how damaging this pattern can become. After the Russian Revolution, the United States experienced its first Red Scare, during which thousands of suspected radicals and immigrants were arrested, many without proper legal process. In the 1950s, Senator Joseph McCarthy used accusations of communist sympathy to destroy careers, often on flimsy evidence. Teachers, writers, scientists, and civil servants lost their livelihoods. Later generations widely judged that period as a betrayal of the country’s own principles. The lesson is not that genuine threats never exist. Espionage and political violence are real dangers that democracies must confront. The lesson is that sweeping labels, applied to large groups of people with differing views, make it easier to punish dissent and harder to identify actual threats.

Some will argue that strong language is a normal part of politics. Campaigns have always exaggerated, and voters are capable of recognizing hyperbole. Moreover, some political movements genuinely do contain extremists, and pointing them out is not unfair. These points are reasonable. Vigorous debate and pointed criticism are healthy, and specific extreme positions should be named and challenged. The problem arises when a label meant for the most radical fringe is stretched to cover an entire party or ideology, or when emotional words replace any discussion of actual proposals. At that point, rhetoric does not sharpen debate. It destroys it, because citizens are no longer arguing about policies but about whether their opponents are loyal members of the nation at all.

What can citizens do? When they hear a loaded label, they can ask which dimension is really being described. Is the disagreement about economic policy, democratic procedures, religious freedom, or the use of violence? They can evaluate the specific proposals instead of the slogan attached to them. They can hold politicians and commentators on their own side to the same standard they apply to opponents. And journalists can help by explaining what candidates actually propose, instead of repeating labels uncritically.

The suitcase at the flea market is easy to refuse once we open it and see what is inside. Political labels are harder, because they are designed to be accepted without inspection. Yet democracy depends on that inspection. When we unpack loaded words and examine their contents honestly, we can argue fiercely about the future while still recognizing that the people on the other side are fellow citizens, not enemies.

37. Return of the Red Scare: how the US right is weaponising the word ‘communism’

1. Title of the Work

**The Ghosts in the Lexicon: How Weaponized Words Paralyze Democracy**

2. Creative Work

In the theater of modern politics, language is rarely used merely to describe reality; it is frequently deployed to distort it. Among the most potent weapons in the rhetorical arsenal is the deliberate resurrection of historical trauma. By invoking the ideological monsters of the twentieth century, political actors can instantly short-circuit rational debate, replacing nuanced policy discussions with primal fear. The recurring weaponization of the term "communism" in contemporary democratic discourse perfectly illustrates this dark art. When the complex machinery of a mixed economy is falsely equated with totalitarianism, the electorate is subjected to a masterclass in linguistic manipulation, one that threatens to drag civil society back into the darkest paranoid eras of our past.

The effectiveness of this rhetorical tactic relies on a mechanism that can be described as "connotative compression." A single, heavily burdened word is used to squeeze a vast array of frightening concepts—such as state-mandated atheism, the abolition of private property, violent revolution, and single-party dictatorship—into one small, explosive package. When deployed against a political opponent, the word functions as a dysphemism, replacing an accurate description of a rival's platform with a deliberately disparaging and terrifying label.

In practice, this operates as a semantic bait-and-switch. A politician might advocate for entirely conventional features of a modern mixed economy, such as universal healthcare, public education, or robust labor unions—policies successfully implemented across various thriving, free-market democracies worldwide. However, by affixing the label of "communism" to these moderate proposals, opponents are able to smuggle in all the horrifying historical baggage of the twentieth century's most brutal regimes. The electorate is manipulated into believing that an increase in government regulation is merely the first inevitable step toward a gulag.

History provides a grim, exhausting blueprint for this specific brand of linguistic warfare. The United States has already endured the fever dreams of two major Red Scares: the Palmer Raids of the early 1920s, which saw thousands arrested without warrants, and the McCarthyism of the 1950s, where the mere allegation of radical association was sufficient to destroy careers and enforce strict ideological conformity. In these eras, the word "communist" ceased to be a descriptor of economic philosophy and became synonymous with subversion and treason. To revive this rhetoric today is to deliberately invoke the same mechanics of hysteria, where the accusation itself matters far more than the absence of evidence.

The ultimate casualty of this semantic warfare is not merely the truth, but the very foundation of democratic society. A healthy republic requires its citizens to view one another as legitimate participants in a shared project, even when their visions for the future clash. However, when routine policy differences are consistently framed as apocalyptic, extremist threats, political opponents are immediately stigmatized as dangerous, foreign outsiders. In an environment where every debate is painted as an existential battle between freedom and totalitarianism, rational compromise becomes an act of treason. By allowing the ghosts of history's worst regimes to haunt our modern lexicon, we risk paralyzing the democratic process entirely, sacrificing our shared reality to the altar of political fear.

An affluent household may absorb higher food prices while a poorer household struggles to maintain adequate nutrition.

These differences matter.

An effective response should recognize that equal exposure to a market shock does not imply equal capacity to endure it.

Equity therefore requires attention to the distribution of vulnerability.

This is a central principle of humanitarian economics.

The severity of a crisis cannot be measured solely through aggregate financial losses.

Its significance also depends upon who experiences those losses and what consequences follow.

A modest price increase may be manageable for one population and devastating for another.

A temporary interruption of farm income may be survivable for a large business with financial reserves but threatening to a smaller producer.

The same economic event can create different human outcomes.

Policy should therefore identify vulnerable groups and prioritize appropriate support.

However, vulnerability should not be treated as a permanent identity.

Farmers, workers, and consumers possess agency and practical knowledge.

They can adapt when provided with viable options.

The purpose of assistance should be to preserve and strengthen that capacity.

A farmer who gains access to alternative markets may recover income.

A community with reliable food assistance may avoid harmful coping strategies.

A transport network with multiple routes may continue operating during disruption.

These improvements support resilience.

Yet resilience should not become an expectation that civilians must simply endure the consequences of repeated military attacks.

The responsibility to prevent unlawful harm remains with parties to conflict.

Humanitarian assistance can reduce suffering, but it does not make deliberate attacks upon protected civilian systems acceptable.

This distinction is essential.

The ability of communities to adapt should not be used to minimize the seriousness of the conditions imposed upon them.

Nor should the existence of alternative export routes justify indifference toward the safety of established maritime corridors.

Adaptation is valuable, but prevention remains important.

The long-term objective should be an international environment in which food trade can proceed without military coercion.

This aspiration may appear difficult during active conflict, but it provides a necessary standard.

International institutions exist partly to establish rules limiting the consequences of war.

Their effectiveness may be imperfect, but the importance of those rules remains.

The protection of civilians and essential supplies should not be regarded as optional concessions granted by stronger states.

It belongs to the broader framework of legal and humanitarian responsibility.

This principle also supports the pursuit of negotiated measures even when comprehensive peace remains elusive.

A limited agreement protecting commercial shipping can reduce suffering.

A functioning transit corridor can preserve agricultural income.

International support can help prevent storage and financing crises.

These measures do not settle the underlying political conflict.

They address particular harms.

Their value should be recognized without exaggerating their significance.

The deeper challenge is to prevent temporary arrangements from becoming substitutes for lasting security.

A shipping agreement may need renewal.

Alternative routes may remain expensive.

Farmers may continue facing uncertainty.

The most durable solution requires reducing the military threats that make ordinary trade dangerous.

However, while that goal remains unresolved, practical efforts to protect civilian economic activity are essential.

The broader significance of Ukraine's disrupted grain exports lies in what the crisis reveals about the organization of global food systems.

Agricultural production can be extensive, yet access to markets may remain fragile.

Trade can connect regions efficiently, yet dependence upon concentrated routes can create vulnerability.

International markets can adapt to shocks, yet the adjustment may impose severe costs upon poorer households and smaller producers.

Governments can provide support, yet their fiscal capacity may be weakened by the same crisis.

These contradictions demonstrate that food security requires more than maximizing harvests.

It depends upon stable relationships among production, transport, finance, governance, and humanitarian protection.

The consequences of maritime conflict expose the importance of every link.

A field cannot feed distant consumers if its harvest cannot leave storage.

A ship cannot transport grain safely if crews face unacceptable danger.

An importer cannot guarantee affordable food if replacement supplies become too expensive.

A government cannot protect vulnerable households effectively without resources and institutional capacity.

The resulting challenges are interconnected.

Their solutions must be equally coordinated.

Ultimately, the disruption of agricultural exports during war demonstrates how modern conflict can transform food into an instrument of economic pressure. The consequences reach beyond the immediate combatants, affecting farmers, commercial workers, government finances, international markets, and households dependent upon imported food.

The most visible events may occur at sea, but their effects spread across a much wider economic landscape.

A threatened shipping corridor can reduce export capacity.

Reduced exports can create storage shortages.

Storage shortages can place downward pressure upon farm income.

Lower income can weaken future production and public revenue.

International buyers may search for replacement suppliers, increasing costs and uncertainty.

The resulting chain can affect food security far beyond the region where military operations occur.

This is why the protection of agricultural trade deserves serious international attention.

Food systems are not merely commercial arrangements.

They are networks through which essential human needs are met.

Their disruption can create suffering even when physical supplies remain abundant.

The challenge is therefore to preserve both production and access.

Immediate responses should seek to reduce maritime risks, support alternative transport where feasible, maintain agricultural financing, and protect vulnerable consumers.

Longer-term strategies should strengthen storage, diversify supply routes, improve regional cooperation, and develop institutions capable of responding rapidly to future disruptions.

However, these measures cannot replace the responsibility to protect civilians and comply with applicable international law.

Humanitarian adaptation should not normalize the use of economic deprivation as a method of coercion.

The deeper lesson concerns the limits of treating war as a struggle occurring only between armies.

Modern states are connected through networks that sustain everyday life.

Attacks upon ports, vessels, and logistical infrastructure can transmit harm through those networks.

The resulting suffering may occur far from the original military operation and long after its immediate effects have disappeared.

Understanding these connections is essential to responsible public judgment.

It also reveals why the preservation of international rules matters.

When commercial food supplies become vulnerable to unrestricted military pressure, the consequences are not confined to the countries at war.

The predictability of global trade weakens.

Importing countries face greater insecurity.

Civilian workers encounter danger.

Vulnerable households bear costs they did not create.

A more stable international order requires recognizing these shared risks.

It requires protecting lawful commerce, developing resilient supply chains, and pursuing diplomatic arrangements that reduce foreseeable civilian harm.

The fundamental principle is straightforward: the capacity to interrupt food supplies should not become an unquestioned entitlement of military power.

Agricultural production represents the labor of farmers and the possibility of nourishment for people across the world.

Its value extends beyond national revenue and strategic competition.

A grain shipment may be recorded in commercial statistics as a quantity of cargo, but behind it stand fields, workers, families, transport systems, and consumers.

When that shipment is prevented from reaching its destination, the loss is not purely financial.

It is part of a wider disruption to the relationships through which societies sustain themselves.

The future of food security will depend upon whether governments and international institutions can respond to this vulnerability with cooperation rather than fragmentation.

No country can eliminate every geopolitical risk.

No trade route can be made completely immune to disruption.

However, states can reduce exposure through infrastructure, preparedness, diversified connections, and credible legal protections.

They can also recognize that food security is a collective interest extending beyond national borders.

The most important achievement would not simply be restoring the movement of grain after one crisis.

It would be strengthening the systems that make future interruptions less damaging and making the deliberate endangerment of civilian food trade more difficult to sustain.

The distinction between agricultural abundance and genuine food security lies at the heart of this challenge.

A world capable of producing food is not necessarily a world capable of distributing it fairly and reliably.

Political conflict can interrupt access.

Economic inequality can make available supplies unaffordable.

Infrastructure failures can prevent harvests from reaching consumers.

Effective food security policy must confront all these dimensions.

The war affecting Ukraine's agricultural trade illustrates their consequences with particular clarity.

It shows that a maritime route is more than a line on a map.

It is a connection between rural livelihoods and international markets, between national economic stability and global access to essential goods.

Protecting such connections is therefore a matter of humanitarian responsibility as well as economic policy.

The ultimate lesson is that hunger can spread through systems long before it appears as an absence of food.

It may begin with a port that cannot operate, a vessel that cannot sail, a farmer who cannot sell, or a government that cannot afford replacement imports.

The effects accumulate until people far from the battlefield experience the consequences of decisions over which they have no control.

Preventing this transformation requires more than emergency relief after prices rise or supplies disappear.

It requires preserving the ordinary civilian systems that allow food to move from those who produce it to those who need it.

A durable approach to global food security must therefore recognize the inseparable relationship between peace, lawful trade, economic resilience, and human dignity.

War may begin through disputes over territory, security, or political authority, but its consequences can reach the dinner tables of people across continents.

The responsibility of the international community is to ensure that essential food networks are not treated as expendable instruments of conflict.

The harvests of one nation may sustain livelihoods and nourishment far beyond its borders.

When those harvests are trapped by war, the resulting crisis belongs not only to the people who cultivated them, but to an interconnected world whose security depends upon their safe passage.

The most meaningful defense of food security is therefore not simply the ability to grow enough grain.

It is the ability to protect the human relationships, infrastructure, and rules that allow that grain to reach the people for whom it was grown.

38. Russia is cutting off Ukraine’s grain exports again, threatening a critical harvest and global food security

1. Title of the Work

Bread Is Not a Weapon: Why the World Must Keep Grain Moving Through Wartime Seas

2. Creative Work

In a bakery in Cairo, the price of a flatbread may seem to have nothing to do with a burning ship off the coast of Odesa. Yet the connection is direct. Egypt is one of the world’s largest wheat importers, and much of its grain has traditionally come across the Black Sea. When cargo ships stop sailing from Ukrainian ports, when insurance rates soar and contracts collapse, the effects travel along shipping lanes and supply chains until they reach kitchens and market stalls thousands of kilometers away. A missile aimed at a vessel in one sea can raise the cost of a family’s dinner on another continent.

That is why attacks on grain shipping in the Black Sea should alarm the entire world, not only the countries at war. Ukraine is among the leading exporters of sunflower oil, barley, corn, and wheat, and nearly all its agricultural exports have depended on sea routes. Renewed strikes on merchant ships and port infrastructure have killed civilian sailors, driven commercial vessels away from Ukrainian ports, and threatened the country’s harvest. Retaliatory attacks on Russian ports have added to the disruption. Whatever the broader course of the war, one principle must be defended firmly: food and the civilian ships that carry it must not become weapons. The international community should press for an immediate halt to attacks on civilian maritime targets, help expand alternative routes in ways that are fair to neighboring countries, and enforce existing norms against using hunger as a tool of war.

Begin with the people closest to the crisis. Ukrainian farmers depend on exports to earn a living. When ships cannot leave port, harvested grain piles up with nowhere to go. Storage space runs short, crops risk spoiling, and contracts with foreign buyers are broken. Farmers lose income, rural communities suffer, and governments lose tax revenue needed to fund public services and support a population already living through war. Economists warn that such disruptions can cost an economy a meaningful share of its total output within a single year. A blockade of food exports is not merely a military tactic. It is a blow aimed at the livelihoods of ordinary people.

The consequences spread far beyond Ukraine. Global food markets are tightly connected, and when a major exporter is cut off, prices rise everywhere. Wealthy countries can usually absorb the shock, but poorer countries in the Middle East, Africa, and Asia, many of which rely heavily on imported grain and cooking oil, feel it acutely. Higher prices mean families eat less, skip meals, or switch to cheaper and less nutritious foods. Humanitarian agencies, which purchase grain to feed people in crisis zones, find their budgets stretched further. In an era already marked by climate shocks and other conflicts disrupting trade, an additional blow to food supplies can push vulnerable populations toward hunger.

There is also a moral dimension that history makes impossible to ignore. Food has been used as a weapon many times, often with devastating results for civilians who have no role in decisions about war. Recognizing this, the United Nations Security Council in 2018 unanimously adopted a resolution condemning the starvation of civilians as a method of warfare and the unlawful denial of humanitarian access. International humanitarian law likewise protects objects indispensable to civilian survival, including foodstuffs and agricultural production. Attacks on civilian merchant ships and the deliberate disruption of food exports sit uneasily with these principles. The norms already exist. What is lacking is the will to enforce them.

Experience shows that solutions are possible. In 2022, after the start of the full-scale invasion, the United Nations and Turkey brokered the Black Sea Grain Initiative, an agreement that allowed ships carrying Ukrainian grain to sail safely through a protected corridor. During its operation, it enabled millions of tonnes of food to reach world markets and helped ease global prices. The deal eventually collapsed, but its success proved that even warring parties can agree to keep food moving when international pressure and diplomacy are sustained. Reports of new offers to halt attacks on civilian targets in the Black Sea suggest that a similar arrangement may again be within reach.

Alternative routes over land and rivers offer another partial solution, but they come with real challenges. Moving grain by rail or road through neighboring countries is far more expensive than shipping by sea, and river transport can be hampered by low water levels. Neighboring farmers have also protested when large volumes of cheaper grain entered their markets, leading some governments to impose restrictions. These concerns are legitimate. Transit countries should not be asked to bear the costs alone. Regional and international partners, including the European Union, can help by funding infrastructure, compensating affected farmers, and ensuring that transit grain reaches its intended destinations instead of flooding local markets.

Some may argue that in wartime, economic pressure is a legitimate tool, and that disrupting an enemy’s exports is a normal part of conflict. Governments do use sanctions and trade restrictions, and military targets in ports may sometimes be lawful. But there is a fundamental difference between targeting military capabilities and attacking civilian vessels carrying food. Deliberately making food scarce harms civilians most, both in the targeted country and among distant populations who have nothing to do with the conflict. A world that accepts such tactics invites their repetition in future wars.

The path forward is clear. All parties should immediately stop attacking civilian merchant ships and grain infrastructure. International mediators should work urgently toward a renewed maritime arrangement that guarantees safe passage for food exports, ideally with independent monitoring. Partners should support alternative export routes while sharing the burden fairly with transit countries. And governments should treat violations of the norms protecting food and civilians with consequences, not just statements of concern.

The flatbread in Cairo and the grain in Odesa are links in the same chain. Breaking that chain does not bring victory on any battlefield. It brings hunger to people far from the fighting. Keeping grain moving through wartime seas is not a favor to one side. It is a responsibility shared by everyone who believes that bread should never be a weapon.

38. Russia is cutting off Ukraine’s grain exports again, threatening a critical harvest and global food security

1. Title of the Work

**The Weaponization of the Harvest: Starvation as Statecraft in the Black Sea**

2. Creative Work

The modern world operates on the fragile assumption that the global food supply chain, though complex, is fundamentally insulated from the worst impulses of war. Yet, as international attention frequently drifts toward highly publicized geopolitical standoffs in the Middle East, a far more insidious blockade has been quietly strangling the Black Sea. By systematically severing Ukraine’s maritime grain exports, Russia is not merely executing a regional military maneuver; it is weaponizing the very foundation of global sustenance. This deliberate chokehold on one of the world's most critical agricultural hubs is a stark reminder that in the theater of modern warfare, starvation and economic asphyxiation remain deeply entrenched instruments of statecraft.

To understand the gravity of this blockade, one must recognize Ukraine's outsized role in feeding the planet. As a dominant global supplier—producing half of the world's sunflower exports and acting as a top-five supplier of barley, corn, and wheat—Ukraine serves as an indispensable artery of global agriculture. When military forces repeatedly strike civilian cargo vessels, resulting in tragic civilian casualties and effectively paralyzing commercial shipping out of Odesa, they are intentionally inducing a global supply shock. The immediate victim is the Ukrainian farmer, who faces the catastrophic domino effect of a severed logistics chain: a massive impending harvest with rapidly depleting storage capacity, broken international contracts, and a devastating financial blow projected to erase up to 1.5% of the nation's entire GDP by year's end.

However, the underlying ambition of this blockade extends far beyond immediate economic sabotage; it is a dark historical echo. Observers note that the strategy actively seeks to artificially elevate Russia's own position in global agricultural markets by forcibly eliminating its primary competitor. More chillingly, the weaponization of Ukraine's food supply mirrors the grim playbook of the 1920s and 30s, when Soviet leadership orchestrated the Holodomor—a manufactured famine designed to break the political and cultural will of the Ukrainian people. Today, the methodology has shifted from domestic grain requisition to international naval blockades, but the core philosophy remains terrifyingly identical: using the harvest as a geopolitical weapon to subjugate a sovereign population.

In response to this maritime strangulation, the desperate pivot to alternative export routes has exposed the severe limitations of terrestrial logistics. While neighboring nations like Moldova and Romania have offered vital transit solutions, and complex negotiations continue with Poland, the reality is that moving millions of tonnes of grain via road or rail is prohibitively expensive and logistically fraught. These terrestrial lifelines are further compromised by environmental factors, such as low water levels on the Danube, and domestic political frictions, evidenced by the protests of European farmers threatened by the sudden influx of cheaper Ukrainian grain. Ultimately, the land cannot adequately absorb what the sea was meant to carry.

The escalating tit-for-tat strikes on Black Sea port infrastructure underscore a terrifying reality: the line between regional conflict and global catastrophe is razor-thin. If a sustainable truce regarding civilian maritime transit cannot be brokered, the consequences will cascade far beyond Eastern Europe, plunging vulnerable populations worldwide into deep food insecurity. The international community must recognize that holding the global food supply hostage is an intolerable escalation. The freedom of the harvest is not merely a matter of economic trade; it is a fundamental pillar of global survival that must be defended as fiercely as any sovereign border.

A society that protects formal choice but maintains severe economic dependence may offer incomplete freedom.

A society that pursues equality through rigid prescriptions concerning acceptable female behavior may undermine autonomy.

The challenge is to avoid both extremes.

A more comprehensive framework supports individuals' capacity to make decisions while seeking to reduce the inequalities shaping those decisions.

It recognizes that consent is necessary but not sufficient to evaluate every social practice.

It understands that economic success can coexist with dependence.

It treats cultural representation as important without assuming that every image has identical effects.

And it refuses to reduce women to symbols of political virtue or social failure.

The deeper philosophical lesson concerns the relationship between recognition and self-determination.

Human beings seek to participate in society, but participation often requires navigating existing norms.

When those norms are unequal, individuals may gain influence by conforming to expectations that limit them.

Their success can be both genuine and compromised.

This does not make their autonomy meaningless.

It reveals that personal power is shaped through relationships.

A woman may control substantial resources while still facing cultural restrictions concerning how she can use them.

She may attract public admiration while remaining valued primarily for one aspect of her identity.

She may reject conventional femininity while adopting another form that satisfies dominant expectations.

These possibilities demonstrate why empowerment must be examined through more than outward appearance.

The important question is not whether a woman appears powerful.

It is whether she possesses meaningful authority over her life and whether the institutions around her recognize that authority without demanding disproportionate sacrifice.

The distinction is essential because systems of inequality can sometimes reward individuals who reinforce them.

A successful participant may become evidence cited in defense of the system.

Her wealth or visibility may suggest that existing arrangements already provide sufficient opportunity.

Yet the experiences of those unable or unwilling to follow the same path remain relevant.

Collective equality cannot be established through isolated examples of success.

It requires examining the distribution of choices and burdens across society.

This includes the consequences for women who do not conform to profitable or culturally approved roles.

Do they possess access to income and professional recognition?

Can they establish boundaries without losing social standing?

Are caregiving responsibilities shared fairly?

Can they pursue leadership without being judged primarily through appearance or likability?

Are their bodies and decisions respected?

These questions provide a stronger foundation for evaluating social progress.

They also shift attention away from the personal morality of exceptional individuals toward the institutions shaping ordinary lives.

Ultimately, the controversies surrounding extreme sexual performance reveal a broader contradiction within contemporary gender politics. A woman may achieve financial independence and public visibility through activities that appear to challenge traditional sexual morality, while the commercial success of those activities may depend upon deeply familiar expectations concerning female availability and male desire.

This contradiction cannot be resolved by declaring the woman either liberated or degraded.

Both judgments can overlook essential dimensions of the situation.

The individual may possess genuine agency, entrepreneurial skill, and personal satisfaction.

The market may also reward representations that deserve criticism for their possible effects upon gender expectations.

These realities can coexist.

The appropriate response is to examine them separately and carefully.

Sexual autonomy is an important component of personal freedom, but it does not automatically transform every sexualized commercial activity into a political achievement.

Economic success can expand independence, but it does not establish that the surrounding system is equitable.

Public visibility can create influence, but it may also produce dependence upon audience approval.

The deeper question concerns whether women can pursue power without being required to satisfy restrictive ideals of femininity.

Traditional domestic roles and sexualized public personas may appear to represent opposing lifestyles.

Yet both can become limiting when society defines women's value primarily through service to men.

The objective of equality should therefore be to expand the range of legitimate identities and opportunities.

Women should be able to pursue caregiving, professional leadership, sexual expression, creative work, or different combinations without being confined to a prescribed role.

Their choices should be meaningful because alternatives are available.

Their dignity should not depend upon public approval.

And their autonomy should not be treated as evidence that every institution surrounding them is beyond criticism.

The broader lesson is that individual success and collective liberation are distinct achievements.

A woman can become wealthy within an unequal system.

She can gain influence through a role that reinforces expectations limiting others.

She can challenge one convention while preserving another.

Recognizing these contradictions does not require condemning her humanity.

It requires examining the social conditions that shape power.

A constructive response should therefore move beyond moral fascination with controversial individuals.

It should investigate economic incentives, cultural expectations, digital platforms, and the distribution of opportunity.

It should also recognize that audiences participate in creating the demand that makes certain performances profitable.

Responsibility cannot be assigned exclusively to the person receiving the most public attention.

The larger environment deserves scrutiny.

The same principle applies to political figures who gain influence through the defense of traditional gender roles.

Their strategies may reflect genuine beliefs, practical calculations, or a combination of motives.

The significance of their conduct depends upon its consequences for freedom and equality, not upon speculative psychological explanations.

A society committed to women's autonomy should allow vigorous criticism of ideas while refusing to reduce women to caricatures.

It should recognize personal agency without romanticizing every choice.

It should confront exploitation without assuming that every participant is powerless.

And it should understand that structural reform requires more than exceptional individual achievement.

The deepest measure of empowerment is the ability to pursue meaningful goals without being forced to exchange dignity, bodily autonomy, or social belonging for influence.

A woman should not have to become an idealized caregiver to receive respect.

She should not have to make herself sexually desirable to gain economic opportunity.

She should not have to disguise ambition to exercise authority.

Nor should she have to prove liberation through increasingly extreme public performances.

These expectations are different expressions of the same underlying limitation: the idea that female value must be established through conformity to roles defined by others.

Genuine equality requires challenging that assumption.

It requires social institutions that recognize women's interests as legitimate in their own right.

It requires economic conditions that expand alternatives.

It requires cultural norms supporting consent, reciprocity, and diverse forms of identity.

And it requires a conception of power that includes both personal independence and the ability to participate in society without compulsory self-denial.

Such a transformation cannot be achieved through the success or failure of a single public figure.

It depends upon changes in workplaces, families, markets, media, and political institutions.

The purpose is not to determine one correct model of womanhood.

It is to make the freedom to define one's own life more substantial.

A society becomes more equal when women can pursue wealth without being reduced to commodities, relationships without surrendering autonomy, and public influence without performing a prescribed identity.

The enduring lesson is therefore not that sexual openness guarantees liberation or that traditional femininity necessarily represents submission.

It is that freedom becomes incomplete when recognition is conditional upon satisfying narrow expectations.

The challenge is to create a world in which women possess both autonomy and belonging, both economic opportunity and social respect, both the right to express sexuality and the right to establish boundaries.

These are not privileges that should require extraordinary performances or exceptional personal success.

They are dimensions of human dignity.

The ultimate achievement of gender equality will not be a society in which every woman's choice is praised as empowering.

It will be a society in which women's choices can be evaluated with the same complexity granted to others, where disagreement does not become dehumanization, and where meaningful freedom no longer depends upon adopting a role designed to secure the approval of those already holding power.

In such a society, a woman could be ambitious without disguising ambition, sexual without being treated as universally available, nurturing without being confined to caregiving, and independent without being excluded from community.

Her value would not need to be demonstrated through wealth, desirability, or submission.

It would be recognized as inherent.

That is the distinction between a culture that rewards selected performances of female power and one that makes genuine autonomy available across the diversity of women's lives.

The first can produce spectacular individual success.

The second offers the possibility of lasting liberation.

39. Sex with 1,000 men in 12 hours: why Bonnie Blue is neither a feminist nor a monster

1. Title of the Work

The Price of the Mask: Why Women Should Not Have to Trade Freedom for Influence

2. Creative Work

In the 1840s, three sisters living in a remote English parsonage sent their novels to publishers under the names Currer, Ellis, and Acton Bell. The names were deliberately ambiguous. The Brontë sisters later explained that they had feared critics would judge their work differently if they were known to be women. Their disguise worked. Their books were read, debated, and admired. But the strategy carried a hidden cost: to gain a public voice, they first had to hide who they were. Their success depended on accepting a world in which a woman’s authority was suspect from the start.

More than a century and a half later, the masks have changed, but the bargain they represent has not disappeared. Women seeking power, money, or visibility still often find that the most available routes run through roles defined by what men want from them. One route rewards women for embodying idealized domestic devotion, positioning themselves as guardians of traditional family life and critics of women who demand more. Another rewards them for offering themselves as objects of sexual fantasy, turning availability into a business. These roles appear to be opposites, and their champions often attack each other. Yet both can lead to influence while quietly limiting the autonomy of the women who adopt them and of women in general. Instead of condemning individual women as villains or praising them as liberated pioneers, we should recognize the social double bind that shapes their choices, and work to open paths to power that do not require women to trade freedom for recognition.

Begin with what power requires. To be powerful is, in part, to be free to make one’s own choices. But power also depends on being embedded in society, recognized by others, and able to influence institutions and opinions. For many men, especially those from dominant groups, these two aspects reinforce each other. Expressing ambition and independence usually strengthens their standing. For many women, the two pull apart. A woman who acts with full autonomy, speaking bluntly, competing openly, or rejecting traditional expectations, may find herself punished, labeled unlikable, or pushed aside. Research on leadership has repeatedly found that women who display assertiveness are often judged more harshly than men who behave the same way. To gain acceptance, many women soften, disguise, or redirect their ambitions.

This dynamic helps explain why some women build careers by defending the very structures that limit women’s choices. Throughout modern history, certain women have found that the surest path to public influence lay not in pursuing their original interests but in championing traditional roles for women, often opposing reforms that would have expanded opportunities for others. Their influence was real, yet it came at the price of narrowing the possibilities of the women they claimed to represent. At the other extreme, some women gain wealth and fame by commercializing a fantasy of unlimited sexual availability. They may describe themselves as empowered and independent, and they may indeed have more money and control over their circumstances than many people. But when the product being sold is the idea that women exist to satisfy male desires, the power earned is tightly bound to serving those desires.

Psychoanalysts and feminist thinkers have long described how societies sort women into a small number of categories based on what they offer men: the pure, nurturing figure on one side and the sexual object on the other. Each category is used to judge and police the other. The devoted homemaker is held up to shame women seen as promiscuous, while the sexually liberated woman may mock homemakers as dull or repressed. The two images depend on each other, and both leave out the vast range of ways women actually live and think. When women’s routes to visibility are confined to these poles, even those who succeed spectacularly remain inside a framework they did not design.

Some will object that this analysis denies women agency. Adult women, they argue, have the right to make their own choices, whether that means embracing traditional family roles or working in the sex industry, and it is condescending to suggest they are merely responding to social pressure. This objection deserves respect. Women are not puppets, and many make deliberate, informed decisions about their lives. Recognizing the double bind does not mean dismissing those choices. It means asking why the menu of choices that bring influence and money is so narrow, and why so many of them involve serving male expectations. Agency always operates within conditions. Questioning those conditions is not an insult to the women who navigate them.

Others argue that the women who take these routes should simply be condemned for harming other women. It is fair to criticize specific actions and messages, particularly when they encourage contempt or entitlement toward women. But treating such figures as monsters or oddities obscures the larger pattern. If the same pressures shape the lives of countless women, then focusing on a few individuals lets the system escape scrutiny. The more useful question is not what is wrong with these women, but what kind of society keeps producing these bargains.

What would a better arrangement look like? Workplaces and institutions can examine how they evaluate ambition and leadership, ensuring that women are not penalized for traits rewarded in men. Media and cultural industries can tell stories about women whose influence comes from expertise, creativity, and leadership instead of from their appeal to male desire. Policymakers can protect hard-won rights that expand women’s choices in education, work, and family life, especially at a time when those gains face pressure in many countries. And individuals can resist the habit of sorting women into narrow categories, recognizing the full complexity of their lives.

The Brontë sisters eventually dropped their pen names and became celebrated under their own. Their genius did not change. What changed was the world’s willingness to accept that women could possess it. The goal today should be similar: a society in which women do not need a mask, whether domestic or sexual, to be heard, paid, or respected. When women no longer have to choose between freedom and influence, the bargains that now seem so puzzling will lose their power.

1. Title of the Work

**The Masquerade of Agency: Decoding the Economy of Infinite Availability**

2. Creative Work

When a woman publicly monetizes an act of extreme hyper-promiscuity—such as servicing an unfathomable thousand men in a single day—society instinctively scrambles to categorize her. The public discourse immediately splinters into two reductive extremes: she is either heralded as a radical, unapologetic pioneer of sex-positive feminism who has conquered the digital economy, or she is condemned as a sociopathic monster, a grotesque aberration of human morality. However, both of these labels are fundamentally flawed. To dismiss such a figure as an anomaly, or to blindly celebrate her as a liberated icon, is to ignore the dark, underlying machinery of her success. She is neither a feminist savior nor a mutant outlier; rather, she is a flawless, tragic reflection of a patriarchal marketplace that only rewards female ambition when it is disguised as female submission.

To understand the architecture of this spectacle, one must examine the inherent paradox of female power. True power requires the marriage of two elements: the autonomy to determine one's own life, and the social integration necessary to exert widespread influence. For men, these ingredients work in seamless harmony, compounding one another. But for women navigating a marginalized existence, these two forces pull violently in opposite directions. To achieve towering visibility, wealth, and influence within our current social framework, women are frequently forced to mortgage their autonomy, achieving status only through profound subservience to male values. A woman who builds an empire by selling the fantasy of her own infinite, boundless availability to men is not conquering male entitlement; she is merely functioning as its most efficient and highly compensated employee.

This mechanism of power-through-submission is not limited to the realm of explicit digital sexuality; it is the exact same engine that drives its superficial opposite. The modern cultural landscape has birthed a spectrum of female performance where the hyper-sexual creator and the hyper-domestic, conservative "tradwife" exist as two sides of the same counterfeit coin. They cleanly inhabit the opposite poles of the ancient Madonna-whore complex—one offering the fantasy of the insatiable object, the other the fantasy of the endlessly deferential, saintly mother. Though they position themselves as bitter rivals, both women generate their immense influence and capital by protecting, validating, and soothing male access to women. They have simply chosen different costumes in which to serve the same master.

The psychology driving this bargain is a defense mechanism born of necessity. Nearly a century ago, psychoanalysts noted a phenomenon known as "womanliness as a masquerade," observing that women who harbored ambitious desires for public power—traits heavily policed and coded as "masculine"—often masked their ambition behind an exaggerated, theatrical performance of femininity to avoid patriarchal retribution. This masquerade remains vibrantly alive today. The ruthless, entrepreneurial pursuit of wealth is rendered acceptable to society only because it is shrouded in the performance of extreme feminine service.

Ultimately, the phenomenon of extreme sexual stunts is a symptom of a deeply broken social contract. Our systems actively punish women who demand power, money, or visibility on their own terms, forcing them into a double bind where they must either abandon their ambitions or make themselves infinitely available to men to achieve them. As long as this paradigm persists, the culture will continue to produce women who trade genuine, collective liberation for a lucrative caricature of subservience. The true measure of an equitable society will not be found in finding new, shocking ways to monetize the male gaze, but in dismantling the system entirely—forging a world where a woman’s power is never contingent upon her willingness to serve.

The international community should seek to reduce incentives for continued conflict while supporting credible civilian participation.

The precise mechanisms may require negotiation and adaptation, but the fundamental standards should remain clear.

Military authority is not equivalent to democratic legitimacy.

Control over resources does not establish a right to exploit them without accountability.

Regional grievances deserve recognition without requiring the acceptance of abusive armed leadership.

Humanitarian assistance should reach people according to need rather than political affiliation.

And a durable national settlement must provide meaningful opportunities for Sudanese citizens to influence the institutions governing their lives.

These principles offer a framework for evaluating competing political projects.

A faction that promises unity should be judged by whether it supports inclusive and accountable institutions.

A faction that promises autonomy should be judged by whether it protects local rights and permits genuine participation.

International mediators should be judged by whether their involvement reduces violence and supports a credible political process.

Such evaluation is more useful than treating either military organization as an automatic source of national salvation.

The future of Sudan cannot be secured solely through the victory of one army over another.

Even a decisive military outcome would leave questions concerning representation, resource distribution, historical violence, and civilian rights.

The challenge is therefore political as well as military.

A lasting solution requires transforming the institutions and incentives that allowed armed rivalry to dominate public life.

This transformation will be difficult.

Communities possess legitimate grievances.

Armed leaders control resources.

Foreign actors have competing interests.

The humanitarian crisis has weakened civilian society.

Yet these difficulties make political reconstruction more necessary, not less.

The alternative is a prolonged process in which territorial division becomes institutionalized and ordinary citizens continue bearing the costs.

The most important question is therefore not which administration can claim the greatest territory or appoint the largest number of officials.

It is whether any political arrangement can establish accountable authority capable of serving the people across Sudan's diverse regions.

A country does not become united simply because a central government declares that it is one.

Nor does it become free simply because a regional armed coalition announces autonomy.

Unity and freedom require institutions through which people can participate, resolve disputes, and receive protection without dependence upon military patronage.

The deeper philosophical issue concerns the relationship between power and legitimacy.

Power can be obtained through force, financial resources, or control of territory.

Legitimacy requires a different foundation.

It depends upon defensible authority, public accountability, and respect for rights.

A government that relies exclusively upon coercion may compel compliance, but it cannot assume that compliance represents consent.

A political movement that invokes historical injustice may attract support, but its claims must still be evaluated through its treatment of civilians and its willingness to accept institutional limits.

This distinction is the foundation of sustainable peace.

A durable political order should reduce the need for coercion by creating institutions people have reasons to regard as legitimate.

Such institutions do not eliminate disagreement.

They provide ways to manage it without returning to war.

The purpose of reconstruction is therefore not to produce unanimous support for a single leadership group.

It is to establish a shared political framework in which competing communities and movements can pursue their interests peacefully.

Sudan's history makes this objective especially important.

The failure to accommodate regional grievances has contributed to repeated conflict.

The militarization of political competition has weakened civilian institutions.

The emergence of rival administrations threatens to make fragmentation more permanent.

Addressing these problems requires a transformation in how authority is organized and justified.

Regional representation should become meaningful rather than symbolic.

Resource distribution should be transparent and fair.

Security institutions should operate under accountable civilian authority.

Political participation should not depend upon possession of weapons.

And the rights of displaced people and marginalized communities should remain central.

These objectives provide a more substantive meaning of national unity.

A country can be politically unified while allowing substantial regional autonomy.

It can preserve common institutions while recognizing diverse identities.

It can maintain national sovereignty without concentrating every decision within a distant center of power.

The challenge is to design arrangements that make such coexistence credible.

That credibility cannot be established through constitutional language alone.

It requires implementation.

People must experience improvements in security, services, and political participation.

Institutions must demonstrate that they can resolve disputes fairly.

Leaders must accept limits upon their authority.

These practices create legitimacy gradually.

They cannot be manufactured immediately through announcements of new governments or military victories.

The importance of time is therefore profound.

Every additional period of war can deepen distrust and destroy capacity.

Yet genuine reconstruction also requires patience.

A rushed settlement that ignores underlying inequalities may be unstable.

A prolonged negotiation that allows civilian suffering to continue indefinitely is equally unacceptable.

The appropriate strategy must therefore combine immediate humanitarian protection with sustained institutional reform.

This balance is difficult, but it is necessary.

The future of a fragmented state depends upon whether political actors can move beyond the assumption that authority is a prize to be captured.

Governance should instead be understood as a public responsibility.

Its purpose is to protect rights, administer resources, and create conditions for collective life.

When armed factions treat territory primarily as a source of political and economic advantage, that responsibility becomes secondary.

The resulting institutions may possess the appearance of government without its deeper legitimacy.

The challenge for Sudan is to reverse this relationship.

Political authority must become accountable to society rather than society being subordinated to armed authority.

This transformation requires a shift from military bargaining toward inclusive governance.

It also requires rejecting the assumption that civilians must wait for commanders to determine the future.

Communities possess knowledge of their needs and histories.

Their participation can contribute to more legitimate solutions.

However, participation must be protected against intimidation and manipulation.

The ability to speak freely is essential.

A consultation conducted under coercive military conditions may not reveal genuine preferences.

The design of political processes must therefore consider security and independence.

Without them, the appearance of inclusion can conceal continued domination.

International actors should recognize this danger.

Supporting civilian participation requires more than inviting selected representatives to diplomatic meetings.

It involves creating conditions in which diverse Sudanese voices can contribute meaningfully.

This is particularly important for people whose political influence has been weakened by displacement or conflict.

Their absence should not be mistaken for indifference.

Their rights remain central to the future state.

The same principle applies to local communities living under rival administrations.

They should not be treated simply as populations belonging to whichever armed group controls their territory.

Their political identities and interests may be more complex.

A durable settlement must recognize their independence from military factions.

This is essential to avoiding permanent political division along wartime front lines.

Front lines reflect the distribution of military power at particular moments.

They do not necessarily represent the preferences or identities of the populations on either side.

Transforming them into permanent political boundaries can therefore create new injustices.

The challenge is to prevent temporary military geography from determining the long-term political future without legitimate public participation.

This is another reason the creation of parallel governments deserves serious concern.

It can transform provisional control into claims of enduring authority.

The longer such claims become institutionalized, the more difficult they may be to reconcile with national structures.

However, the existence of rival administrations can also reveal the depth of dissatisfaction with centralized governance.

A sustainable response must address that dissatisfaction rather than merely seek to eliminate its institutional expression through force.

This requires a political process capable of separating legitimate demands for autonomy from the interests of armed leaders.

The distinction is difficult but essential.

A community's desire for greater control over local affairs does not necessarily imply support for a particular paramilitary organization.

The creation of a rival government does not automatically mean that every resident seeks national partition.

Political preferences must be established through meaningful and safe participation.

The objective should be to allow those preferences to inform constitutional reconstruction.

This approach offers a possible foundation for unity that does not require uniformity.

It recognizes that a stable state can accommodate regional differences while maintaining common institutions.

However, such accommodation requires trust.

Communities must believe that agreements will be implemented.

National authorities must accept meaningful limits upon central power.

Regional institutions must protect minority rights.

Security forces must cease operating as independent political actors.

These conditions are demanding.

Yet the alternative is an increasingly fragmented political order sustained through coercion and competition for resources.

The humanitarian costs of that alternative are profound.

Prolonged war destroys more than buildings and livelihoods.

It weakens social relationships, educational opportunities, and institutional memory.

Children grow up amid insecurity.

Families become separated.

Professional expertise is lost through displacement.

Local economies become dependent upon unstable and coercive networks.

These consequences can shape the future long after armed conflict ends.

Preventing further deterioration should therefore be a central international priority.

However, humanitarian concern must lead to practical action.

Diplomatic statements should be connected to efforts that improve access, reduce weapons flows, and support credible negotiations.

The effectiveness of these efforts should be evaluated honestly.

No single external measure can guarantee peace.

Arms restrictions may face enforcement challenges.

Mediation may be obstructed by competing interests.

Humanitarian corridors may remain insecure.

Nevertheless, coordinated action can reduce particular forms of harm and create opportunities for political progress.

The important principle is that the absence of a comprehensive solution should not justify inaction.

Partial measures can save lives.

Their limitations should be acknowledged, but their value remains.

At the same time, temporary relief should not become a substitute for addressing structural causes.

Sudan's crisis is rooted partly in longstanding disputes concerning power, representation, and resources.

A settlement that ignores these questions may reproduce conflict.

The purpose of diplomacy should therefore extend beyond persuading armed leaders to stop fighting temporarily.

It should support the emergence of political institutions capable of managing disagreement peacefully.

This requires a conception of sovereignty grounded in public legitimacy.

The state should not be treated as the property of military commanders.

Its institutions should serve citizens across regions and communities.

Its resources should support public welfare.

Its security forces should protect the population.

Its political processes should permit meaningful participation.

These principles provide a foundation for a more durable national order.

They also clarify the limits of parallel military administrations.

A new government can be announced through an agreement among armed factions.

A legitimate political community cannot be created so easily.

It requires trust, accountability, and recognition of rights.

The existence of ministries and councils may signal organizational ambition, but it does not demonstrate that these foundations exist.

The same is true of established central institutions.

Historical continuity and international recognition are important, but they do not eliminate the need for reform.

A national government cannot restore legitimacy solely by defeating its rivals while preserving systems of exclusion.

The challenge requires deeper change.

The enduring lesson of Sudan's fragmentation is therefore that political unity must be built rather than merely asserted.

A country can survive a temporary division of authority if its institutions and communities retain pathways toward reconciliation.

It becomes more vulnerable when military control hardens into competing systems of permanent rule.

The difference depends upon whether armed actors, civilian organizations, and international institutions can create credible alternatives to continued conflict.

The future remains shaped by political choices.

Fragmentation may deepen, but it is not an unavoidable destiny.

Negotiations can establish new arrangements.

Institutions can be reformed.

Communities can rebuild relationships.

However, each possibility requires conditions that cannot be created through military coercion alone.

The ultimate challenge is to restore the principle that legitimate authority comes from responsibility to the governed.

Without that principle, the names and boundaries of administrations may change while the underlying struggle for power continues.

A nation divided among armed factions may possess several governments but little accountable governance.

It may have competing claims to peace while civilians remain exposed to violence.

It may contain abundant resources while its people face severe deprivation.

These contradictions reveal the distance between political power and public legitimacy.

Closing that distance is essential to Sudan's recovery.

The most meaningful outcome would not simply be the disappearance of one rival administration or the victory of one military institution.

It would be the establishment of a political order in which regional diversity is respected, historical grievances are addressed, civilian rights are protected, and disputes can be resolved without armed force.

Such an order would allow national unity to emerge through shared institutions rather than compulsory submission.

It would recognize that meaningful autonomy and common sovereignty need not be incompatible.

And it would place the interests of ordinary Sudanese people above the survival of military organizations.

That is the deeper challenge of peacebuilding in a fragmented state.

The central question is not who can claim to govern the largest territory, command the strongest army, or obtain the greatest number of diplomatic supporters.

It is who can establish institutions that deserve public trust.

Sudan's future depends upon transforming that question from a competition among armed leaders into a process of legitimate political reconstruction.

The longer the war continues, the greater the danger that rival structures will become entrenched and civilian society will lose further capacity to shape the outcome.

Yet the possibility of a different future remains grounded in the distinction between military control and political legitimacy.

Weapons can seize territory.

They cannot by themselves create a just constitutional order.

Political announcements can claim representation.

They cannot substitute for meaningful public consent.

Foreign recognition can confer diplomatic advantages.

It cannot replace the trust of the people being governed.

A lasting Sudanese peace must therefore be built upon the rights and participation of those who have endured the conflict rather than solely upon agreements among those commanding it.

The preservation of a nation requires more than keeping its borders unchanged.

It requires creating a political community in which people across those borders possess reasons to remain connected.

That connection cannot survive indefinitely through coercion, exclusion, or competition for resources.

It must be supported by security, justice, representation, and fair governance.

The deepest lesson is that a state can be divided long before its formal borders change, and it can begin to recover only when political authority becomes accountable to the society it claims to serve.

Sudan's struggle is therefore not merely a contest over which government will prevail.

It is a test of whether military power can give way to institutions capable of making shared national life possible again.

40. Sudan’s rebel force has declared a parallel government: what this means for the war

1. Title of the Work

Two Flags Over One Nation: Why Rival Governments Will Not Heal Sudan

2. Creative Work

In 2014, Libya found itself with two governments. One sat in Tripoli, the other in the eastern city of Tobruk, each claiming to be the country’s legitimate authority, each backed by armed forces and foreign patrons. What began as a temporary standoff hardened into years of division. Central bank funds, oil revenues, and even official postage stamps became objects of rivalry. Ordinary Libyans endured repeated rounds of fighting, collapsing services, and economic chaos, while outside powers poured in weapons and mercenaries. More than a decade later, the country has still not fully reunified. Rival governments did not resolve Libya’s conflict. They gave it institutions.

Sudan now risks following a similar path. After more than two years of devastating war between the national army and the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces, an alliance led by the paramilitary group has announced a parallel government based in Darfur, controlling large parts of the country’s west. Its leaders present it as a voice for Sudan’s long-marginalized regions and promise a more decentralized and representative state. Those grievances are real, and they deserve to be addressed. But the parallel government is better understood as a product of military stalemate than as a genuine path to justice. It is an attempt to entrench control, repair a badly damaged reputation, and seek outside recognition, and it threatens to lock Sudan into permanent division. The international community should respond not by legitimizing rival authorities, but by cutting off the flow of weapons, building a stronger peace process, delivering aid directly to civilians, and ensuring that the peripheries’ legitimate demands are met through an inclusive national settlement.

To understand why the parallel government has emerged, it helps to look at the battlefield. The paramilitary forces quickly seized much of western Sudan at the start of the war, including most of Darfur, a vast region rich in gold, farmland, and gum arabic, a valuable export used in foods and medicines. But they have struggled to push further east, where the army remains entrenched and enjoys overwhelming air power. Neither side appears close to outright victory. In that situation, forming a government allows the paramilitary group to consolidate its hold over territory it already controls, collect resources, build alliances with local groups, and create institutions that can deal with foreign actors. It turns military occupation into an administration.

The project also serves as an effort at political reinvention. The paramilitary force grew out of militias accused of atrocities in Darfur two decades ago, and during the current war it has faced extensive reports of ethnic killings, sexual violence, and abuses against civilians. By partnering with other armed movements and community leaders, including groups from historically excluded populations who have themselves suffered attacks, the coalition seeks to present itself as a champion of the marginalized. Yet a new name and a broader coalition cannot erase the record of violence against civilians. Legitimacy earned through representation must be built on accountability, not on rebranding.

There is no doubt that Sudan’s peripheral regions have endured deep injustice. For decades, political and economic power has been concentrated among elites from the country’s center and north, while communities in Darfur, Kordofan, and elsewhere suffered neglect, discrimination, and repeated wars. Demands for decentralization and fair control over local resources are reasonable and widely shared. The tragedy is that these legitimate aspirations are being harnessed by armed actors seeking to entrench their own power. If the parallel government becomes permanent, the outcome is unlikely to be justice for marginalized communities. It is more likely to be another militarized authority, dependent on foreign patrons and resource extraction, presiding over a fractured land.

Some might argue that recognizing de facto authorities is simply realistic. If a group controls territory and provides some degree of order, engaging with it may help deliver aid and stabilize regions abandoned by the central state. Humanitarian organizations already work with local authorities wherever they must to reach people in need, and that pragmatism is necessary to save lives. But practical engagement for humanitarian purposes is different from formal recognition. Rewarding the creation of a rival government would encourage further fragmentation and signal that territory seized by force can be converted into international legitimacy. Libya’s experience shows how hard it is to reverse such divisions once they take root.

The risks of continued stalemate are severe. Fighting is likely to intensify around remaining contested cities, both sides may seek more advanced weapons from abroad, and access to humanitarian aid may become another weapon, with each side trying to control routes and crossings to gain recognition or punish opponents. Meanwhile, Sudan’s civilians face mass displacement, hunger, and disease on a catastrophic scale.

What should be done? First, the existing arms embargo on Sudan should be expanded and strictly enforced, with consequences for any country or company supplying weapons to either side. Reducing the flow of arms is one of the few tools capable of shifting the warring parties’ calculations toward negotiation. Second, a new political process is needed, one less vulnerable to rivalries among the regional powers that currently dominate mediation and that often back opposing sides. Broader involvement from the African Union, the United Nations, and Sudanese civilian groups could make talks more credible. Third, humanitarian aid must reach civilians directly, including through air drops when necessary, so that neither side can use access to food and medicine as leverage. Finally, any settlement must address the root grievances of Sudan’s peripheries through genuine decentralization, fair resource sharing, and accountability for atrocities committed by all sides.

Libya’s two governments became symbols of a nation unable to end its war. Sudan still has a chance to avoid that fate. The answer to centuries of exclusion is not a second flag raised by armed men, but a shared state in which every region has a real voice. Achieving that will require patience, pressure, and principled diplomacy. The alternative, a country split between rival authorities and endless conflict, would betray the very communities in whose name the parallel government claims to act.
